knowledge_statements.statement_title: Levenberg–Marquardt regularized least-squares step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\), with residual \(r_k=R(x_k)\), Jacobian \(J_k=R'(x_k)\), and trust-region radius \(\Delta_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares using the Gauss–Newton trust-region model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Levenberg–Marquardt step is a solution of \[\min_p\ \tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|p\|_2\le\Delta_k.\] Equivalently, a feasible \(p_k\) is a solution exactly when there exists \(\lambda_k\ge0\) such that \[(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)p_k=-J_k^Tr_k,\qquad \lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|p_k\|_2)=0.\] Local Levenberg–Marquardt theory studies accepted iterates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) near a stationary solution. When the trust region eventually becomes inactive, \(\lambda_k=0\) and the method takes Gauss–Newton steps, inheriting the corresponding zero- or nonzero-residual local rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt minimizes the norm of the linearized residual inside a trust region. Its step is equivalently characterized by a nonnegative diagonal regularization parameter and a complementarity condition. Once the trust region is inactive near a solution, the step becomes the ordinary Gauss–Newton step.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The regularized step minimizes \(\|J_kp+r_k\|_2^2+\lambda_k\|p\|_2^2\) for fixed \(\lambda_k\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: If the Gauss–Newton step lies strictly inside the trust region, then \(\lambda_k=0\).
If \(J_k\) is rank deficient and \(\lambda_k>0\), the regularized coefficient matrix is positive definite.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive regularization makes the step uniquely defined even when \(J_k^TJ_k\) is singular.
boundary_notes: The step definition alone does not specify the acceptance ratio or radius-update rule.
Damped formulations that prescribe \(\lambda_k\) directly are nearby variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Least-Squares Local Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-rank, zero-residual convergence of the minimum-norm Gauss–Newton correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be twice continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), let \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(J(x)\) has constant rank \(r<n\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Then the local solution set \(S=\{x:F(x)=0\}\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(n-r\). For the minimum-norm Gauss–Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-J(x_k)^\dagger F(x_k)\), constants \(C,\delta>0\) exist such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le C\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2\) whenever \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under constant rank and zero residual, pseudoinverse Gauss–Newton reduces the distance to the local solution manifold quadratically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) is locally an \((n-r)\)-dimensional manifold and \(\operatorname{dist}(x_{k+1},S)\le C\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)^2\).
review_flags: A dedicated constant-rank Gauss–Newton source is required to confirm the stated manifold-distance estimate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-rank manifold conclusion is standard, but the quadratic pseudoinverse Gauss–Newton distance estimate requires a dedicated source. The estimate must also explicitly restrict x_k to a neighborhood of x_*, since small distance to S alone does not ensure that the iterate lies where the local constant-rank assumptions hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-deficient Gauss–Newton model and minimum-norm step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(J_k=R'(x_k)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}J_k=r_k<n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linearized least-squares geometry when the Jacobian lacks full column rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The rank-deficient Gauss–Newton step set is \[\mathcal P_k:=\arg\min_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\|J_kp+R(x_k)\|_2.\] It is generally non-singleton and equals \[\mathcal P_k=-J_k^\dagger R(x_k)+\ker J_k.\] The canonical minimum-norm step is \(p_k^{\min}=-J_k^\dagger R(x_k)\), characterized by \(p_k^{\min}\perp\ker J_k\). Rank-deficient local theory must therefore distinguish convergence to a particular solution from convergence to a solution set and must replace inversion of \(J_k^TJ_k\) by a pseudoinverse, rank-revealing factorization, or positive regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the residual Jacobian loses column rank, the linearized least-squares subproblem still has solutions but normally has infinitely many. Every solution is the minimum-norm pseudoinverse step plus an arbitrary null-space vector. Selecting the orthogonal minimum-norm member provides a canonical step, while local convergence may naturally be measured relative to a solution manifold.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The minimum-norm step satisfies \(J_k^T(J_kp_k^{\min}+R(x_k))=0\) and \(p_k^{\min}\in\operatorname{range}J_k^T\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J_k\) has full column rank, \(J_k^\dagger=(J_k^TJ_k)^{-1}J_k^T\).
Levenberg–Marquardt regularization replaces \(J_k^TJ_k\) by \(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The unregularized normal equations do not uniquely determine a step when \(J_k\) is column-rank deficient.
boundary_notes: Constant-rank and error-bound assumptions are needed for specific local convergence rates.
A numerical rank threshold is algorithm-dependent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-to-solution error bound at a singular root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(S:=\{x\in D:F(x)=0\}\), and let \(x_*\in S\) be singular in the sense that \(F'(x_*)\) is not invertible as a square linear map.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual error bounds near singular or nonisolated solutions; no particular iterative method is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local Hölder residual error bound of exponent \(\theta\in(0,1]\) holds at \(x_*\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|^\theta\qquad\text{for every }x\in B_\delta(x_*)\cap D.\] The case \(\theta=1\) is a local Lipschitz error bound, also called metric subregularity of the residual mapping at \((x_*,0)\). For an isolated solution, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\|x-x_*\|\) after shrinking the neighborhood. Singular-root error-bound theory uses this inequality as the replacement for the inverse-Jacobian estimate unavailable at a singular root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular-root error bound controls distance to the local solution set by a power of the residual norm. The exponent one gives the Lipschitz form associated with metric subregularity; smaller exponents allow weaker Hölder control. For an isolated root, distance to the solution set reduces locally to ordinary error relative to that root.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an isolated root, the bound is \(\|x-x_*\|\le\kappa\|F(x)\|^\theta\).
special_cases_latex: \(\theta=1\) gives a Lipschitz residual error bound.
For a nonisolated solution, distance must be measured to the set \(S\), not to one selected point.
immediate_consequences_latex: A residual stopping tolerance \(\|F(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) implies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\varepsilon^\theta\) inside the error-bound neighborhood.
boundary_notes: No supplied authoritative locator was found for this singular-root error-bound definition.
An error bound does not by itself specify a Newton-type iteration or its convergence rate.

Convergence Degradation at Multiple Roots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar Newton convergence at a root of known multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)^m h(x)\), where \(m\ge2\), \(h\) is continuously differentiable near \(a\), and \(h(a)\ne0\). For ordinary Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\), with \(e_k=x_k-a\), one has \(e_{k+1}=((m-1)/m)e_k+O(e_k^2)\). Hence the simple-root quadratic rate degrades to q-linear convergence with asymptotic factor \((m-1)/m\). The factor approaches one as \(m\) increases, quantifying worsening local convergence at increasingly multiple roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method becomes linearly convergent at a root of multiplicity m, with asymptotic factor (m−1)/m instead of a quadratic rate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of quadratic Newton convergence at a scalar multiple root
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:I\subseteq\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be sufficiently differentiable near \(x_*\), and suppose \(x_*\) is a root of multiplicity \(m\ge2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical scalar exact Newton iteration at an isolated multiple root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Multiplicity \(m\) means that locally \[f(x)=(x-x_*)^m g(x),\qquad g(x_*)\ne0.\] For the unmodified Newton iteration \(x_{k+1}=x_k-f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\), convergence degradation at the multiple root is the replacement of the simple-root quadratic rate by the asymptotic q-linear relation \[x_{k+1}-x_*=\frac{m-1}{m}(x_k-x_*)+O((x_k-x_*)^2).\] Equivalently, for a convergent sequence not terminating finitely, \[\frac{|x_{k+1}-x_*|}{|x_k-x_*|}\longrightarrow\frac{m-1}{m}.\] The singularity \(f'(x_*)=0\) is therefore the mechanism that invalidates the regular-root quadratic estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar root has multiplicity at least two when the function factors into the corresponding power of the root displacement times a nonzero local factor. Standard Newton iteration then loses the simple-root quadratic rate and becomes asymptotically linear, with contraction factor determined by the multiplicity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Multiplicity \(m\) is equivalently characterized by \(f(x_*)=f'(x_*)=\cdots=f^{(m-1)}(x_*)=0\) and \(f^{(m)}(x_*)\ne0\), when these derivatives exist.
special_cases_latex: For a double root, the asymptotic factor is \(1/2\).
For \(m=1\), the displayed degradation factor is zero and the simple-root quadratic regime is recovered under standard smoothness.
immediate_consequences_latex: As \(m\) increases, the factor \((m-1)/m\) approaches one and the unmodified iteration becomes progressively slower.
boundary_notes: The inspected source explicitly supports linear degradation at a multiple root but does not state the full multiplicity-factor formula at the cited passage.
Multivariate multiplicity and singular Jacobians require additional algebraic or geometric definitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multiplicity-Resolving Reformulation of a Singular Residual System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(x_*\in U\) satisfy \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(F'(x_*)\) is rank deficient. Let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and let \(Z\) be a finite-dimensional auxiliary space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, exact, local residual equations. The definition covers augmentation, deflation, lifting, or multiplicity-aware transformations through their common projection and regularity properties; it does not prescribe one construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local multiplicity-resolution method for \(F(x)=0\) at \(x_*\) is a construction of a residual map \(\Phi:V\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times Z\to\mathbb R^{n+\dim Z}\) and a point \(z_*\in Z\) such that \(\Phi(x_*,z_*)=0\), the projected transformed zero set agrees locally with the original zero set, \[\pi_x\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(0)\cap V_0\bigr)=S\cap U_0,\] for neighborhoods \(V_0\) of \((x_*,z_*)\) and \(U_0\) of \(x_*\), and the transformed root is regular, \[D\Phi(x_*,z_*):\mathbb R^n\times Z\to\mathbb R^{n+\dim Z}\quad\text{is nonsingular}.\] A multiplicity-resolution method family is a collection of such constructions indexed by admissible auxiliary data, with every transformed solution projecting to an original solution and every original solution sufficiently near \(x_*\) admitting at least one local lift.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplicity-resolution method replaces a singular residual equation by an augmented local equation whose zeros project exactly onto the nearby zeros of the original equation. The augmented residual vanishes at a lift of the target root and has a nonsingular derivative there. Thus ordinary regular-root solvers may be applied in the lifted variables without introducing spurious projected roots locally. Different choices of auxiliary variables or equations constitute different members of the family.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the local lift is unique, there is a map \(z=z(x)\) on \(S\cap U_0\) such that \(\Phi^{-1}(0)\cap V_0=\{(x,z(x)):x\in S\cap U_0\}\).
special_cases_latex: For an isolated scalar root, multiplicity correction may be represented without auxiliary variables by a transformed scalar residual having a nonzero derivative at the root.
Deflation methods are included when auxiliary null-vector or derivative constraints reduce the nullity until the final augmented Jacobian is nonsingular.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inverse function theorem applies to the square transformed residual at \((x_*,z_*)\).
Any sufficiently accurate transformed solution has a projection belonging to the original local solution set.
boundary_notes: The stated regularity condition excludes transformations that merely rescale the residual while leaving the augmented Jacobian singular.

For a positive-dimensional solution manifold, a square nonsingular augmentation generally selects or parametrizes a local lift; additional geometric conditions are needed to preserve the entire manifold.
No inspected source in the supplied corpus established this exact umbrella definition across all multiplicity-resolution constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Deflation Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative deflation for a scalar root whose multiplicity is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a scalar function \(f\), an initial point \(x_0\), and a known multiplicity \(m\ge2\) of a nearby root \(a\). Form the derivative-deflated function \(g=f^{(m-1)}\). Provided \(f\) is \(m+1\) times continuously differentiable and \(f^{(m)}(a)\ne0\), the root \(a\) is simple for \(g\). Iterate \(x_{k+1}=x_k-g(x_k)/g'(x_k)\) while \(|g(x_k)|>\varepsilon_g\) and \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|>\varepsilon_x\); otherwise output \(x_{k+1}\). For sufficiently close \(x_0\), this deflated Newton iteration converges quadratically to \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiate a scalar function m−1 times to turn a multiplicity-m root into a simple root, then apply Newton's method with standard stopping tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Newton iteration on \(g=f^{(m-1)}\) converges quadratically to the simple root \(a\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a differentiable scalar function \(f\), an initial point \(x_0\), and the known multiplicity \(m\ge2\) of a nearby root \(a\). At iteration \(k\), compute \(x_{k+1}=x_k-m f(x_k)/f'(x_k)\). Stop and output \(x_{k+1}\) when both \(|f(x_{k+1})|\le\varepsilon_f\) and \(|x_{k+1}-x_k|\le\varepsilon_x\). knowledge_statements.title: Correction Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar boundary for Newton correction using an incorrect multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-a)^m h(x)\), where \(m\ge2\), \(h\) is continuously differentiable near \(a\), and \(h(a)\ne0\). Apply the correction \(x_{k+1}=x_k-qf(x_k)/f'(x_k)\) with a fixed estimate \(q>0\), and define \(e_k=x_k-a\). Then \(e_{k+1}=(1-q/m)e_k+O(e_k^2)\). Quadratic convergence occurs when \(q=m\). If \(0<q<2m\) and \(q\ne m\), the iteration is locally q-linear with asymptotic factor \(|1-q/m|\). If \(q=2m\), the leading factor is \(-1\), so local contraction is not guaranteed; if \(q>2m\), the root is locally repelling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently smooth scalar multiple-root problem, using the wrong multiplicity leaves linear convergence inside the contraction interval, loses guaranteed contraction at twice the true multiplicity, and makes the root repelling beyond that boundary.
assumptions_latex: The correction uses a fixed estimate \(q>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local factor is \(1-q/m\); contraction requires \(0<q<2m\), and quadratic cancellation occurs when \(q=m\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order expansion of multiplicity-scaled Newton iteration
A source for the sharp incorrect-multiplicity boundary should be added.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Theory near Nonisolated Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-rank manifold structure and residual error bound near a nonisolated zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(x_*\), with \(F(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(J(x)\) has constant rank \(r<n\) on a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Then, after restricting the neighborhood if necessary, the zero set \(S=\{x:F(x)=0\}\) is a continuously differentiable embedded manifold of dimension \(n-r\). Moreover, constants \(\kappa,\delta>0\) exist such that \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|\) whenever \(\|x-x_*\|\le\delta\). Thus residual decay controls distance to the solution set, but does not select a unique solution point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-rank nonisolated zero lies on a smooth solution manifold, and the residual locally bounds distance to that manifold, not to a unique point.
review_flags: The constant-rank manifold claim is standard, but the residual error bound needs an exact authoritative locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Solution-Set Framework at a Nonisolated Zero
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed, let \(F:X\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuous, and let \(S=\{x\in X:F(x)=0\}\). Fix \(\bar x\in S\) that is nonisolated, meaning every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a point of \(S\setminus\{\bar x\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local theory in which error and convergence are measured relative to the full solution set rather than to a distinguished isolated solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local solution-set theory near the nonisolated solution \(\bar x\) uses the set distance \[d_S(x)=\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{z\in S}\|x-z\|\] as its primal error and a residual \(r(x)\ge 0\) satisfying \(r(x)=0\iff x\in S\) locally. It has a Lipschitz residual-to-solution bound at \(\bar x\) when there exist \(\delta>0\) and \(\kappa>0\) such that \[\|x-\bar x\|\le\delta,\ x\in X\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa r(x).\] For the equation residual, \(r(x)=\|F(x)\|\). More generally, for a set-valued residual \(\Psi\) with \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\), take \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\); the displayed condition is metric subregularity at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nonisolated solution, distance to one selected solution is not the intrinsic error because iterates may approach another nearby member of the solution set. The local theory therefore measures error by distance to the whole zero set. A residual is locally adequate when small residual forces small distance to that set through a uniform Lipschitz inequality. For a set-valued equation this property is metric subregularity at the reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le\kappa\|F(x)\|\) for every \(x\in X\cap\mathbb B(\bar x,\delta)\) in the residual-bounded regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\), the condition is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\Psi^{-1}(0))\le\kappa\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\) locally at \(\bar x\).
If a sequence satisfies \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\to0\), its convergence is to the solution set even when \(x_k\) does not converge to the selected reference point \(\bar x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\bar x\) is isolated in \(S\), then locally \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\|x-\bar x\|\), recovering the usual pointwise error measure.
If \(S\) is a smooth solution manifold, \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\) measures the normal error and ignores harmless tangential displacement along the manifold.
immediate_consequences_latex: A stopping test based on \(r(x)\) certifies proximity to some local solution, not necessarily to \(\bar x\).
Any estimate \(r(x_{k+1})\le q r(x_k)\) with \(q<1\), together with the error bound, yields a corresponding residual-controlled estimate for distance to \(S\).
boundary_notes: Metric subregularity does not imply local uniqueness of the solution.
Pointwise convergence of iterates requires additional control of tangential motion along a nonisolated solution set.
The definition does not assert differentiability or manifold structure of \(S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-to-Solution Error Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Hölder error bound for a possibly singular or nonisolated zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), and let \(\bar x\in S\). A local residual-to-solution error bound of order \(\theta\in(0,1]\) holds at \(\bar x\) if there exist \(\kappa>0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\leq \kappa\lVert F(x)\rVert^{\theta}
\quad\text{whenever}\quad \lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\delta.
\]
The case \(\theta=1\) is a local Lipschitz error bound; \(\theta<1\) permits the weaker behavior typical near singular roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a solution, distance to the zero set is bounded by a constant times a power of the residual norm.
assumptions_latex: Distance and residual are measured using fixed finite-dimensional norms.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-to-Solution Error Bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(S\subseteq T\) be a nonempty target solution set, and define \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=\inf_{z\in S}\|x-z\|\). Let \(r_S:T\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(r_S(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic error bounds. Both Lipschitz and Hölder residual bounds are distinguished, and locality may be defined by residual size or by proximity to a reference solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The residual \(r_S\) defines a residual-to-solution Lipschitz error bound for \(S\) relative to \(T\) if there is \(c>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in T.\] It is a local error bound in the residual sense if the same inequality holds on \(T_\varepsilon=\{x\in T:r_S(x)\le\varepsilon\}\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\). At a reference point \(\bar x\in S\), it is local in the neighborhood sense if there are \(c,\delta>0\) such that the inequality holds for every \(x\in T\cap\mathbb B(\bar x,\delta)\). A Hölder error bound of exponent \(\theta\in(0,1]\) replaces the right-hand side by \(c\,r_S(x)^\theta\). For a residual equation \(F(x)=0\), the canonical choice is \(S=F^{-1}(0)\) and \(r_S(x)=\|F(x)\|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual-to-solution error bound is an inequality that turns a computable residual into an upper bound on the generally unknown distance to the solution set. A global bound holds throughout the test set. A local bound holds either where the residual is sufficiently small or in a neighborhood of a reference solution. The linear power gives a Lipschitz error bound; a fractional power gives a Hölder error bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)\) on the specified test region, or \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\,r_S(x)^\theta\) in the Hölder variant.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(S=F^{-1}(0)\), the Lipschitz form is \(\operatorname{dist}(x,F^{-1}(0))\le c\|F(x)\|\).
For a set-valued mapping \(\Psi\), take \(r_S(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\Psi(x))\) and \(S=\Psi^{-1}(0)\).
special_cases_latex: When \(S=\{x_*\}\) locally, the bound becomes \(\|x-x_*\|\le c\,r_S(x)\).
For an affine system \(Ax=b\), a suitable constant gives \(\operatorname{dist}(x,\{z:Az=b\})\le c\|Ax-b\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(r_S(x_k)\to0\) and the iterates remain in the bound's region, then \(\operatorname{dist}(x_k,S)\to0\).
A residual termination threshold \(r_S(x)\le\tau\) certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(x,S)\le c\tau\) in the Lipschitz case.
boundary_notes: The reverse inequality is not part of the definition.
An error bound does not by itself guarantee existence or uniqueness of a nearest solution.
The numerical size of the modulus \(c\) matters for certification even when existence of some modulus is known.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Structured Nonlinear Least-Squares Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be twice continuously differentiable and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\). Let \(J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be the residual Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth, finite-dimensional, unconstrained nonlinear least squares. Constrained least-squares variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A nonlinear least-squares method is residual-structured if, at each iterate \(x_k\), it constructs a step from \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and optionally approximations to the residual-curvature term \[S(x_k)=\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x_k)
abla^2r_i(x_k),\] exploiting \[
abla f(x_k)=J_k^Tr_k,\qquad 
abla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+S(x_k).\] Its local model has the form \[m_k(p)=	frac12\|r_k\|^2+p^TJ_k^Tr_k+	frac12p^T igl(J_k^TJ_k+C_k igr)p,\] where \(C_k=0\) gives Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt structure, \(C_k=S(x_k)\) gives full Newton structure, and an updated \(C_k\approx S(x_k)\) gives a structured quasi-Newton method. A method family is determined by the rule for \(C_k\), the step constraint or regularization, the inner linear least-squares solve, and the acceptance mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear least-squares methods minimize one half of the squared norm of a smooth residual vector. Their defining feature is use of the exact gradient and the decomposition of the Hessian into the positive-semidefinite Gauss–Newton term plus a residual-weighted second-derivative term. The principal families omit, retain, or approximate the latter term and combine the resulting model with line-search, trust-region, damping, or regularization controls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method model uses \(J_k^Tr_k\) as its linear term and \(J_k^TJ_k+C_k\) as its residual-structured curvature matrix.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Gauss–Newton model is exactly \(m_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\).
The stationarity residual for the least-squares objective is \(\|J(x)^Tr(x)\|\).
special_cases_latex: If every \(r_i\) is affine, then \(S(x)=0\) and the Gauss–Newton curvature equals the exact Hessian.
If \(r(x_*)=0\), then \(S(x_*)=0\) even when the residual components are nonlinear.
immediate_consequences_latex: The matrix-vector product \(J_k^TJ_kv\) can be evaluated as \(J_k^T(J_kv)\) without explicitly forming the normal matrix.
Residual structure permits linear least-squares solvers to compute Gauss–Newton-type steps.
boundary_notes: This definition does not include nonsmooth robust losses that are not expressed as ordinary squared residuals.
Bounds or nonlinear constraints require a constrained optimization framework.
Derivative-free residual methods require separate models because \(J_k\) is unavailable.

notation.meaning: Residual-weighted second-derivative contribution to the Hessian.
Exact or approximate correction to Gauss–Newton curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hybrid and Structured Quasi-Newton Constructions for Large-Residual Least Squares
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the omitted-curvature failure boundary, a residual-regime switching construction, and the Dennis–Gay–Welsch structured secant update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2$, $\nabla^2f(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x)\nabla^2r_j(x)$. When the residual-weighted second-order term is significant, the Gauss–Newton model omits significant curvature and Gauss–Newton or Levenberg–Marquardt has only linear asymptotic convergence in the described large-residual regime. A switching construction accepts a sufficiently successful Gauss–Newton step and resets $B_k$ to $J_k^TJ_k$; otherwise it computes a step from $B_k$ with a line search, after which a BFGS-like update is applied in either case. The construction eventually takes Gauss–Newton steps in the zero-residual case and eventually reduces to BFGS in the nonzero-residual case. A structured alternative sets $B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k$ and imposes $S_{k+1}s=y^\sharp$, where $s=x_{k+1}-x_k$ and $y^\sharp=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_{k+1}$. With $y=J_{k+1}^Tr_{k+1}-J_k^Tr_k$, the displayed symmetric update is $S_{k+1}=S_k+\frac{(y^\sharp-S_ks)y^T+y(y^\sharp-S_ks)^T}{y^Ts}-\frac{(y^\sharp-S_ks)^Ts}{(y^Ts)^2}yy^T$. To prevent the correction from interfering near a zero-residual solution, replace $S_k$ on the right-hand side by $\tau_kS_k$, where $\tau_k=\min\!\left(1,\frac{|s^Ty^\sharp|}{|s^TS_ks|}\right)$, and omit the correction when the Gauss–Newton model produces a sufficiently good step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Large residuals can make the Hessian term omitted by Gauss–Newton significant, limiting the residual-structured methods to linear asymptotic convergence. One hybrid switches between successful Gauss–Newton steps and BFGS-like steps. A structured alternative approximates only the omitted Hessian term with a symmetric secant update, scales that correction near zero-residual solutions, and suppresses it when the Gauss–Newton model is already adequate.
assumptions_latex: y^Ts\neq0\text{ for the displayed structured update}
s^TS_ks\neq0\text{ when the displayed scaling ratio is evaluated}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{k+1}s=y^\sharp,\qquad B_k=J_k^TJ_k+S_k;\quad \text{the switching construction eventually uses Gauss--Newton in the zero-residual case and BFGS in the nonzero-residual case}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth nonlinear least-squares objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a smooth nonlinear least-squares objective. The condition m at least n is a standing assumption of the source chapter, not an intrinsic requirement of nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $r_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be smooth for $j=1,\ldots,m$. A nonlinear least-squares objective has the form
\[
f(x)=\frac12\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x)^2,
\]
where each $r_j$ is called a residual. In the setting of this source chapter, $m\ge n$ is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth nonlinear least-squares objective is one half the sum of the squares of smooth scalar residual functions. Each scalar function is called a residual. The source chapter additionally assumes that the number of residuals is at least the number of variables.
assumptions_latex: r_j:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ is smooth for }j=1,\ldots,m
m\ge n\text{ is the source chapter's standing assumption}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton Method Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\), and write \(r_k=r(x_k)\) and \(J_k=J(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth, finite-dimensional, unconstrained nonlinear least squares. The family permits exact or approximate solution of the linearized least-squares subproblem and separate global step control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton method generates a trial direction \(p_k\) by minimizing, exactly or approximately, the linearized residual model \[\ell_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2.\] An exact minimizer satisfies the normal equations \[J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k.\] The next iterate is formed as \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), where \(s_k\) is either \(p_k\), a line-search scaling \(\alpha_kp_k\), or a controlled approximation obtained from a trust region or regularized version of \(\ell_k\). The family is characterized by replacing the exact Hessian \(J_k^TJ_k+\sum_i r_i(x_k)\nabla^2r_i(x_k)\) with the Gauss–Newton matrix \(J_k^TJ_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton family minimizes a nonlinear sum of squares by repeatedly solving the linear least-squares problem obtained from the first-order model of the residual vector. Its curvature approximation is the Jacobian Gram matrix. Exact normal-equation, QR, SVD, iterative, line-search, trust-region, and damped implementations belong to the family when they retain this linearized-residual model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p}\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\), equivalently \(J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)=0\), for an exact Gauss–Newton direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact direction solves \(J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k\).
The quadratic model is \(f(x_k)+p^T\nabla f(x_k)+\tfrac12p^TJ_k^TJ_kp\).
special_cases_latex: If \(J_k\) has full column rank, the exact Gauss–Newton direction is unique.
If \(J_k\) is rank deficient, the linearized least-squares problem remains solvable but may have multiple minimizers; the minimum-norm minimizer is \(-J_k^\dagger r_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For an exact direction, \(p_k^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|J_kp_k\|^2\le0\).
The step can be computed without explicitly forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
boundary_notes: The family omits the residual-curvature term and therefore differs from full Newton least squares.
A raw full step need not be globally convergent; acceptance control is a separate component.
Normal equations can square the condition number, so the defining equations do not prescribe their direct numerical solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm; V_M and f_M are the regularized Gauss–Newton map and model value defined in the standing setting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{Fix }L_0\in(0,L]\text{ and }x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n.\ \text{For every }k\ge0,\text{ choose }M_k\in[L_0,2L]\text{ such that }f(V_{M_k}(x_k))\le f_{M_k}(x_k),\text{ and set }x_{k+1}=V_{M_k}(x_k).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix L0 strictly positive and no larger than L, and choose any initial point in R^n. At each iteration, select M_k between L0 and 2L satisfying the stated model-acceptance inequality, then set the next iterate equal to the corresponding regularized Gauss–Newton point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Model Decrease
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the improvement available from a model within a closed ball centered at the current point; the definition is model-generic rather than Gauss–Newton-specific.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{E}_1\to\mathbb{R} and \psi:\mathbb{E}_1\times\mathbb{E}_1\to\mathbb{R}. For x\in\mathbb{E}_1 and r>0, define
\Delta_r(x)=f(x)-\min\left\{\psi(x;y):y\in\mathbb{E}_1,\ \lVert y-x\rVert\leq r\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local model decrease at a point and positive radius is the current objective value minus the minimum model value attainable within the corresponding closed ball.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence of equation feasibility and zero merit optimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes solvability of a nonlinear system through an attained minimum of its sharp-merit reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2 be real vector spaces, let F:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2, and let \phi:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb R_+ be a sharp merit function, so that \phi(z)=0 if and only if z=0. Define f(x):=\phi(F(x)) and suppose f^*:=\min_{x\in\mathbb E_1}f(x) is attained. Then F(x)=0 has a solution in \mathbb E_1 if and only if f^*=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Provided the composite objective attains its minimum and the sharp merit function vanishes exactly at zero, the nonlinear equation is solvable exactly when the minimum merit value is zero.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_1,\mathbb E_2\text{ are real vector spaces}
\phi:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb R_+\text{ is a sharp merit function with }\phi(z)=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tail estimates for the modified Gauss–Newton process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For the iterates and quantities defined by the modified Gauss–Newton algorithm under Assumption 4.4.2.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(k\ge 0\) and \(r>0\), the modified Gauss--Newton iterates satisfy
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\ge \frac{L_0}{2}\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}r_{M_i}^2(x_i)\ge \frac{L_0}{2}\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}r_{2L}^2(x_i),
\]
and
\[
f(x_k)-f^*\ge r^2\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}M_i\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x_i)}{M_i r^2}\right)\ge 2Lr^2\sum_{i=k}^{\infty}\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x_i)}{2Lr^2}\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every iterate and for every positive radius, the objective gap bounds the stated tails of the modified Gauss–Newton residual and progress measures, including their uniform-parameter counterparts.
assumptions_latex: \(\{x_i\}\) is generated by modified Gauss--Newton Algorithm 4.4.1.
\(F\), \(f\), \(L_0\), \(L\), \(M_i\), \(r_M\), \(\Delta_r\), and \(\chi\) satisfy the cited definitions and Assumption 4.4.2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratically Regularized Modified Gauss–Newton Iterate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the iterate and associated radius, regularized model value, and decrement for the modified Gauss–Newton construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let M>0 and x\in\mathcal{F}. Choose
V_M(x)\in\operatorname*{Argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{E}_1}\left\{\psi(x;y)+\frac{M}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},
where the auxiliary objective is convex in y and \operatorname*{Argmin} denotes its global minimizers. Define
r_M(x)=\lVert V_M(x)-x\rVert,\qquad
f_M(x)=\psi(x;V_M(x))+\frac{M}{2}r_M^2(x),\qquad
\delta_M(x)=f(x)-f_M(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive regularization parameter and a feasible point, a modified Gauss–Newton iterate is any global minimizer of the convex Gauss–Newton model plus a quadratic displacement penalty. Its step radius, regularized model value, and model decrement are defined by the displayed formulas.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local quadratic error bound for the modified Gauss–Newton update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-step local error bound and nonexpansion result near a nondegenerate zero-residual solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x^*\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) satisfy \(F(x^*)=0\) and
\[
\sigma:=\sigma_{\min}(F'(x^*))>0.
\]
If \(x_k\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) and
\[
\|x_k-x^*\|\le \frac{2}{L}\frac{\sigma\gamma_\phi}{3+5\gamma_\phi},
\]
then the modified Gauss--Newton update satisfies \(x_{k+1}\in\mathcal L(f(x_0))\) and
\[
\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|\le \frac{3(1+\gamma_\phi)L\|x_k-x^*\|^2}{2\gamma_\phi\bigl(\sigma-L\|x_k-x^*\|\bigr)}\le \|x_k-x^*\|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Within the stated neighborhood of a nondegenerate zero-residual solution, one modified Gauss–Newton update remains in the initial level set and satisfies an explicit quadratic error bound as well as nonexpansion.
assumptions_latex: \(x_{k+1}\) is produced by Algorithm 4.4.1 under Assumption 4.4.2 and the cited definitions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic regularity and limit points of modified Gauss–Newton iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence consequences for the sequence generated by the modified Gauss–Newton process under its standing assumptions; \(r\) is the parameter occurring in the cited definition of \(\Delta_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) be generated by Algorithm 4.4.1 under its standing assumptions. Then
\[
\lim_{k\to\infty}\|x_k-x_{k+1}\|=0,\qquad \lim_{k\to\infty}\Delta_r(x_k)=0.
\]
Consequently, the set \(X^*\) of limit points of \(\{x_k\}\) is connected, and every \(\bar x\in X^*\) satisfies \(\Delta_r(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modified Gauss–Newton iterates are asymptotically regular, their stated progress measure tends to zero, their limit-point set is connected, and every limit point has zero progress measure.
assumptions_latex: \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) is generated by modified Gauss--Newton Algorithm 4.4.1.
The cited definitions and Assumption 4.4.2 hold.
\(X^*\) denotes the set of limit points of \(\{x_k\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{k\to\infty}\|x_k-x_{k+1}\|=0,\quad \lim_{k\to\infty}\Delta_r(x_k)=0,\quad X^*\text{ is connected},\quad \Delta_r(\bar x)=0\ \forall\bar x\in X^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteration Bound for Entering the Quadratic-Convergence Region

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the setting of Theorem 4.4.3 and Proposition 4.4.8, let \(N\) be the number of iterations of method (4.4.17) necessary to reach the region of quadratic convergence. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Regime Descent of the Modified Gauss–Newton Method
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-iteration objective bounds for Algorithm 4.4.1 under Assumptions 4.4.1–4.4.3, including the sharper constant-parameter case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Assumptions 4.4.1, 4.4.2, and 4.4.3 hold, and let \(\{x_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}\) be generated by Algorithm 4.4.1. If \(f(x_k)\geq \frac{\sigma^2}{2L}\gamma_\phi^2\), then \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\frac{\sigma^2}{4L}\gamma_\phi^2\). Otherwise, \(f(x_{k+1})\leq \frac{L}{\sigma^2\gamma_\phi^2}f(x_k)^2\leq \frac12f(x_k)\). If the sequence is generated with \(M_k\equiv L\), then, when \(f(x_k)\geq \frac{\sigma^2}{L}\gamma_\phi^2\), \(f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\frac{\sigma^2}{2L}\gamma_\phi^2\); otherwise, \(f(x_{k+1})\leq \frac{L}{2\sigma^2\gamma_\phi^2}f(x_k)^2\leq \frac12f(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the three cited assumptions, a modified Gauss–Newton step either decreases the objective by the stated fixed amount or, below the stated threshold, satisfies a quadratic bound and reduces the objective by at least one half. Choosing every M_k equal to L gives the sharper stated thresholds and constants.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the sharpened bounds, Algorithm 4.4.1 is run with }M_k\equiv L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}f(x_{k+1})\leq f(x_k)-\frac{\sigma^2}{4L}\gamma_\phi^2,&f(x_k)\geq\frac{\sigma^2}{2L}\gamma_\phi^2,\\f(x_{k+1})\leq\frac{L}{\sigma^2\gamma_\phi^2}f(x_k)^2\leq\frac12f(x_k),&f(x_k)<\frac{\sigma^2}{2L}\gamma_\phi^2,\end{cases}\quad\text{with the stated sharper pair when }M_k\equiv L.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic accuracy of the sharp-merit composite Gauss–Newton model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the discrepancy between the merit objective and its affine-residual composite model, making explicit the metric property of the merit function needed for the stated constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(y):=\phi(F(y)) and \psi(x;y):=\phi\!\left(F(x)+F'(x)(y-x)\right). Suppose \phi is a sharp merit function satisfying |\phi(u)-\phi(v)|\le \|u-v\|, and suppose F' is L-Lipschitz on a region containing the segment [x,y]. Then |f(y)-\psi(x;y)|\le \tfrac12L\|y-x\|^2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the sharp merit function is one-Lipschitz and the residual derivative is L-Lipschitz along the step, the composite Gauss–Newton model differs from the true merit objective by at most one half L times the squared step length.
assumptions_latex: [x,y]\subseteq\mathcal F\text{, or the stated smoothness hypotheses otherwise hold along the segment}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity of the Regularized Model Value
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes how the optimal regularized model value and modified Gauss–Newton step radius vary with the positive regularization parameter at a fixed feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed x\in\mathcal{F}, let
f_M(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb{E}_1}\left\{\psi(x;y)+\frac{M}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\},\qquad M>0.
Then M\mapsto f_M(x) is concave. Moreover,
\frac{d}{dM}f_M(x)=\frac12 r_M^2(x),
and hence M\mapsto\frac12 r_M^2(x) is decreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a fixed feasible point, the minimum regularized model value is concave in the positive quadratic-regularization parameter. Its derivative is one half of the squared modified Gauss–Newton step radius, so the squared radius decreases as the parameter increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\mapsto f_M(x)\text{ is concave},\qquad \frac{d}{dM}f_M(x)=\frac12 r_M^2(x),\qquad M\mapsto\frac12r_M^2(x)\text{ is decreasing}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global stationarity of line-search Gauss–Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence of the nonlinear least-squares gradient to zero under uniform full rank and Wolfe step lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2 and \mathcal L=\{x\mid f(x)\le f(x_0)\}. If x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}, where J_k^TJ_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tr_k and \alpha_k satisfies the Wolfe conditions, then \lim_{k\to\infty}J_k^Tr_k=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the initial level set is bounded, the residuals have Lipschitz-continuous derivatives nearby, the Jacobian remains uniformly full column rank there, and Gauss–Newton uses Wolfe line-search steps, then the gradients J-transpose-r converge to zero.
assumptions_latex: f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2,\quad \mathcal L=\{x\mid f(x)\le f(x_0)\}\text{ is bounded}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local-Model Lower Bound for the Regularized Decrement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the modified Gauss–Newton decrement using the best model decrease in an arbitrary positive-radius neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every x\in\mathbb{E}_1, r>0, and M>0,
\delta_M(x)\geq Mr^2\,\chi\!\left(\frac{\Delta_r(x)}{Mr^2}\right),
where
\chi(t)=\begin{cases}t-\frac12,&t\geq1,\\[2pt]\frac12t^2,&0\leq t\leq1.\end{cases}
For fixed x and r, the right-hand side is a decreasing function of M.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any point, positive radius, and positive regularization parameter, the modified Gauss–Newton decrement is bounded below by the stated piecewise function of the normalized local model decrease. With the point and radius fixed, this lower bound decreases as the regularization parameter increases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sharp-merit composite Gauss–Newton model and update rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the affine-residual composite model and the conditional model-minimizing update without asserting that a minimizer always exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix x\in\mathbb E_1. Let F:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2 be differentiable at x and let \phi:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb R_+ be a sharp merit function whose defining properties include convexity. Define \psi(x;y):=\phi\!\left(F(x)+F'(x)(y-x)\right) for y\in\mathbb E_1. Then \psi(x;\cdot) is convex. If \operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in\mathbb E_1}\psi(x;y) is nonempty, a next approximation may be selected from that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearize the residual at the current point inside the convex sharp merit function. This gives a convex trial-point model; when the model has a minimizer, a next approximation may be chosen from its minimizers.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2\text{ is differentiable at }x
\phi:\mathbb E_2\to\mathbb R_+\text{ is a sharp merit function and is convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \psi(x;y):=\phi\!\left(F(x)+F'(x)(y-x)\right)\text{ is convex in }y,\qquad \operatorname{Argmin}\psi(x;\cdot)\ne\varnothing\Longrightarrow x^+\in\operatorname{Argmin}_{y\in\mathbb E_1}\psi(x;y)\text{ may be selected}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solvability bound from dual nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general finite-dimensional linear-operator result used in the Gauss–Newton analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A:\mathbb E_1\to\mathbb E_2\) be linear and suppose \(\sigma_{\min}(A^*)>0\). Then, for every \(b\in\mathbb E_2\), there exists \(x(b)\in\mathbb E_1\) such that
\[
Ax(b)=b,\qquad \|x(b)\|\le \frac{\|b\|}{\sigma_{\min}(A^*)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the adjoint of a linear operator has positive smallest singular value, every right-hand side is attainable, with a solution norm bounded by the reciprocal singular value.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton direction from a linearized residual model

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Composite residual merit objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a residual-composite minimization model and records the standard squared-Euclidean merit choice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For residual functions \(f_i:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) and a merit function \(\phi:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\phi(u)\ge 0\) and \(\phi(u)=0\iff u=0\), define \(f(x)=\phi(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\) and consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb E}f(x)\). A standard choice is \(\phi(u)=\|u\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^m(u^{(i)})^2\), whose squared form supports a smoother objective than the unsquared norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual problem may minimize a nonnegative merit function of the residual vector, where the merit vanishes exactly when all residuals vanish. The standard squared Euclidean merit is the sum of squared residuals and is chosen for its favorable smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Classical Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undamped Gauss–Newton iteration for smooth finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a continuously differentiable residual \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), minimize \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\). From \(x_0\), at iteration \(k\) form \(J_k=F'(x_k)\) and compute any minimizer
\[
p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n}\tfrac12\lVert F(x_k)+J_kp\rVert_2^2.
\]
If \(J_k\) has full column rank, this is equivalently \((J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k)p_k=-J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\), and stop when a prescribed residual, gradient, or step tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration minimizes the linearized residual in least squares and takes the resulting full step.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the iterates.
The linearized least-squares subproblem has a selected minimizer at every iteration.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of F at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Line-Search Gauss–Newton Iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\) with continuously differentiable \(r:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\). At \(x_k\), set \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and assume \(J_k\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical deterministic Gauss–Newton with an exact direction and line-search step length; trust-region, regularized, and inexact-inner-solve variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The classical Gauss–Newton method computes the unique direction \(p_k^{GN}\) from \[J_k^TJ_kp_k^{GN}=-J_k^Tr_k\] and updates \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k^{GN},\qquad \alpha_k\in(0,1].\] The step length is selected by a standard line search applied to \(f\), commonly to satisfy Armijo decrease or Wolfe conditions. Because \(J_k\) has full column rank, \(J_k^TJ_k\) is positive definite; whenever \(J_k^Tr_k\ne0\), \[(p_k^{GN})^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|J_kp_k^{GN}\|^2<0,\] so the direction is a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The classical method solves the Gauss–Newton normal equations exactly and globalizes the resulting descent direction with a scalar line search. Full column rank makes the direction unique. A unit step is allowed when accepted by the line search, while shorter steps protect the iteration away from a local solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p_k^{GN}=\operatorname*{argmin}_p\|J_kp+r_k\|^2\).
A QR factorization of \(J_k\) may solve the same exact linear least-squares subproblem without forming \(J_k^TJ_k\).
special_cases_latex: With \(\alpha_k=1\), the iteration is the undamped classical Gauss–Newton method.
For a square nonsingular \(J_k\), the direction also satisfies \(J_kp_k^{GN}=-r_k\), coinciding with the Newton step for the residual equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: An Armijo backtracking line search is well-defined whenever the direction is strict descent.
The iteration terminates at a first-order stationary point when \(J_k^Tr_k=0\).
boundary_notes: Rank-deficient Jacobians fall outside this classical unique-direction definition.
The line search controls only the outer step; it does not define an inexact inner solve.
The method does not include Levenberg–Marquardt regularization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Gauss–Newton step and its least-squares representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Gauss–Newton for smooth nonlinear least squares, including its model, descent condition, and standard computational realizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For f(x)=	frac12\|r(x)\|^2 with Jacobian J(x), the Gauss	ext{--}Newton direction p_k^{\mathrm{GN}} satisfies J_k^T J_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tr_k and equivalently minimizes 	frac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2. It replaces 
abla^2f(x_k)=J_k^TJ_k+\sum_{j=1}^m r_j(x_k)
abla^2r_j(x_k) by J_k^TJ_k. If \operatorname{rank}J_k=n and 
abla f_k
e0, then (p_k^{\mathrm{GN}})^T
abla f_k=-\|J_kp_k^{\mathrm{GN}}\|^2<0. The subproblem may be solved directly from J_k by QR, SVD, or iterative products with J_k and J_k^T; when m is large, J^TJ and J^Tr may instead be accumulated residual by residual. A line search commonly selects \alpha_k using Armijo or Wolfe conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton step minimizes the squared norm of the linearized residual, or equivalently solves its normal equations. Its matrix is the Hessian approximation J-transpose-J, which omits the residual-weighted second derivatives and is especially accurate when residuals are small or nearly affine. With a full-column-rank Jacobian and nonzero gradient, the step is a strict descent direction. It can be computed by direct or iterative least-squares methods, with residual-wise accumulation available when storing a large Jacobian is undesirable, and is commonly globalized by an Armijo or Wolfe line search.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Step-Controlled Gauss–Newton Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), and let \(\ell_k(p)=\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|^2\) be the Gauss–Newton model at \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained least squares. The definition concerns outer-step magnitude and acceptance, independently of how accurately the linearized subproblem is solved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton step-control method chooses a trial step from the Gauss–Newton model and restricts or scales it before acceptance. In a line-search member, \[p_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_p\ell_k(p),\qquad s_k=\alpha_kp_k,\quad \alpha_k\in(0,1],\] with \(\alpha_k\) satisfying a prescribed sufficient-decrease or curvature condition for \(f\). In a trust-region member, \[s_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|p\|\le\Delta_k}\ell_k(p),\qquad \Delta_k>0,\] and acceptance is governed by the ratio \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{\ell_k(0)-\ell_k(s_k)}.\] The iterate is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when the trial is accepted and remains \(x_k\) otherwise; the control parameter is updated from the acceptance information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family retains the Gauss–Newton residual model while controlling how far the outer iteration moves. Line-search methods scale an unconstrained direction. Trust-region methods constrain the step while solving the model. In both cases acceptance compares predicted behavior with the actual nonlinear objective, separating step control from the choice of inner linear algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted displacement is either \(s_k=\alpha_kp_k\) for a line search or a minimizer of \(\ell_k\) over \(\|p\|\le\Delta_k\) for a trust region.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a spherical trust region, a solution satisfies \((J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_k I)s_k=-J_k^Tr_k\), \(\lambda_k\ge0\), and \(\lambda_k(\Delta_k-\|s_k\|)=0\).
special_cases_latex: The full-step method is obtained when \(\alpha_k=1\) is accepted.
Levenberg–Marquardt trust-region steps are the spherical trust-region specialization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Step control can reject or shorten a direction even when the linearized subproblem is solved exactly.
When the unconstrained Gauss–Newton step lies inside an inactive trust region, the trust-region step equals that unconstrained step.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe Armijo, Wolfe, or trust-region thresholds numerically.
Regularization imposed for inverse-problem stability is distinct from globalization-only damping.
Accuracy conditions for iterative inner solves belong to the inner-solve family.

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual to predicted reduction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Line-search Gauss–Newton iteration for minimizing a nonlinear sum-of-squares objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose an initial estimate \(x_0\). For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), form the residual vector \(f_k=(f_i(x_k))_i\) and its Jacobian \(J_k\), obtain \(p_k\) by solving \((J_k^T J_k)p_k=-J_k^T f_k\), choose \(s\) so that \(F(x_k+s p_k)\) satisfies Wolfe conditions 2 and 3, and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s p_k\). Stop when the norm of the stationarity residual is sufficiently small.

(J_k^T J_k)p_k=-J_k^T f_k\text{ is solvable at each performed iteration}
\text{A step length }s\text{ satisfying Wolfe conditions 2 and 3 is found at each performed iteration}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Levenberg–Marquardt trust-region step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region and diagonally scaled damping formulations for smooth nonlinear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2, J_k=J(x_k), and r_k=r(x_k). The classical Levenberg\text{--}Marquardt trust-region step solves
\[
\min_{\|s\|_2\leq\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|J_ks+r_k\|_2^2.
\]
A solution satisfies, for some \mu_k\geq0,
\[
(J_k^TJ_k+\mu_kI)s_k=-J_k^Tr_k,
\]
with \mu_k=0 in an inactive-boundary Gauss\text{--}Newton regime and \mu_k>0 with \|s_k\|_2=\Delta_k in the active-boundary regime. If \mu_k>0 and s_k\neq0, then J_k^TJ_k+\mu_kI\succ0 and
\[
(J_k^Tr_k)^Ts_k=-s_k^T(J_k^TJ_k+\mu_kI)s_k<0.
\]
As \mu_k becomes large, s_k is approximately -\mu_k^{-1}J_k^Tr_k. With a diagonal matrix D_k\succ0, the scaled equation is
\[
(J_k^TJ_k+\mu_kD_k)s_k=-J_k^Tr_k,
\]
and its large-damping direction is proportional to -D_k^{-1}J_k^Tr_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Levenberg–Marquardt minimizes the Gauss–Newton linearized least-squares model inside a trust region. An inactive boundary permits an undamped Gauss–Newton step, while an active boundary uses positive damping. Positive damping produces a descent direction whenever the step is nonzero, and large damping approaches steepest descent. Positive diagonal damping gives the corresponding metric-scaled variant.
assumptions_latex: D_k\succ0\text{ is diagonal in the scaled variant}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_k\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\|s\|_2\leq\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|J_ks+r_k\|_2^2\text{ is generated through the stated damped normal-equation regimes, with descent for }\mu_k>0\text{ and }s_k\neq0.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton direction combined with Armijo backtracking on the least-squares objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\) and \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\). Compute a direction \(p_k\) from the Gauss–Newton model, requiring \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\). Fix \(c\in(0,1)\) and \(\beta\in(0,1)\). Choose the smallest integer \(j_k\geq0\) for which
\[
f(x_k+\beta^{j_k}p_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\beta^{j_k}g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k.
\]
Set \(\alpha_k=\beta^{j_k}\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\). Stop under a prescribed residual, gradient, or step tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking shortens a descent Gauss–Newton direction until the least-squares objective satisfies sufficient decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the trial points.
The selected direction satisfies \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\) whenever \(g_k\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted step satisfies the Armijo inequality and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\).

notation.meaning: gradient of the least-squares objective at x_k

knowledge_statements.title: Step-Acceptance Safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent-angle and sufficient-decrease safeguards for a trial Gauss–Newton step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), let \(g_k=F'(x_k)^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), and let \(p_k\neq0\) be a trial direction at an iterate for which \(g_k\neq0\). Fix \(\sigma\in(0,1]\) and \(c\in(0,1)\). A descent-angle safeguard requires
\[
g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\leq-\sigma\lVert g_k\rVert_2\lVert p_k\rVert_2.
\]
A step length \(\alpha_k>0\) is accepted only if
\[
f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k.
\]
If either test fails, the trial is shortened, rejected, or replaced by a nonzero direction satisfying the descent-angle test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonstationary iterate, a nonzero trial direction must make a uniformly acute angle with the negative gradient, and its step length is accepted only after it produces sufficient objective decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable at the current iterate and at every trial point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted trial satisfies \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\leq-\sigma\lVert g_k\rVert_2\lVert p_k\rVert_2\) and \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\leq f(x_k)+c\alpha_k g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\).

notation.meaning: least-squares gradient at the current iterate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact and Inexact Gauss–Newton Inner Solves
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an outer iterate \(x_k\), let \(r_k\in\mathbb R^m\), \(J_k\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(g_k=J_k^Tr_k\). The Gauss–Newton inner problem is \(\min_p\tfrac12\|J_kp+r_k\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional inner linear algebra for Gauss–Newton models, including rank-aware direct solvers and residual-controlled iterative solvers; outer acceptance is not specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Gauss–Newton inner-solve method returns \(p_k\) satisfying either the exact optimality condition \[J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)=0\] or an inexact condition \[\|J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)\|\le\eta_k\|g_k\|,\qquad 0\le\eta_k<1.\] Direct members compute an exact or rank-revealing minimizer using QR or SVD. Normal-equation members solve \(J_k^TJ_kp=-g_k\). Matrix-free iterative members access \(J_kv\) and \(J_k^Tw\) and stop when the displayed forcing condition is met. If the exact minimizer is nonunique, the canonical rank-aware selection is the minimum-norm solution \(p_k=-J_k^\dagger r_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inner-solve family consists of numerical methods for the linear least-squares model inside a Gauss–Newton iteration. Exact QR, SVD, and normal-equation methods satisfy the model optimality condition. Iterative methods may terminate early when the normal residual is small relative to the current gradient. Matrix-free variants need only products with the Jacobian and its transpose.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step satisfies \(\|J_k^T(J_kp_k+r_k)\|\le\eta_k\|J_k^Tr_k\|\), with \(\eta_k=0\) for an exact solve.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact condition is the normal equation \(J_k^TJ_kp_k=-J_k^Tr_k\).
The augmented least-squares residual is \(J_kp_k+r_k\), whose orthogonality to \(\operatorname{range}(J_k)\) characterizes an exact minimizer.
special_cases_latex: QR avoids explicitly forming the normal matrix when \(J_k\) has full column rank.
SVD supplies a minimum-norm solution and rank information when \(J_k\) is deficient.
Krylov methods evaluate \(J_k^TJ_kv\) through successive products \(J_kv\) and \(J_k^T(J_kv)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The inner solver can be changed without altering the outer Gauss–Newton model.
A decreasing forcing sequence \(\eta_k\) demands progressively more accurate inner solutions.
boundary_notes: The forcing inequality alone does not define an outer globalization rule.
Direct normal equations may be less stable than QR or SVD for ill-conditioned Jacobians.
Preconditioning changes the inner numerical method but not the target linearized least-squares problem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton scoring updates for weighted nonlinear Gaussian regression
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint mean-parameter and variance estimation with known observation weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let independent responses satisfy \(x_i\sim N(\mu_i(\theta),\sigma^2/w_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\). Define \(G_n=\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\nabla\mu_i(\theta_n)\nabla\mu_i(\theta_n)^T\). Fisher scoring gives the Gauss--Newton updates
\[
\theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+G_n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\bigl(x_i-\mu_i(\theta_n)\bigr)\nabla\mu_i(\theta_n),
\qquad
\sigma_{n+1}^2=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m w_i\bigl(x_i-\mu_i(\theta_n)\bigr)^2.
\]
The \(\theta\)-iteration is independent of the current value and update of \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent nonlinear Gaussian observations with known weights, Fisher scoring updates the mean parameter by the weighted Gauss–Newton normal-equation step and updates the variance by the mean weighted squared residual. The mean-parameter iterations can be performed without iterating the variance parameter.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton step as a linearized least-squares solve
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the Gauss–Newton step through its linearized least-squares subproblem, normal equations, and pseudoinverse realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At x_c, let J_c=R'(x_c). Choose the minimum-norm step among the minimizers of \[\min_s\ \tfrac12\|R(x_c)+J_cs\|_2^2,\] and set x_+=x_c+s. If J_c has full column rank, then \[s=-(J_c^TJ_c)^{-1}J_c^TR(x_c)=-(J_c^TJ_c)^{-1}\nabla f(x_c),\] which entails M\ge N. The linear least-squares formulation also covers M<N; its minimum-norm step is s=-J_c^\dagger R(x_c) and may be computed using an SVD. The Hessian term discarded by Gauss–Newton, R''(x_c)^TR(x_c), vanishes at a zero-residual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauss–Newton minimizes the locally linearized residual and adds a minimum-norm step to the current iterate. With a full-column-rank Jacobian this gives the normal-equation formula; the linear least-squares or pseudoinverse form also covers underdetermined problems. The omitted second-order Hessian term vanishes at a zero-residual point.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{rank}J_c=N\text{ when the inverse normal-equation formula is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{u}\|R(x_c)+J_cu\|_2\text{ with minimum norm},\qquad x_+=x_c+s;\quad \operatorname{rank}J_c=N\Rightarrow s=-(J_c^TJ_c)^{-1}J_c^TR(x_c),\quad s=-J_c^\dagger R(x_c)\text{ for the minimum-norm least-squares realization}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: QR Realization and Conditioning of the Gauss–Newton Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: QR-based computation of a full-column-rank Gauss–Newton step and its condition-number advantage over forming normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $J_k=J(x_k)$ have full column rank and singular values $\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n>0$. For the normal equations $J_k^TJ_k s=-J_k^Tr_k$, the stated perturbation estimate is $\frac{\|\delta s\|}{\|s\|}\leq\kappa_2(J_k^TJ_k)\frac{\|E\|}{\|J_k^TJ_k\|}$, with $\kappa_2(J_k^TJ_k)=\sigma_1^2/\sigma_n^2$. If an orthogonal factorization gives $J_k=Q\begin{bmatrix}R_1\\0\end{bmatrix}$, where $R_1$ is nonsingular and upper triangular, then the step is computed by back substitution from $R_1s=-(Q^Tr_k)_{1:n}$. Moreover, $\kappa_2(R_1)=\sigma_1/\sigma_n$, so QR avoids the squared condition number associated with the normal equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-column-rank Gauss–Newton Jacobian, forming the normal equations squares the Jacobian's spectral condition number. QR factorization instead computes the step through an upper-triangular solve whose condition number equals that of the Jacobian, reducing conditioning-based error amplification.
assumptions_latex: J_k=Q\begin{bmatrix}R_1\\0\end{bmatrix},\quad Q^TQ=I,\quad R_1\text{ nonsingular and upper triangular}
E\text{ and }\delta s\text{ denote the stated matrix and step perturbations, respectively.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton quadratic model and full-rank step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical smooth nonlinear least squares with an objective induced by a residual map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), let \(J_k=J(x_k)\) and \(g_k=J_k^Tr(x_k)\). Omitting the residual-weighted second-derivative term from the Hessian gives
\[
\bar q_k(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x_k)\|^2+g_k^T(x-x_k)+\tfrac12(x-x_k)^TJ_k^TJ_k(x-x_k).
\]
If \(J_k\) has full column rank, then \(J_k^TJ_k\) is positive definite and the uniquely defined Gauss–Newton update is
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k-(J_k^TJ_k)^{-1}J_k^Tr(x_k).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gauss–Newton replaces the nonlinear least-squares Hessian by J transpose J. When the current residual Jacobian has full column rank, the normal-equations matrix is invertible and yields a unique step.
assumptions_latex: r_i\text{ is twice differentiable near }x_k\text{ for each residual component }i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-residual representation and descent property of the Gauss–Newton step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-equations and affine-residual interpretations of classical smooth Gauss–Newton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|^2\), \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and \(g_k=J_k^Tr(x_k)\). If
\[
J_k^TJ_k s_k=-g_k,
\]
then \(s_k\) solves the affine-residual least-squares model
\[
\min_s\ \tfrac12\|r(x_k)+J_ks\|^2.
\]
Moreover,
\[
s_k^T\nabla f(x_k)=-s_k^TJ_k^TJ_ks_k=-\|J_ks_k\|^2\leq0.
\]
If \(J_k\) has full column rank and \(g_k\neq0\), then \(s_k^T\nabla f(x_k)<0\). The model uses only first derivatives of \(r\), and \(J_k^TJ_k\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton equations are the optimality equations for least-squares minimization of the affine residual model. Their curvature matrix is positive semidefinite and requires only first residual derivatives. With full column rank and a nonzero gradient, the step is a strict descent direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_k\in\arg\min_s\tfrac12\|r(x_k)+J(x_k)s\|^2,\qquad s_k^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|J(x_k)s_k\|^2<0\text{ under the strict-descent assumptions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic convergence of Gauss–Newton at a zero-residual solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero residual removes the residual-dependent linear error term in the local Gauss–Newton recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m and f(x)=\tfrac12R(x)^TR(x) be twice continuously differentiable on an open convex set D. Suppose J\in\operatorname{Lip}_\gamma(D), \|J(x)\|_2\le\alpha on D, J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0, \lambda=\lambda_{\min}(J(x_*)^TJ(x_*)), \|(J(x)-J(x_*))^TR(x_*)\|_2\le\sigma\|x-x_*\|_2 on D, and \sigma<\lambda. If R(x_*)=0, then some \varepsilon>0 exists such that every x_0\in N(x_*,\varepsilon) generates a well-defined Gauss\text{--}Newton sequence that converges q-quadratically to x_*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the local smoothness, bounded-Jacobian, stationarity, and positive-curvature assumptions of the Gauss–Newton convergence theorem, a zero-residual solution attracts every sufficiently close Gauss–Newton sequence with q-quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: R:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m,\quad f(x)=\tfrac12R(x)^TR(x)\in C^2(D),\quad D\text{ open and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall x_0\in N(x_*,\varepsilon):\ \text{the Gauss\text{--}Newton sequence is well defined and converges q-quadratically to }x_*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local quadratic convergence of Gauss–Newton to the zero-residual set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers square and underdetermined problems, where the nearby limit may differ from the reference zero-residual point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M\le N and define \mathcal Z=\{x:R(x)=0\}. Suppose x^*\in\mathcal Z minimizes \|R\|_2^2, R is Lipschitz continuously differentiable near x^*, and R'(x^*) has maximal rank \min(M,N). Then there exists \delta>0 such that, whenever \|x_0-x^*\|\le\delta, the iterates \[x_{n+1}=x_n-R'(x_n)^\dagger R(x_n)\] are well defined and converge r-quadratically to some z^*\in\mathcal Z. The limit z^* need not equal the reference point x^*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square or underdetermined zero-residual problem with a locally Lipschitz Jacobian of maximal rank, every sufficiently nearby pseudoinverse Gauss–Newton sequence exists and converges r-quadratically to a zero-residual point, which may differ from the initially chosen reference solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\delta>0:\quad x_{n+1}=x_n-R'(x_n)^\dagger R(x_n)\text{ exists for all }n\text{ and }x_n\xrightarrow{r\text{-quadratically}}z^*\in\mathcal Z.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Grade-partitioned corrected Gauss–Newton direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines an SVD-based Gauss–Newton correction for weak singular-value directions, including its endpoint cases, adaptive grade, and correction-information variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J_k=U\begin{pmatrix}S\\0\end{pmatrix}V^T, with \sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n\ge0, and choose a grade r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}. Partition V=[V_1\ V_2], S=\operatorname{diag}(S_1,S_2), and the first n components of U^Tf_k as \bar f=(\bar f_1,\bar f_2). Require \sigma_r>0 when r>0 and set \bar p_1=-S_1^{-1}\bar f_1. For a residual second-order matrix or approximation \widehat Q_k, compute \bar p_2 from (S_2^2+V_2^T\widehat Q_kV_2)\bar p_2=-S_2\bar f_2-V_2^T\widehat Q_kV_1\bar p_1, and define p_C=V_1\bar p_1+V_2\bar p_2. With r=n and full column rank, this is the Gauss--Newton direction; with r=0 and \widehat Q_k=Q_k, it is the Newton construction when the Newton system is solvable. The grade is adjusted according to achieved objective decrease. The correction may use exact second derivatives, directional finite differences, or a quasi-Newton approximation, with a stabilized factorization used when needed to obtain descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Corrected Gauss–Newton splits the Jacobian singular directions into a dominant subspace treated by Gauss–Newton and a complementary subspace corrected using residual second-order information. Its grade is adapted according to objective decrease. Under the appropriate rank and exact-correction conditions, its endpoints are the Gauss–Newton and Newton constructions.
assumptions_latex: \text{Terms involving }Q_k\text{ in the dominant-subspace equations are treated as negligible}
\widehat Q_k=Q_k\text{ for the exact Newton endpoint at }r=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_C=V_1(-S_1^{-1}\bar f_1)+V_2\bar p_2,\qquad (S_2^2+V_2^T\widehat Q_kV_2)\bar p_2=-S_2\bar f_2-V_2^T\widehat Q_kV_1(-S_1^{-1}\bar f_1).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauss–Newton direction and rank-aware computation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the Gauss–Newton inner solve, its Newton approximation and zero-residual local regime, and its numerical boundaries under ill-conditioning or rank deficiency.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At x_k, a Gauss--Newton direction satisfies p_{\mathrm{GN}}\in\arg\min_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n}\tfrac12\|J_kp+f_k\|_2^2 and hence J_k^TJ_kp_{\mathrm{GN}}=-J_k^Tf_k. The minimizer is unique when J_k has full column rank. If the Newton direction p_N exists, p_N\ne0, J_k has full column rank, and \|Q(x_k)\|=\epsilon is sufficiently small, then \|p_N-p_{\mathrm{GN}}\|/\|p_N\|=O(\epsilon). Thus, at a zero-residual solution with a full-column-rank Jacobian, the method can attain quadratic local convergence. Directly forming J_k^TJ_k squares the two-norm condition number, so an orthogonal factorization or SVD is preferable. If J_k is rank deficient, the least-squares minimizer is nonunique; a standard choice is the minimum-Euclidean-norm minimizer, whose computation requires a scale-dependent numerical-rank decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gauss–Newton direction minimizes the norm of the linearized residual and is unique under full column rank. It approaches the Newton direction as the omitted residual-Hessian term vanishes and can be quadratically convergent in the zero-residual, full-rank regime. Stable implementations solve the least-squares problem directly; rank-deficient cases require a minimum-norm choice and a scaling-sensitive rank estimate.
assumptions_latex: J_k\text{ has full column rank for uniqueness and the Newton-direction comparison}
p_N\text{ exists and }p_N\ne0\text{ for the relative-error comparison}
x_k\to x^*,\quad f(x^*)=0,\quad \operatorname{rank}J(x^*)=n\text{ for the stated quadratic regime}

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton iteration whose normal equations are solved only to a forcing tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lVert F(x)\rVert_2^2\), set \(J_k=F'(x_k)\), \(g_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}F(x_k)\), and \(B_k=J_k^{\mathsf T}J_k\). Choose a forcing number \(\eta_k\in[0,1)\) and compute \(p_k\) such that
\[
\lVert B_kp_k+g_k\rVert_2\leq\eta_k\lVert g_k\rVert_2.
\]
Apply the prescribed full-step or globalization rule to obtain \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), where \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\). Stop when the outer residual, gradient, or step tolerance is met; the inner solve may terminate as soon as the displayed inequality holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal equations need only be solved until their residual is a controlled fraction of the outer gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: An inner solver can produce a step satisfying the forcing inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inexact Gauss–Newton construction for large sparse problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate Gauss–Newton system solution when exact Jacobian or normal-equation factorization is expensive.

The approximation satisfies J_k^TJ_k\succeq0, which simplifies the resulting inexact algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For large sparse nonlinear least-squares problems, an inexact Gauss–Newton method applies the approximate-solve pattern of inexact Newton to the positive-semidefinite matrix J-transpose-J, avoiding the need to compute every step by exact factorization.
