knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonquadratic Robust Residual Objective and Method Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(\sigma_i>0\), and let \(\rho_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be loss functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise robust residual objectives in finite dimensions; the losses may be smooth or nonsmooth and convex or nonconvex, provided the chosen algorithm declares the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonquadratic robust residual problem is \[\min_{x\in\mathcal D}\;F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i\!\left(\frac{r_i(x)}{\sigma_i}\right),\] where at least one \(\rho_i\) is not a positive quadratic on all of \(\mathbb R\), and large arguments receive less than quadratic marginal influence in the robust case. A robust residual method is any iteration whose model, generalized gradient, or reweighting rule is constructed from this declared \(F\), rather than from the unqualified least-squares objective \(\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\). For differentiable losses, \[\nabla F(x)=J(x)^TD_\sigma^{-1}\psi(D_\sigma^{-1}R(x)),\qquad \psi_i=\rho_i',\] with componentwise evaluation of \(\psi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family minimizes a sum of declared nonquadratic losses of scaled residual components. Robust losses reduce the marginal influence of sufficiently large residuals. Methods in the family must construct their local equations or models from this objective, not silently replace it by ordinary least squares.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\sum_i\rho_i(r_i(x)/\sigma_i)\), with at least one globally nonquadratic loss and, in the differentiable case, \(\nabla F(x)=J(x)^TD_\sigma^{-1}\psi(D_\sigma^{-1}R(x))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With a vector loss \(\rho:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\), the objective is \(F(x)=\rho(R(x))\); the componentwise form is the separable-loss specialization.
special_cases_latex: Huber loss is quadratic near zero and linear in magnitude beyond its threshold.
A bounded redescending loss, such as the Beaton–Tukey loss, yields vanishing influence beyond its cutoff.
immediate_consequences_latex: Ordinary least squares is recovered when every \(\rho_i(t)=t^2/2\), but then the objective is not nonquadratic.
boundary_notes: Robustness is not guaranteed merely by using a nonquadratic loss; its influence or tail behavior must be specified.
Redescending losses are generally nonconvex and may have multiple stationary points.

notation.meaning: Influence function, equal to the derivative of the ith loss where differentiable.
Diagonal matrix of positive residual scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteratively Reweighted Least-Squares Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth robust-loss IRLS with weights derived from the loss derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i(r_i(x))\), initialize \(x_0\). At iteration \(k\), assign \(w_i^k=\rho_i'(r_i(x_k))/r_i(x_k)\) when \(r_i(x_k)\ne0\), using the continuous nonnegative extension at zero. Compute \(s_k\) by minimizing \(\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m w_i^k(r_i(x_k)+\nabla r_i(x_k)^\top s)^2+\tfrac{\mu_k}{2}\lVert s\rVert_2^2\), where \(\mu_k\ge0\), and accept or damp the step according to decrease in \(F\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_k s_k\). Stop when the robust gradient or step norm meets its tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly convert a robust residual objective into a weighted least-squares model, solve it, and globalize or damp the resulting step.
assumptions_latex: Each loss \(\rho_i\) is differentiable and yields nonnegative finite weights.
The regularized weighted subproblem has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed iteration defines the smooth-loss iteratively reweighted least-squares family.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^m\), scales \(\sigma_i>0\), and differentiable even losses \(\rho_i\) with influence functions \(\psi_i=\rho_i'\). Put \(t_i(x)=r_i(x)/\sigma_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component-separable differentiable M-estimation; zero residuals require a declared continuous extension of the weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iteratively reweighted least-squares method for \(F(x)=\sum_i\rho_i(t_i(x))\) defines at iterate \(x_k\) nonnegative weights \[w_i^{(k)}=\begin{cases}\psi_i(t_i(x_k))/t_i(x_k),&t_i(x_k)\ne0,\\ \lim_{t\to0}\psi_i(t)/t,&t_i(x_k)=0,\end{cases}\] whenever these quantities exist, and computes \(x_{k+1}\) by solving or approximately solving the weighted nonlinear least-squares surrogate \[\min_{x\in\mathcal D}\;Q_k(x)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m w_i^{(k)}\left(\frac{r_i(x)}{\sigma_i}\right)^2,\] possibly with damping, a trust region, or proximal regularization. The family is distinguished by recomputation of residual-dependent weights between least-squares subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IRLS alternates between calculating weights from the current scaled residuals and solving a weighted least-squares problem. For a differentiable M-loss, the canonical weight is its influence divided by the residual, with a continuous value assigned at zero.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For fixed weights, \(Q_k(x)=\tfrac12\|W_k^{1/2}D_\sigma^{-1}R(x)\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: For quadratic loss, every weight is constant and IRLS reduces to a single weighted least-squares model family.
For Huber loss, \(w(t)=1\) inside the threshold and is proportional to \(1/|t|\) outside it.
immediate_consequences_latex: The weighted normal-equation gradient at \(x_k\) matches the robust-objective gradient when the stated weight identity is used.
boundary_notes: Negative weights do not define an ordinary weighted least-squares subproblem and are excluded here.
The definition alone does not assert descent or convergence for nonconvex losses.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square-summability and asymptotic regularity of IRLS steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite squared-step bound and vanishing successive differences for sparse-recovery IRLS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((x^n)\) be the IRLS iterates and let \(B\) be the constant defined by \(B=\mathcal J(x^1,w^0,\varepsilon_0)\). Then
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\|x^{n+1}-x^n\|_2^2\le2B^2.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}(x^{n+1}-x^n)=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The squared Euclidean lengths of successive IRLS steps have sum at most 2B squared. Consequently, consecutive iterates become asymptotically equal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local linear convergence of IRLS for exact sparse recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global exact-sparse convergence and eventual linear contraction after entering a support-dependent neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times N}\) satisfies the stable null-space property of order \(s\) with constant \(\rho<1/3\). Let \(\kappa\in(0,1)\) satisfy
\[
\mu:=\frac{3\rho(1+\rho)}{2(1-\kappa)}<1.
\]
For an \(s\)-sparse \(x\in\mathbb C^N\), let \(y=Ax\), and generate \((x^n)\) by IRLS with \(\gamma=1/(2N)\) and sparsity parameter \(s\). Then \(x^n\to x\). Moreover, if \(n_0\ge1\) satisfies
\[
\|x-x^{n_0}\|_1\le R:=\kappa\min_{j\in\operatorname{supp}(x)}|x_j|,
\]
then for every \(n\ge n_0\),
\[
\|x-x^{n+1}\|_1\le\mu\|x-x^n\|_1,
\]
and therefore
\[
\|x^n-x\|_1\le\mu^{n-n_0}\|x^{n_0}-x\|_1.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stable null-space property with rho below one third, IRLS with gamma equal to 1/(2N) converges to an s-sparse signal consistent with the data. Once an iterate lies within the stated neighborhood determined by the smallest nonzero signal entry, subsequent l1 errors contract linearly by the factor mu.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb C^{m\times N}\text{ satisfies the stable null-space property of order }s\text{ with constant }\rho<1/3
(x^n)\text{ is generated by IRLS with }\gamma=1/(2N)\text{ and sparsity parameter }s
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^n\to x;\quad \text{if }\|x-x^{n_0}\|_1\le\kappa\min_{j\in\operatorname{supp}(x)}|x_j|,\text{ then }\|x-x^{n+1}\|_1\le\mu\|x-x^n\|_1\text{ for all }n\ge n_0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: IRLS for equality-constrained sparse recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteratively reweighted least-squares scheme for approximating a sparsest solution of a consistent linear system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times N}\), \(y\in\mathbb C^m\), \(\gamma>0\), and \(s\in[N]\), initialize \(w^0=\mathbf1\in\mathbb R^N\) and \(\varepsilon_0=1\). Repeatedly compute
\[
x^{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathbb C^N}\mathcal J(z,w^n,\varepsilon_n)\quad\text{subject to }Az=y,
\]
set
\[
\varepsilon_{n+1}=\min\{\varepsilon_n,\gamma (x^{n+1})^*_{s+1}\},
\]
and compute
\[
w^{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w>0}\mathcal J(x^{n+1},w,\varepsilon_{n+1}).
\]
Stop when \(\varepsilon_n=0\) or another stopping criterion is met, and return the prescribed final feasible iterate as an approximation to a sparsest solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IRLS alternates a weighted least-squares minimization over Az=y, a reduction of the smoothing parameter using the (s+1)-st ordered coordinate magnitude, and a weight update. It returns a feasible iterate intended to approximate a sparsest solution.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: IRLS descent identity and iterate boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-objective identities, descent, iterate boundedness, and lower bounds on the weights for sparse-recovery IRLS.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For IRLS iterates \((x^n,w^n,\varepsilon_n)\) and every \(n\ge1\),
\[
\mathcal J(x^n,w^n,\varepsilon_n)=\sum_{j=1}^N\sqrt{|x_j^n|^2+\varepsilon_n^2}=F_{\varepsilon_n}(x^n),
\]
and
\[
\mathcal J(x^n,w^n,\varepsilon_n)
\le \mathcal J(x^n,w^{n-1},\varepsilon_n)
\le \mathcal J(x^n,w^{n-1},\varepsilon_{n-1})
\le \mathcal J(x^{n-1},w^{n-1},\varepsilon_{n-1}).
\]
With
\[
B:=\mathcal J(x^1,w^0,\varepsilon_0),
\]
one also has
\[
\|x^n\|_1\le B\quad(n\ge1),\qquad w_j^n\ge B^{-1}\quad(j\in[N],\ n\ge1).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every IRLS iterate, the auxiliary objective equals the smoothed l1 functional and satisfies the stated descent chain. The iterates are uniformly bounded in l1 norm, and every weight is uniformly bounded below by 1/B.
assumptions_latex: (x^n,w^n,\varepsilon_n)\text{ are iterates of the stated IRLS algorithm}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal J(x^n,w^n,\varepsilon_n)=F_{\varepsilon_n}(x^n),\quad \mathcal J\text{ satisfies the stated descent chain},\quad \|x^n\|_1\le B,\quad w_j^n\ge B^{-1}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence and recovery guarantees for sparse-recovery IRLS
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit characterization and branch-dependent approximation bounds under the stable null-space property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(A\in\mathbb C^{m\times N}\) satisfies the stable null-space property of order \(s\in[N]\) with constant \(\rho<1\), let \(x\in\mathbb C^N\), \(y=Ax\), and let \((x^n,\varepsilon_n)\) be generated by IRLS with parameters \(\gamma>0\) and \(s\). Then \(x^n\to x^\sharp\). If \(\varepsilon_n\to0\), then \(x^\sharp\) is an \(s\)-sparse \(\ell_1\)-minimizer of the equality-constrained recovery problem and
\[
\|x-x^\sharp\|_1\le \frac{2(1+\rho)}{1-\rho}\sigma_s(x)_1.
\]
Thus \(x^\sharp=x\) when \(x\) is \(s\)-sparse. If \(\varepsilon_n\to\varepsilon>0\), then \(x^\sharp\) minimizes the corresponding smoothed problem and, whenever
\[
\widetilde s<s+1-\frac{(1+\rho)N\gamma}{1-\rho},
\]
obeys
\[
\|x-x^\sharp\|_1\le
\frac{3+\rho}{(1-\rho)-(1+\rho)N\gamma/(s+1-\widetilde s)}\sigma_{\widetilde s}(x)_1.
\]
In particular, if \(\rho<1/3\) and \(\gamma=1/(2N)\), then
\[
\|x-x^\sharp\|_1\le\frac{2(3+\rho)}{1-3\rho}\sigma_s(x)_1.
\]
Under these latter conditions, an \(s\)-sparse \(x\) necessarily satisfies \(x^\sharp=x\) and \(\varepsilon_n\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stable null-space property, the IRLS iterates converge. Vanishing smoothing yields an s-sparse l1 minimizer and a best-s-term error bound. A positive smoothing limit yields a smoothed-problem minimizer with a parameter-dependent bound. Stronger constants ensure exact recovery and vanishing smoothing for s-sparse signals.

(x^n,\varepsilon_n)\text{ is generated by IRLS with parameters }\gamma,s
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^n\to x^\sharp\text{ with the stated branch-dependent minimizer characterizations, error bounds, and exact-recovery conclusion}

knowledge_statements.title: Robust Gauss–Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gauss–Newton linearization for differentiable robust sums of scalar residual losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i(r_i(x))\). At \(x_k\), form \(r_k=r(x_k)\), \(J_k=J_r(x_k)\), and diagonal \(W_k\) with \((W_k)_{ii}=\rho_i'(r_{k,i})/r_{k,i}\), continuously extended at zero. Compute \(s_k\) from \((J_k^\top W_kJ_k+\mu_k I)s_k=-J_k^\top W_kr_k\), with \(\mu_k\ge0\). Choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) by a line-search or trust-region acceptance test for \(F\), then set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\). Terminate when \(\lVert J_k^\top W_kr_k\rVert\) is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use robust-loss weights in a Gauss–Newton system, globalize the computed direction, and stop when the weighted first-order residual is small.
assumptions_latex: The loss-derived weights are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration is a robust Gauss–Newton method with loss-dependent curvature approximation \(J_k^\top W_kJ_k\).

notation.meaning: Residual Jacobian at the current iterate.
Regularization parameter ensuring a solvable model system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the terminal container, but no evidence supports this particular weight formula, curvature approximation, regularization, and globalization combination. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Robust Gauss–Newton Step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m\rho_i(r_i(x)/\sigma_i)\), let \(J_k=R'(x_k)\), and suppose \(w_i^{(k)}=\psi_i(t_i(x_k))/t_i(x_k)\geq0\) is defined with a continuous convention at zero. Let \(D_\sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth residual maps with differentiable component losses and nonnegative local weights; globalization is optional but must be declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A robust Gauss–Newton method forms \[g_k=J_k^TD_\sigma^{-1}\psi(D_\sigma^{-1}R_k),\qquad B_k=J_k^TD_\sigma^{-1}W_kD_\sigma^{-1}J_k,\] and selects a step from the weighted Gauss–Newton model \[m_k(p)=F(x_k)+g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TB_kp.\] An undamped step satisfies \(B_kp_k=-g_k\) when this system is solvable; damped or trust-region variants replace it by a regularized system or constrained model minimization. The method is robust only relative to the declared losses and scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robust Gauss–Newton replaces the ordinary least-squares normal matrix by a residual-weighted normal matrix derived from a robust loss. It then solves the corresponding quadratic model, optionally with damping or a trust region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_k=J_k^TD_\sigma^{-1}W_kD_\sigma^{-1}J_k\) and an undamped robust Gauss–Newton step satisfies \(B_kp_k=-J_k^TD_\sigma^{-1}\psi(D_\sigma^{-1}R_k)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step is a Gauss–Newton step for the locally weighted residual \(W_k^{1/2}D_\sigma^{-1}(R_k+J_kp)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\rho_i(t)=t^2/2\), \(W_k=I\) and the ordinary scaled Gauss–Newton method is recovered.
immediate_consequences_latex: If all weights are nonnegative, \(B_k\) is positive semidefinite.
Zero weights suppress the corresponding residual rows in the local curvature model.
boundary_notes: Indefinite exact robust Hessian terms involving derivatives of the weights are omitted, as in the Gauss–Newton approximation.
No inspected locator states this combined robust Gauss–Newton construction exactly.

notation.meaning: Diagonal matrix of robust weights evaluated at the current residual.

Other-Norm Residual Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual minimization under an explicitly chosen non-Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual map \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and a norm \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal R}\), minimize \(F(x)=\lVert r(x)\rVert_{\mathcal R}\). At \(x_k\), construct the linearized residual model \(r(x_k)+J_k s\) and compute \(s_k\) as a minimizer of \(\lVert r(x_k)+J_ks\rVert_{\mathcal R}\) over \(\lVert s\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\), or an accuracy-controlled approximation thereof. Accept \(x_k+s_k\) when actual reduction in \(F\) is commensurate with predicted reduction; otherwise reduce \(\Delta_k\). Stop using a norm-appropriate stationarity measure and return the accepted iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a residual norm other than the Euclidean norm by solving norm-matched linearized subproblems within a globalization mechanism.
assumptions_latex: \(r\) is continuously differentiable on an open set containing the iterates.
\(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal R}\) is a specified norm on \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
Each trust-region model subproblem is solved to prescribed accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure defines a derivative-based residual method adapted to \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{\mathcal R}\).

notation.meaning: Residual Jacobian at the current iterate.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is appropriate, but the statement proposes a specific trust-region framework without evidence and leaves the norm-dependent stationarity measure unspecified. In addition, the plain statement excludes the Euclidean norm while the mathematical statement permits any norm. A source is needed to determine and support the intended other-norm variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Minimization in a Non-Euclidean Norm
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be nonsingular, and let \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathsf R}\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional residual minimization using a norm other than the Euclidean norm; smoothness is not assumed for the norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An other-norm residual problem is \[\min_{x\in\mathcal D}\;F_{\mathsf R}(x)=\|D^{-1}R(x)\|_{\mathsf R},\] where \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathsf R}\) is not a positive multiple of \(\|\cdot\|_2\). An other-norm residual method constructs its steps from this objective or an equivalent epigraph formulation and uses subgradients, linear programs, convex programs, or smooth approximations appropriate to the selected norm. The norm, scaling, constraint set, and exact or smoothed interpretation must be fixed as part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Other-norm residual methods minimize the size of a scaled residual vector in a specified norm that is not Euclidean. Their models and optimality objects must match that norm; ordinary least-squares normal equations do not define the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathsf R}(x)=\|D^{-1}R(x)\|_{\mathsf R}\) with \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathsf R}\not\equiv c\|\cdot\|_2\) for every \(c>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any norm, \(\|z\|_{\mathsf R}=\max_{\|u\|_{\mathsf R,*}\leq1}u^Tz\), where \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathsf R,*}\) is the dual norm.
special_cases_latex: For \(\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|\), the problem is least-absolute-residual fitting.
For \(\|z\|_\infty=\max_i|z_i|\), the problem is minimax residual fitting.
immediate_consequences_latex: The \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_\infty\) objectives are generally nonsmooth even when \(R\) is smooth.
boundary_notes: A componentwise robust loss need not be a norm because it may fail positive homogeneity or the triangle inequality.
Squaring a norm preserves minimizers but changes its first-order representation at zero and its model scaling.

notation.meaning: Dual norm of the selected residual norm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative-Free Nonlinear Least-Squares Method
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be available through residual evaluations and define \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional nonlinear least squares in which analytic or automatic residual derivatives are not used by the iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative-free nonlinear least-squares method generates trial points using values \(\{R(y):y\in Y_k\}\) at a finite sample set \(Y_k\), without evaluating \(J(y)\) or derivatives of \(f\). It may construct residual models \(m_{i,k}(p)\) satisfying interpolation or regression conditions at sampled displacements and then use the structured objective model \[q_k(p)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m m_{i,k}(p)^2,\] or it may construct a scalar model of \(f\) directly. Acceptance, sample-set maintenance, and radius control are based solely on evaluated residuals and declared model-quality tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative-free nonlinear least-squares method uses sampled residual values, not evaluated derivatives, to choose steps. A structure-exploiting version models each residual and minimizes the sum of squares of those models; a scalar-model version models the least-squares objective directly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Trial steps depend on sampled values \(R(Y_k)\) and not on evaluated \(J\), with a structured model optionally given by \(q_k(p)=\tfrac12\sum_i m_{i,k}(p)^2\).
special_cases_latex: Finite-difference least squares is derivative-free with respect to the user interface but forms a derivative approximation and is treated as a distinct subfamily.
Residual-interpolation methods are structure-exploiting derivative-free least-squares methods.
immediate_consequences_latex: If each residual model is affine, \(q_k\) is a quadratic sum-of-squares model.
boundary_notes: A method is not derivative-free if it obtains exact Jacobian-vector products from automatic differentiation.
The inspected derivative-free source treats general scalar objectives, not this residual-structured family exactly.

notation.meaning: Finite set of sampled points used at iteration k.
Derivative-free local model of the ith residual component.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local contraction and quadratic convergence of Levenberg–Marquardt
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local error bounds for bounded nonnegative regularization parameters, with quadratic convergence under zero residual and vanishing regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the smooth nonlinear least-squares conditions: f(x)=\tfrac12R(x)^TR(x)\in C^2(D) on an open convex D, J\in\operatorname{Lip}_\gamma(D), \|J(x)\|_2\le\alpha, J(x_*)^TR(x_*)=0, \lambda=\lambda_{\min}(J(x_*)^TJ(x_*)), and \|(J(x)-J(x_*))^TR(x_*)\|_2\le\sigma\|x-x_*\|_2, with \sigma<\lambda. Let 0\le\mu_k\le b. For every c\in(1,(\lambda+b)/(\sigma+b)), some \varepsilon>0 exists such that every x_0\in N(x_*,\varepsilon) generates a well-defined sequence x_{k+1}=x_k-(J(x_k)^TJ(x_k)+\mu_kI)^{-1}J(x_k)^TR(x_k) satisfying \|x_{k+1}-x_*\|_2\le\frac{c(\sigma+b)}{\lambda+b}\|x_k-x_*\|_2+\frac{c\alpha\gamma}{2(\lambda+b)}\|x_k-x_*\|_2^2\le\frac{c(\sigma+b)+(\lambda+b)}{2(\lambda+b)}\|x_k-x_*\|_2<\|x_k-x_*\|_2. If additionally R(x_*)=0 and \mu_k=O(\|J(x_k)^TR(x_k)\|_2), then x_k converges q-quadratically to x_*.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded nonnegative Levenberg–Marquardt regularization and the stated smoothness, stationarity, curvature, and residual-nonlinearity assumptions, every sufficiently close initial point produces a well-defined strictly contracting iteration satisfying the stated error recurrence. At a zero-residual solution, convergence is q-quadratic if the regularization parameters are of the order of the gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: f(x)=\tfrac12R(x)^TR(x)\in C^2(D),\quad D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\text{ open and convex}
R(x_*)=0\text{ and }\mu_k=O(\|J(x_k)^TR(x_k)\|_2)\text{ for the quadratic-convergence conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\varepsilon>0\ \forall x_0\in N(x_*,\varepsilon):\ \text{the Levenberg\text{--}Marquardt sequence is well defined and }\|e_{k+1}\|_2\le\frac{c(\sigma+b)}{\lambda+b}\|e_k\|_2+\frac{c\alpha\gamma}{2(\lambda+b)}\|e_k\|_2^2\le\frac{c(\sigma+b)+(\lambda+b)}{2(\lambda+b)}\|e_k\|_2<\|e_k\|_2;\quad R(x_*)=0,\ \mu_k=O(\|J_k^TR_k\|_2)\Rightarrow x_k\to x_*\text{ q-quadratically}.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Interpolation Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-free least squares using separate interpolation models of residual components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given sampled points \(Y_k\) near \(x_k\), construct for every component \(i\) an interpolation model \(m_{i,k}\) satisfying \(m_{i,k}(y)=r_i(y)\) for designated \(y\in Y_k\). Define \(M_k(s)=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m m_{i,k}(x_k+s)^2\), compute an approximate minimizer \(s_k\) subject to \(\lVert s\rVert_2\le\Delta_k\), and evaluate \(r(x_k+s_k)\). Accept the trial point and update \(\Delta_k\) according to the ratio of actual to predicted least-squares reduction. Update \(Y_k\) to maintain poised interpolation geometry. Stop when the radius and model-gradient tests meet their tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interpolate each residual from sampled values, minimize the induced least-squares trust-region model, and update both the radius and sample geometry.
assumptions_latex: Residual values are available but derivatives need not be available.
The interpolation set is poised for the selected component-model class.
Trial residual evaluations can be obtained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Interpolation Least-Squares Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(Y_k=\{y^0,\ldots,y^s\}\) be sampled points. Let \(\Pi_d^n\) denote scalar polynomials in \(n\) variables of degree at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic derivative-free nonlinear least squares using componentwise polynomial interpolation; regression and underdetermined minimum-change variants require separately declared fitting conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A residual-interpolation model selects \(m_{i,k}\in\Pi_d^n\) for each \(i=1,\ldots,m\) such that \[m_{i,k}(y^j-x_k)=r_i(y^j),\qquad j=0,\ldots,s,\] and forms the structured least-squares model \[q_k(p)=\tfrac12\|m_k(p)\|_2^2=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m m_{i,k}(p)^2.\] A residual-interpolation method computes a step by approximately minimizing \(q_k\) over a declared region, evaluates \(R(x_k+p_k)\), and updates both the sample set and model region according to interpolation-geometry and agreement tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method interpolates every residual component at a common set of sampled points, squares and sums the component models, and chooses a step from that structured model inside a controlled region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_{i,k}(y^j-x_k)=r_i(y^j)\) for all sampled points, and \(q_k(p)=\tfrac12\sum_i m_{i,k}(p)^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For affine residual models \(m_k(p)=c_k+G_kp\), the objective model has Gauss–Newton form \(q_k(p)=\tfrac12\|c_k+G_kp\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: With \(d=1\) and \(n+1\) affinely independent sample points, each residual has a unique affine interpolant.
immediate_consequences_latex: A single residual evaluation at a sample point supplies interpolation data for all \(m\) component models.
boundary_notes: Interpolation geometry must be adequate; the equations need not determine unique models for arbitrary sample sets.
Scalar objective interpolation is not residual interpolation because it need not preserve sum-of-squares structure.

Finite-Difference Least-Squares Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear least squares with a finite-difference approximation to the residual Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F(x)=\tfrac12\lVert r(x)\rVert_2^2\), choose nonzero increments \(h_{k,j}\) and form \((\widehat J_k)_{:,j}=[r(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-r(x_k)]/h_{k,j}\). Compute \(s_k\) from a regularized or trust-region least-squares model, for example by minimizing \(\tfrac12\lVert r(x_k)+\widehat J_ks\rVert_2^2+\tfrac{\mu_k}{2}\lVert s\rVert_2^2\). Accept or damp the step using actual reduction in \(F\), set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\), and adapt the increments to truncation and evaluation error. Stop when a finite-difference first-order measure is below tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate the residual Jacobian by finite differences, solve the resulting least-squares model, globalize the step, and adapt differencing increments.
assumptions_latex: \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is continuously differentiable near the iterates.
All required perturbed residual evaluations are feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure is a finite-difference nonlinear least-squares method with approximate Jacobian \(\widehat J_k\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Difference Nonlinear Least Squares
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(R:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|R(x)\|_2^2\), and let \(e_j\) be the jth coordinate vector. Assume the required perturbed points lie in \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth deterministic residuals evaluated in finite precision; forward and central componentwise Jacobian approximations are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-difference least-squares method replaces the analytic residual Jacobian by a matrix \(A_k\) whose columns are obtained from residual evaluations. The forward formula is \[(A_k)_{:j}=\frac{R(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-R(x_k)}{h_{k,j}},\qquad h_{k,j}\ne0,\] and the central formula is \[(A_k)_{:j}=\frac{R(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-R(x_k-h_{k,j}e_j)}{2h_{k,j}}.\] It then forms a least-squares step from \(R(x_k)+A_kp\), such as \(\min_p\tfrac12\|R(x_k)+A_kp\|_2^2\), with optional damping, bounds, or a trust region. Step sizes may vary by coordinate and must account for scaling and evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method estimates every Jacobian column by perturbing a variable and differencing residual vectors, then uses the approximate Jacobian in a Gauss–Newton, damped, or trust-region least-squares model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A_k)_{:j}=[R(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-R(x_k)]/h_{k,j}\) for forward differences, followed by a step based on \(R(x_k)+A_kp\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The forward approximation uses \(n\) additional residual-vector evaluations when columns are differenced separately.
Central differencing uses two perturbed residual-vector evaluations per coordinate and has higher truncation order for sufficiently smooth residuals.
special_cases_latex: Known Jacobian sparsity may permit simultaneous noninterfering coordinate perturbations.
immediate_consequences_latex: With exact arithmetic and differentiable \(R\), each forward-difference column converges to the corresponding Jacobian column as \(h_{k,j}\to0\).
boundary_notes: Arbitrarily small differences can amplify roundoff or residual-evaluation noise.
Secant updates reusing inter-iterate differences are not identical to fresh coordinate finite differences.

notation.meaning: Finite-difference approximation to the residual Jacobian at x_k.

knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Aware Residual-Model Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-free residual modeling with explicit safeguards against evaluation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose evaluations satisfy \(\widetilde r(x)=r(x)+\varepsilon(x)\) with a known or estimated bound \(\lVert\varepsilon(x)\rVert_2\le\eta(x)\). At \(x_k\), fit residual models from samples whose radii exceed the noise-resolution scale. Compute a trust-region step from the induced least-squares model, but accept it only when predicted and observed reductions exceed prescribed multiples of the corresponding uncertainty bounds. If reduction is unresolved, enlarge sampling increments, resample, or terminate with a noise-limited flag rather than shrinking indefinitely. Output an accepted iterate together with the final stationarity and noise-resolution thresholds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build residual models only at resolvable scales, compare reductions against noise uncertainty, and report when further progress is noise-limited.
assumptions_latex: Observed residuals obey the stated deterministic error bound.
The residual model is fitted from a geometrically adequate sample set.
Acceptance thresholds account for uncertainty in both compared evaluations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure prevents model acceptance and radius refinement from relying on reductions indistinguishable from noise.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noise-Aware Residual Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Suppose evaluations return \(\widetilde R(x)=R(x)+\varepsilon(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), with a declared componentwise or normwise bound \(\|\varepsilon(x)\|\leq\delta(x)\). Let \(m_k(p)\) be a local model built from noisy samples.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic bounded evaluation error in residual values; stochastic-noise methods require probabilistic accuracy conditions instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A noise-aware residual-model method is a residual-based iteration whose model construction and acceptance tests explicitly use an error scale \(\delta\). Its interpolation or regression conditions are relaxed to consistency conditions such as \[\|m_k(y-x_k)-\widetilde R(y)\|\leq c\,\delta(y),\qquad y\in Y_k,\] and a trial step is accepted as producing resolved decrease only when the observed change in the merit function exceeds a declared multiple of the uncertainty induced by the noisy residual evaluations. Model radii, difference intervals, and termination tolerances are not reduced below declared noise-dependent floors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noise-aware residual-model method represents residual evaluations as true values plus bounded error, fits models only to the accuracy justified by that error, and refuses to interpret changes smaller than the induced uncertainty as reliable progress.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model fitting satisfies a noise-scaled consistency condition and step acceptance requires observed reduction larger than a declared uncertainty threshold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonlinear Equation Method Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\). A root is \(x_*\in\mathcal D\) satisfying \(F(x_*)=0\). When \(F\) is differentiable, write \(J(x)=F'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square finite-dimensional nonlinear systems; rectangular systems and least-squares stationarity are outside the canonical root-finding form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonlinear equation method is an iteration \[x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\] whose defining local equation, fixed-point map, secant condition, continuation equation, or residual model is constructed with the primary destination \(F(x)=0\). The nonlinear equation method families include exact or inexact Newton methods based on \(F(x_k)+J(x_k)s\), secant or quasi-Newton methods replacing \(J(x_k)\), fixed-point iterations \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\) with \(F(x)=0\iff G(x)=x\), higher-order residual models, and continuation methods tracking solutions of \(H(x,t)=0\) toward \(H(x,1)=F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonlinear equation methods seek an actual root of a square residual map. Their step equations or maps are built to make the residual zero, unlike generic minimization of a residual norm, which may stop at a nonzero stationary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solution set targeted by the family is \(F^{-1}(0)=\{x\in\mathcal D:F(x)=0\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(G:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\) satisfies \(F(x)=0\iff G(x)=x\), root finding is equivalently fixed-point computation.
special_cases_latex: For \(F=\nabla f\), a nonlinear equation method targets stationary points of \(f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every root globally minimizes \(\tfrac12\|F(x)\|_2^2\) with value zero, but a stationary point of that merit function need not be a root.
boundary_notes: The definition does not guarantee existence, uniqueness, or convergence to a root.
Methods whose sole stated destination is an arbitrary stationary point of \(\tfrac12\|F\|^2\) are not placed in this family.

notation.meaning: Set of roots of the nonlinear system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong and strongly Lipschitz stable stationary points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a fixed smooth parameterization and uniformly over all such parameterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_0$ be stationary for $(P_0)$ and let $(f(x,u),G(x,u))$ be a $C^2$-smooth parameterization at $u_0$. The point $x_0$ is strongly stable (respectively, strongly Lipschitz stable) with respect to this parameterization if there are neighborhoods $\mathcal V_X$ of $x_0$ and $\mathcal V_U$ of $u_0$ such that every $u\in\mathcal V_U$ yields a unique stationary point $\bar x(u)\in\mathcal V_X$, and $u\mapsto\bar x(u)$ is continuous (respectively, Lipschitz continuous) on $\mathcal V_U$. It is strongly stable (respectively, strongly Lipschitz stable) without qualification if this holds for every $C^2$-smooth parameterization of $(P_0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point is strongly stable relative to a smooth parameterization when every nearby parameter has one nearby stationary point depending continuously on the parameter; strong Lipschitz stability requires Lipschitz dependence. The unqualified notions require this property for every twice continuously differentiable parameterization.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is a stationary point of }(P_0)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,\mathcal V_X,\mathcal V_U\ \forall u\in\mathcal V_U:\ \exists!\,\bar x(u)\in\mathcal V_X\text{ stationary for }(P_u),\quad u\mapsto\bar x(u)\text{ is continuous (respectively Lipschitz)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong regularity is equivalent to strong stability under conic reducibility and nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional constraint-image space with a locally pointed-conic reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_0$ be a locally optimal solution of $(P_0)$ and let $\lambda_0$ be a corresponding Lagrange multiplier. Suppose $Y$ is finite dimensional, $K$ is $C^2$-reducible at $G(x_0)$ to a pointed closed convex cone, and $x_0$ is nondegenerate with respect to that reduction. Then $(x_0,\lambda_0)$ is a strongly regular solution of the generalized equations (5.47) if and only if $x_0$ is a strongly stable point of $(P_0)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a local solution with a multiplier, finite-dimensional constraint-image space, a twice-smooth reduction to a pointed closed convex cone, and reduction nondegeneracy, strong regularity of the primal-dual generalized equation is equivalent to strong stability of the optimization problem.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_0,\lambda_0)\text{ strongly solves generalized equations (5.47) regularly}\iff x_0\text{ is strongly stable for }(P_0)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative classification of scalar fixed points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local behavior of scalar functional iteration near a differentiable fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f(x_\infty)=x_\infty and suppose f is differentiable at x_\infty. The fixed point is called attractive when |f'(x_\infty)|<1 and repelling when |f'(x_\infty)|>1. If an orbit x_n=f(x_{n-1}) converges to x_\infty without reaching it in finitely many steps, then -1<f'(x_\infty)<0 implies eventual alternation across x_\infty, whereas 0<f'(x_\infty)<1 implies eventual monotone convergence toward x_\infty. If |f'(x_\infty)|>1, then |f(x)-x_\infty|>|x-x_\infty| for every sufficiently close x\neq x_\infty. The boundary case |f'(x_\infty)|=1 is inconclusive under this derivative test alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Derivative magnitude below one classifies a fixed point as attractive, while magnitude above one classifies it as repelling. A convergent nonterminating orbit eventually alternates sides for a negative derivative between minus one and zero and converges monotonically for a positive derivative below one. Magnitude exactly one gives no definitive classification.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the oscillation and monotonicity claims, }x_n\to x_\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |f'(x_\infty)|<1\Rightarrow x_\infty\text{ is attractive};\quad -1<f'(x_\infty)<0\Rightarrow\text{eventual alternation for nonterminating convergent orbits};\quad 0<f'(x_\infty)<1\Rightarrow\text{eventual monotone convergence};\quad |f'(x_\infty)|>1\Rightarrow x_\infty\text{ is repelling};\quad |f'(x_\infty)|=1\Rightarrow\text{the test is inconclusive}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compact interpolatory tensor model and safeguarded step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An algorithmic representation for square nonlinear residual systems; it does not assert a convergence rate or guarantee for degenerate roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) have Jacobian \(J\), let \(q\ge 1\), and set \(s_{jk}=x_{k-j}-x_k\). Define
\[
\widehat M_k(p)=r(x_k)+J(x_k)p+\tfrac12T_kpp,
\qquad
T_kuv=\sum_{\ell=1}^q a_\ell(s_{\ell k}^Tu)(s_{\ell k}^Tv).
\]
If the vectors \(a_\ell\in\mathbb{R}^n\) are chosen so that
\[
\tfrac12T_ks_{jk}s_{jk}=r(x_{k-j})-r(x_k)-J(x_k)s_{jk},
\qquad j=1,\ldots,q,
\]
then
\[
\widehat M_k(s_{jk})=r(x_{k-j}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,q.
\]
The representation stores the \(2q\) vectors \(\{a_\ell,s_{\ell k}\}_{\ell=1}^q\), requiring \(2nq\) scalar locations. If \(\widehat M_k(p)=0\) has no solution, the method may instead choose a minimizer of \(\|\widehat M_k(p)\|_2^2\). If this step is not a descent direction for \(\phi(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2\), it may be replaced, when \(J(x_k)\) is nonsingular, by \(-J(x_k)^{-1}r(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a square nonlinear residual system, the tensor method augments the Newton model with a quadratic tensor term. A compact representation based on previous displacements can be selected to interpolate residual values at retained iterates and uses 2nq scalar storage locations. The tensor-model equation need not have a root; in that case the method may minimize the squared model residual. A resulting non-descent step may be replaced by the Newton step when the Jacobian is nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: a_1,\ldots,a_q\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ satisfy the stated interpolation equations}
J(x_k)\text{ is nonsingular if the Newton fallback is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat M_k(s_{jk})=r(x_{k-j})\ (j=1,\ldots,q),\qquad \operatorname{storage}(T_k)=2nq;\quad \widehat M_k(p)=0\text{ may be unsolvable, in which case }p\in\arg\min_z\|\widehat M_k(z)\|_2^2\text{ may be used and, if non-descent, replaced by }-J(x_k)^{-1}r(x_k).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniqueness and existence for a contraction self-map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The existence conclusion requires a nonempty closed domain; closedness alone permits the empty-set counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(B:\mathcal X\to\mathcal X\). Suppose that for some vector norm and \(\alpha\in[0,1)\), \(\|B(x)-B(y)\|\leq\alpha\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathcal X\). Then \(B\) has at most one fixed point. If, additionally, \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty and closed, then \(B\) has a unique fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction self-map has at most one fixed point. On a nonempty closed subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space, it has exactly one fixed point.
assumptions_latex: There exist a vector norm and \(\alpha\in[0,1)\) such that \(\|B(x)-B(y)\|\leq\alpha\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in\mathcal X\).
For the existence conclusion, \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty and closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\) has at most one fixed point; if \(\mathcal X\) is nonempty and closed, then \(B\) has a unique fixed point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local linear convergence from a stable linearization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral-radius criterion for local linear convergence of a differentiable fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $x^{k+1}=g(x^k)$, let $x^*$ satisfy $g(x^*)=x^*$, and suppose $g$ is differentiable at $x^*$. Set $\rho=\rho(g'(x^*))$ and assume $\rho<1$. For every $\varepsilon$ with $0<\varepsilon<1-\rho$, there exist $\delta>0$ and $c>0$ such that
\[
\|x^k-x^*\|\le c(\rho+\varepsilon)^k\qquad\forall k\ge0
\]
whenever $\|x^0-x^*\|\le\delta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the derivative of a fixed-point mapping has spectral radius below one at the fixed point, then every sufficiently close initial point converges linearly, with any geometric factor strictly between that spectral radius and one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ostrowski Local Attraction Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative spectral-radius criterion for local attraction of a differentiable fixed-point iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^p$ satisfy $G(z^*)=z^*$ and be continuously differentiable on an open set containing $z^*$. If every eigenvalue of $\nabla G(z^*)^{\prime}$ lies strictly inside the complex unit circle, then $z^*$ is a point of attraction of the iteration $z_{k+1}=G(z_k)$. Moreover, whenever a generated sequence converges to $z^*$, the convergence rate of $\{\lVert z_k-z^*\rVert\}$ is at least linear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a continuously differentiable fixed-point map has a fixed point whose Jacobian transpose has all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle, that fixed point is locally attracting. Any generated sequence converging to it has an error-norm sequence whose convergence rate is at least linear.
assumptions_latex: G\in C^1(U)\text{ for some open }U\ni z^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^*\text{ is a point of attraction of }z_{k+1}=G(z_k);\quad z_k\to z^*\implies \{\lVert z_k-z^*\rVert\}\text{ has convergence rate at least linear}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A two-cycle for unit-step Newton iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded global-failure boundary for unsafeguarded Newton and Broyden root-finding, with an explicit Newton two-cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Unit-step Newton and Broyden iterations, when defined, have no general convergence guarantee from arbitrary starting points and may exhibit blow-up or cycling. In particular, for r(x)=-x^5+x^3+4x, unit-step Newton iteration from x_0=1 satisfies x_{2k}=1 and x_{2k+1}=-1 for all k\ge 0, while r(1)=4 and r(-1)=-4.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unsafeguarded unit-step Newton and Broyden iterations are not globally convergent in general. For the scalar residual minus x to the fifth plus x cubed plus four x, Newton's method started at 1 alternates forever between 1 and -1, neither of which is a root.
assumptions_latex: \text{The unit-step Newton or Broyden iteration is defined at each iterate under consideration.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\Omega\supset\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on the open set \(\Omega\), let \(T\) be a linear Newton approximation scheme for \(\mathbf F_{\mathrm{FB}}\), and let the infinite sequence \(\{x^k\}\) be generated by Algorithm 9.1.42. Every limit point is stationary for problem (9.1.53). If a limit point \(x^*\) solves \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\) and \(T(x^*)\) is nonsingular, then the whole sequence converges to \(x^*\), and the convergence rate is Q-superlinear. If, additionally, \(T\) is strong at \(x^*\) and \(\rho(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))=O(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))\) for all \(x\) sufficiently near \(x^*\), then the convergence rate is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every limit point of the infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 9.1.42 is stationary for the associated merit problem. If a limit point solves the NCP and the linear Newton approximation is nonsingular there, the entire sequence converges to that point and does so Q-superlinearly. The rate is Q-quadratic when the approximation scheme is also strong and the stated local residual condition holds.
assumptions_latex: F:\Omega\supset\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuously differentiable on the open set }\Omega
T\text{ is a linear Newton approximation scheme for }\mathbf F_{\mathrm{FB}}
\{x^k\}\text{ is an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 9.1.42
x^*\text{ is a limit point satisfying }x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(\operatorname{NCP}(F))\text{ and }T(x^*)\text{ is nonsingular}
\text{For Q-quadratic convergence, }T\text{ is strong at }x^*\text{ and }\rho(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))=O(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))\text{ for all }x\text{ sufficiently near }x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{limpts}(\{x^k\})\subseteq\operatorname{stat}(9.1.53);\quad x^*\in\operatorname{SOL}(\operatorname{NCP}(F)),\ T(x^*)\text{ nonsingular}\Rightarrow x^k\to x^*\text{ Q-superlinearly};\quad T\text{ strong at }x^*,\ \rho(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))=O(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}(x))\text{ locally}\Rightarrow\text{ Q-quadratic convergence.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trust-region algorithm for nonlinear equations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance and radius-update framework using a linearized residual trust-region subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given $\bar\Delta>0$, $\Delta_0\in(0,\bar\Delta)$, and $\eta\in[0,\tfrac14)$, for $k=0,1,\ldots$ compute an approximate solution $p_k$ of
\[
\min_{\|p\|\leq\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2
\]
and evaluate
\[
\rho_k=\frac{\|r_k\|^2-\|r(x_k+p_k)\|^2}{\|r_k\|^2-\|r_k+J_kp_k\|^2}.
\]
Set
\[
\Delta_{k+1}=\begin{cases}
\tfrac14\|p_k\|,&\rho_k<\tfrac14,\\
\min\{2\Delta_k,\bar\Delta\},&\rho_k>\tfrac34\text{ and }\|p_k\|=\Delta_k,\\
\Delta_k,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad
x_{k+1}=\begin{cases}x_k+p_k,&\rho_k>\eta,\\x_k,&\rho_k\leq\eta.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximately minimize the linearized residual model within the current trust region. Shrink the radius when agreement is below one quarter, double it up to the prescribed maximum when agreement exceeds three quarters and the step reaches the boundary, and otherwise retain it. Accept the step exactly when the agreement ratio is strictly greater than eta.
assumptions_latex: p_k\text{ approximately solves the stated residual trust-region subproblem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_{k+1},\Delta_{k+1})\text{ is determined by the displayed acceptance and radius-update rules for every }k\geq0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction theorem for functional iteration on a closed interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, convergence from every point in the interval, and a geometric error estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I\subseteq\mathbb{R} be a closed interval and let f:I\to I satisfy |f(y)-f(x)|\leq\lambda|y-x| for all x,y\in I, where 0\leq\lambda<1. Then f has a unique fixed point x_\infty\in I. For every x_0\in I, the iterates x_n=f(x_{n-1}) converge to x_\infty and satisfy |x_n-x_\infty|\leq\frac{\lambda^n}{1-\lambda}|x_1-x_0| for n\geq0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction mapping of a closed real interval into itself has a unique fixed point. Iteration converges to it from every starting point in the interval, with the stated geometric error bound.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional sequence convergence and eventual trust-region behavior for Algorithm BTR applied to the stated nonlinear residual problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathrm{AC.1e}\), \(\mathrm{AC.3e}\), \(\mathrm{AN.1}\), \(\mathrm{AM.1e}\text{--}\mathrm{AM.4e}\), and \(\mathrm{AA.1}\) hold. Let \(\{x_k\}\) be generated by Algorithm \(\mathrm{BTR}\) applied to problem (16.1.2), and suppose it has a limit point \(x_*\) satisfying \(c(x_*)=0\). Assume either that the Gauss--Newton model (16.1.6) is used or that \(\mathrm{AM.5e}\) holds, and suppose \(A(x_*)\) has full rank. Then the complete sequence satisfies \(x_k\to x_*\), every sufficiently large iteration is successful, and \(\Delta_k\) is bounded away from zero. In the square case, every sufficiently late trust region contains a root of the residual model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed points and standard convergence orders
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology for an iteration $x^{k+1}=g(x^k)$ and a nonnegative measure of closeness $u_k$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $x^{k+1}=g(x^k)$ with $g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$, a point $x^*$ is a fixed point if $g(x^*)=x^*$; if $x^k=x^*$, then $x^s=x^*$ for every $s\ge k$. Linear convergence means convergence at a geometric-progression rate, superlinear convergence means convergence faster than every geometric progression, and quadratic convergence refers to a process satisfying an estimate $u_{k+1}\le c u_k^2$, where $u_k$ measures closeness to the solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed point is unchanged by the iteration map, and an iteration that reaches it remains there. Linear convergence has a geometric rate, superlinear convergence is faster than every geometric progression, and quadratic convergence satisfies an error estimate of the form u(k+1) at most c times u(k) squared.
assumptions_latex: u_k\ge0\text{ measures closeness to the solution}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(x^*)=x^*\implies\bigl(x^k=x^*\Rightarrow x^s=x^*\ \forall s\ge k\bigr),\qquad u_{k+1}\le c u_k^2\text{ is the stated quadratic-rate estimate}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularized residual trust-region steps and sufficient inexact-step safeguards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual trust-region step representation, Levenberg–Marquardt interpretation, inexact-step requirements, and an LP-representable alternative residual model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For
\[
\min_{\|p\|\leq\Delta_k}\tfrac12\|r_k+J_kp\|_2^2,
\]
an exact solution admits the representation
\[
p_k=-(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)^{-1}J_k^Tr_k
\]
for some $\lambda_k\geq0$ whenever the displayed inverse exists. If the unconstrained step $p_k^{\mathrm J}$ exists and satisfies $\|p_k^{\mathrm J}\|\leq\Delta_k$, then $\lambda_k=0$. This is the residual trust-region form associated with Levenberg--Marquardt regularization.

Exact recovery of the trust-region parameter is unnecessary for the cited global-convergence framework when the computed regularized steps satisfy, for iteration-independent constants $c_1>0$ and $\gamma\geq1$,
\[
m_k(0)-m_k(p_k)\geq c_1\|J_k^Tr_k\|\min\left\{\Delta_k,\frac{\|J_k^Tr_k\|}{\|J_k^TJ_k\|}\right\},
\qquad \|p_k\|\leq\gamma\Delta_k.
\]
An alternative residual model using an $\ell_1$ merit function and an $\ell_\infty$ trust region is
\[
\min_p\|J_kp+r_k\|_1\quad\text{subject to}\quad\|p\|_\infty\leq\Delta,
\]
and this subproblem is representable as a linear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact Euclidean residual trust-region step has a Levenberg–Marquardt regularized Gauss–Newton form with a nonnegative parameter, which is zero when the unconstrained step exists and is feasible. Exact parameter recovery is unnecessary for the cited global-convergence framework if the computed steps uniformly achieve Cauchy-type decrease and obey the stated enlarged-radius bound. With an l1 residual objective and an l-infinity trust region, the residual subproblem can instead be formulated as a linear program.
assumptions_latex: J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI\text{ is invertible whenever the displayed inverse representation is used}
p_k^{\mathrm J}\text{ exists for the stated feasible-unconstrained-step implication}
c_1>0\text{ and }\gamma\geq1\text{ are independent of }k\text{ for the inexact-step guarantee}
p_k\text{ is generated and accepted within the stated residual trust-region framework}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k=-(J_k^TJ_k+\lambda_kI)^{-1}J_k^Tr_k,\ \lambda_k\geq0;\quad \|p_k^{\mathrm J}\|\leq\Delta_k\Rightarrow\lambda_k=0;\quad \text{the displayed decrease and norm conditions are sufficient step hypotheses for the cited global-convergence results; and the }\ell_1/\ell_\infty\text{ subproblem is LP-representable}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unit tangent characterization of an arclength-parameterized zero path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies at a regular point of a continuously differentiable homotopy zero path; orientation by comparison with the preceding tangent is a practical sign-selection heuristic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let H be continuously differentiable near a path (x(s),\lambda(s)) satisfying H(x(s),\lambda(s))=0 and (x(0),\lambda(0))=(a,0), with s denoting arc length. Then H_x(x,\lambda)\dot{x}+H_\lambda(x,\lambda)\dot{\lambda}=0 and \|\dot{x}\|_2^2+|\dot{\lambda}|^2=1. If [H_x\;H_\lambda]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n+1)} has full row rank n, its null space is one-dimensional, so the unit tangent is determined up to sign. A consistent orientation may be selected by requiring an acute angle with the preceding tangent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiating the zero-path equation places the path tangent in the null space of the augmented homotopy derivative. At a full-row-rank point that null space is one-dimensional; unit normalization gives an arclength tangent up to sign, and comparison with the preceding tangent supplies a practical orientation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The quantities $\sigma(x^k,d^k)$, condition $(\mathrm{BD}_\theta)$, and Algorithm 8.3.2 retain their source-defined meanings.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order perturbation asymptotics under nonempty multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional perturbation of a nonlinear program at a uniquely optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose $(P_{u_0})$ has the unique optimal solution $x_0$, Gollan's condition holds in direction $d$, $\Lambda(x_0,u_0)\neq\varnothing$, the sufficient second-order conditions (5.107) hold, and for every sufficiently small $t>0$ the feasible set of $(P_{u(t)})$ is nonempty and uniformly bounded. Then every $o(t)$-optimal solution $\bar x(t)$ satisfies $\|\bar x(t)-x_0\|=O(t^{1/2})$ and
\[v(u(t))=v(u_0)+\tfrac12t\,\operatorname{val}(\mathcal{PQ}^2)+o(t).\]
Every limit point of $t^{-1/2}(\bar x(t)-x_0)$ solves $(\mathcal{PQ}^2)$; conversely, for every solution $h$ of $(\mathcal{PQ}^2)$ there is an $o(t)$-optimal path $x(t)=x_0+t^{1/2}h+o(t^{1/2})$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the unperturbed nonlinear program has a unique optimum, Gollan's directional condition and the stated sufficient second-order conditions hold, its multiplier set is nonempty, and nearby feasible sets are nonempty and uniformly bounded, then all sufficiently accurate perturbed solutions are one-half Hölder stable. The value has the stated order-t expansion, scaled solution displacements can accumulate only at solutions of the second-order auxiliary problem, and every such auxiliary solution generates a matching near-optimal path.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is the unique optimal solution of }(P_{u_0})
\forall t>0\text{ sufficiently small, }\operatorname{feas}(P_{u(t)})\neq\varnothing\text{ and is uniformly bounded}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Min-Based Line-Search Algorithm (minLSA)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible line-search scheme based on a convex quadratic direction subproblem and the minimum-function merit measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x^0\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), at iteration \(k\) choose an optimal solution \(d^k\) of \(\min_d\phi(x^k,d)\) subject to \(x^k+d\ge 0\). Stop if \(d^k=0\). Otherwise choose the smallest \(i_k\in\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying \[\theta_{\min}(x^k+2^{-i_k}d^k)\le \theta_{\min}(x^k)-\gamma 2^{-i_k}\sigma(x^k,d^k),\] set \(\tau_k=2^{-i_k}\), and update \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\tau_kd^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from a nonnegative point, solve the prescribed convex quadratic direction problem under nonnegativity of the trial point. Stop at a zero direction; otherwise backtrack over dyadic step sizes until the stated minimum-merit decrease test holds, then update the iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^{k+1}=x^k+2^{-i_k}d^k\quad\text{for the least }i_k\ge0\text{ satisfying the stated line-search inequality, unless }d^k=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered stopping conditions for nonlinear-equation iterations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A prioritized termination dispatcher with diagnostic codes and explicit warnings against interpreting every termination as successful root finding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mathrm{termcode}=0\). In order, assign code \(3\) when \(\mathrm{retcode}=1\); code \(1\) when \(\max_i S_{F,i}|F_i(x_+)|\leq\mathrm{fvectol}\); code \(2\) when \(\max_i |x_{+,i}-x_{c,i}|/\max\{|x_{+,i}|,1/S_{x,i}\}\leq\mathrm{steptol}\); or code \(4\) when \(\mathrm{itncount}\geq\mathrm{itnlimit}\). Otherwise, if a maximum-length step was taken, increment \(\mathrm{consecmax}\) and assign code \(5\) when it reaches five. If no maximum-length step was taken, reset \(\mathrm{consecmax}=0\) and, only when an analytic Jacobian is used or function evaluation is cheap, assign code \(6\) when the prescribed normalized scaled residual-merit gradient test is at most \(\mathrm{mintol}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the tests in the stated priority order and return zero if none succeeds. Code 1 indicates a small scaled residual, subject to the tolerance not being too large. Code 2 can instead reflect slow progress or an excessive step tolerance. Code 3 can reflect limited attainable accuracy, a faulty analytic Jacobian, an inaccurate secant Jacobian, or an excessive step tolerance. Code 5 can indicate residual asymptoting or an undersized maximum step. Code 6 indicates an apparent local minimizer of the residual norm that is not a root and suggests restarting elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: n\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\quad x_c,x_+\in\mathbb R^n,\quad F_+=F(x_+)\in\mathbb R^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{termcode}\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6\}\text{ records the first satisfied condition, and }\mathrm{consecmax}\text{ is updated as specified.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing forcing values along a bounded-below subsequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A subsequential convergence consequence for the abstract nonsmooth Armijo algorithm under the line-search consistency condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex, let $\theta$ be locally Lipschitz on $X$, and let $\{x^k\}\subset X$ be an infinite sequence generated by the abstract line-search algorithm with directions $d^k$ and forcing values $\sigma(x^k,d^k)$. Let $\kappa$ index a subsequence. Assume $\{\theta(x^k):k\in\kappa\}$ is bounded below and that, for every positive sequence $t_k\to0$ with $k\in\kappa$, $$\limsup_{k\in\kappa,\,k\to\infty}\frac{\theta(x^k+t_kd^k)-\theta(x^k)+t_k\sigma(x^k,d^k)}{t_k}\le0.$$ Then $$\lim_{k\in\kappa,\,k\to\infty}\sigma(x^k,d^k)=0.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along any subsequence on which the objective values are bounded below, if every vanishing positive step sequence satisfies the stated line-search consistency inequality, then the forcing values converge to zero along that subsequence.
assumptions_latex: \{x^k\}\subset X\text{ is an infinite sequence generated by the line-search algorithm}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior-point sequential unconstrained minimization technique
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a barrier transformation and warm-started sequence of local minimization subproblems for inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let R^0=\{x\mid g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\} and R=\{x\mid g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}. Suppose I:R^0\to\mathbb R is continuous and I(x^k)\to+\infty whenever x^k\in R^0 converges to a boundary point x_B with g_i(x_B)=0 for some i. Let s:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) be strictly increasing and satisfy s(r_k)\to0 whenever r_k\to0. An interior-point sequential unconstrained minimization technique chooses x^0\in R^0 and a strictly decreasing positive sequence \{r_k\}, defines U(x,r_k)=f(x)+s(r_k)I(x), and, for each k, finds a local minimizer x(r_k) of U(\cdot,r_k) over R, using x(r_{k-1}) as the next starting point. The barrier behavior places each finite-valued local minimizer in R^0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let the strict feasible region consist of points satisfying every inequality strictly. The barrier is continuous there and diverges to positive infinity along every interior sequence approaching a constraint boundary. Its positive weight decreases to zero with the parameter. Starting from a strictly feasible point, the method minimizes the objective plus the weighted barrier locally for a strictly decreasing sequence of positive parameters, warm-starting each subproblem from the preceding local minimizer; finite-valued subproblem minimizers lie in the strict interior.
assumptions_latex: R^0=\{x\mid g_i(x)>0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\},\quad R=\{x\mid g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}
x^k\in R^0,\ x^k\to x_B,\ (\exists i)\ g_i(x_B)=0\implies I(x^k)\to+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: U(x,r_k)=f(x)+s(r_k)I(x),\qquad x(r_k)\in\operatorname{locmin}_{x\in R}U(x,r_k),\quad x(r_k)\in R^0,\text{ with }x(r_{k-1})\text{ used to initialize subproblem }k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global and local convergence of Algorithm 9.1.39 for an NCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantees for the specified equation-based nonlinear-complementarity algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\Omega\supset\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on the open set \(\Omega\), and let \(\{x^k\}\) be generated by Algorithm 9.1.39. Every accumulation point is stationary for problem (9.1.53), and every such point that is FB-regular solves \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\). If the sequence has an isolated accumulation point, the whole sequence converges to it. If a limit point \(x^*\) is a strongly stable solution of \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\), then \(x^k\to x^*\). Moreover, when \(p>2\) and \(\gamma<\tfrac12\), eventually \(d^k\) solves \(\operatorname{LCP}(q^k,JF(x^k))\), unit steps are accepted so that \(x^{k+1}=x^k+d^k\), and convergence is superlinear; it is quadratic if \(JF\) is Lipschitz continuous at \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For continuously differentiable F, every accumulation point produced by Algorithm 9.1.39 is stationary for the associated merit problem, and an FB-regular one solves the NCP. An isolated accumulation point attracts the whole sequence. A strongly stable NCP solution that is a limit point also attracts the whole sequence; when p > 2 and gamma < 1/2, the method eventually takes LCP directions and full steps, converges superlinearly, and converges quadratically if the Jacobian is Lipschitz at the solution.
assumptions_latex: F:\Omega\supset\mathbb{R}_+^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is continuously differentiable on the open set }\Omega
\text{For the local conclusions, }x^*\text{ is a limit point and a strongly stable solution of }\operatorname{NCP}(F)
\text{For quadratic convergence, }JF\text{ is Lipschitz continuous at }x^*

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MCP Functions and Their Scaling Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines interval MCP functions, their induced system reformulation, the projection-based example, and two invariance transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an interval \([\alpha,\beta]\), allowing infinite endpoints, an MCP function is a map \(\phi_{[\alpha,\beta]}:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\phi_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x_1,x_2)=0\iff \alpha\le x_1\le\beta,\quad (x_1-\alpha)x_2\le0,\quad (x_1-\beta)x_2\le0,\] with the usual one-sided interpretations at infinite endpoints. Consequently, a box MCP is equivalent to \(\phi_{[a_i,b_i]}(u_i,F_i(u))=0\) for all \(i\). The projection residual \[\phi^E_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x_1,x_2)=x_1-P_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x_1-x_2)\] is an MCP function. If \(\sigma>0\), then \((x_1,x_2)\mapsto\phi_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x_1,\sigma x_2)\) is also an MCP function. If \(\phi_{[0,1]}\) is an MCP function and \(-\infty<\alpha<\beta<\infty\), then \[(x_1,x_2)\mapsto\phi_{[0,1]}\!\left(\frac{x_1-\alpha}{\beta-\alpha},x_2\right)\] is an MCP function for \([\alpha,\beta]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An MCP function is a scalar function whose zeros exactly encode the interval complementarity conditions. Applying it componentwise converts a box MCP into equations. The projection residual is one such function, and positive scaling of the complementarity variable or affine normalization of a finite interval preserves the defining zero set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_{[\alpha,\beta]}(x)=0\iff x\text{ satisfies the interval complementarity conditions}

Let $A\in\mathbb{C}^{n\times n}$ be stable, meaning that every eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i<0$. If $B=I+\gamma A$ and
\[
0<\gamma<\min_i\frac{-2\operatorname{Re}\lambda_i}{|\lambda_i|^2},
\]
then $\rho(B)<1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every eigenvalue of A has negative real part, then B = I + gamma A has spectral radius below one for every positive gamma below the stated eigenvalue-dependent bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homotopy tangent calculation by column-pivoted QR factorization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Requires full row rank so that the triangular factor is nonsingular; sign continuity additionally requires a preceding oriented tangent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A=[H_x(x,\lambda)\;H_\lambda(x,\lambda)]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n+1)} have rank n. Compute Q^TA\Pi=[R\;w], where Q\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is orthogonal, R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} is nonsingular upper triangular, \Pi\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+1)\times(n+1)} is a permutation matrix, and w\in\mathbb{R}^n. Set v=\Pi\begin{bmatrix}R^{-1}w\\-1\end{bmatrix}. Then Av=0. Set (\dot{x},\dot{\lambda})=\pm v/\|v\|_2, choosing the sign to make an acute angle with the preceding tangent when orientation continuity is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Column-pivoted QR reduces the augmented homotopy derivative to a triangular system and yields an explicit null vector. Normalizing that vector gives the unit path tangent, whose sign can be selected consistently with the previous tangent.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuation method for a nonlinear system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the continuation framework without asserting that a solution path always exists, remains regular, or can always be tracked successfully.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuation (homotopy) method for F(x)=0 introduces a parameterized system H(x,t)=0, t\in[0,1], such that H(x,0)=G(x) is an easily solved system and H(x,1)=F(x) is the target system. Starting from a known x(0) satisfying G(x(0))=0, the method attempts to track solutions x(t) satisfying H(x(t),t)=0 toward t=1, with the aim of obtaining F(x(1))=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuation or homotopy method continuously transforms an easily solved nonlinear system into the target system. Beginning at a known root of the easy system, it attempts to track a path of roots to the target endpoint. The description does not guarantee that such a path exists or can be followed successfully.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(x(t),t)=0\text{ is tracked from }t=0\text{ toward }t=1,\text{ aiming to obtain }F(x(1))=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be differentiable and f(x)=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2. At iteration k, choose p_k satisfying J(x_k)p_k=-r(x_k). If r(x_k)\ne0, then p_k^T\nabla f(x_k)=-\|r(x_k)\|_2^2<0. Choose a line-search step length \alpha_k, possibly satisfying the Wolfe conditions, and set x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the Newton residual equation, select a line-search step length, and update along the Newton direction. Whenever such a step is defined and the residual is nonzero, it is a strict descent direction for the squared-residual merit function. Wolfe conditions are an admissible step-selection interface, but this extract does not state the subsequent convergence theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moré-style Levenberg–Marquardt step and radius update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract specifies one iteration but does not state initialization or a radius update for cases not covered by the displayed branches; the overlapping boundary at \rho_k=1/4 is retained as written.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \sigma\in(0,1). If \|D_kJ_k^{-}r_k\|\le(1+\sigma)\Delta_k, set \mu_k=0 and s_k=-J_k^{-}r_k. Otherwise choose \mu_k>0 so that s_k solves \min_s\left\|\begin{bmatrix}J_k\\ \mu_k^{1/2}D_k\end{bmatrix}s+\begin{bmatrix}r_k\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\| and satisfies (1-\sigma)\Delta_k\le\|D_ks_k\|\le(1+\sigma)\Delta_k. Compute the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio \rho_k. If \rho_k\le10^{-4}, set x_{k+1}=x_k and J_{k+1}=J_k; if \rho_k>10^{-4}, set x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k and recompute J_{k+1}. If \rho_k\le1/4, choose \Delta_{k+1}\in[\Delta_k/10,\Delta_k/2]. If ([\rho_k\in[1/4,1/3]\ \text{and}\ \mu_k=0]\ \text{or}\ \rho_k\ge3/4), set \Delta_{k+1}=2\|D_ks_k\|. Finally update D_k by the monotone diagonal rule d_i^{(k+1)}=\max\{d_i^{(k)},\|\partial_i r(x_{k+1})\|\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose either the generalized Gauss–Newton step when it lies within the scaled radius tolerance or a regularized least-squares step whose scaled norm is close to the radius. Accept the step only when the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio exceeds 0.0001, update the radius by the stated ratio tests, and then update the diagonal scaling using the largest residual-Jacobian column norms observed so far.
assumptions_latex: J_k^{-}\text{ denotes the generalized inverse used by the algorithm}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_k,s_k,x_{k+1},J_{k+1},\Delta_{k+1},D_{k+1})\text{ are selected by the stated regularized least-squares, acceptance, radius, and scaling rules}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity of a Strongly F-Differentiable Subsequence Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convergence guarantee for Algorithm 8.3.6 and problem (8.2.1), whose definitions remain external to the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be closed and convex, let $\theta$ be B-differentiable on $X$, and let $\{x^k\}\subset X$ be an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 8.3.6. Suppose an infinite $\kappa\subseteq\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ satisfies: there are $c_1,c_2>0$ such that $c_1y^Ty\le y^TH^ky\le c_2y^Ty$ for every $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $k\in\kappa$; $x^k\to x^*$ as $k\in\kappa$ tends to infinity; and $\theta$ has a strong F-derivative at $x^*$. Then $x^*$ is stationary for problem (8.2.1).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For Algorithm 8.3.6 on a closed convex set, any convergent subsequence along which the metric matrices are uniformly positive definite and bounded has a stationary limit for problem (8.2.1), provided the B-differentiable merit function is strongly F-differentiable at that limit.

\exists c_1,c_2>0\;\forall k\in\kappa\;\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ c_1y^Ty\le y^TH^ky\le c_2y^Ty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contractivity and derivative-based contraction criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global and local contraction criteria for scalar differentiable fixed-point maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A map f defined on an interval I is contractive on I if there exists \lambda\in[0,1) such that |f(x)-f(y)|\leq\lambda|x-y| for all x,y\in I. If f is continuous on I, differentiable on \operatorname{int}(I), and |f'(z)|\leq\lambda<1 throughout \operatorname{int}(I), then f is contractive on I. Separately, if f(x_\infty)=x_\infty, f is continuously differentiable near x_\infty, and |f'(x_\infty)|<1, then there exists d_0>0 such that for every 0<d\leq d_0, with I_d=[x_\infty-d,x_\infty+d], one has \lambda_d:=\sup_{z\in I_d}|f'(z)|<1 and f(I_d)\subseteq I_d.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contraction has a Lipschitz factor below one. A uniform derivative bound below one supplies such a factor. Near a fixed point whose derivative magnitude is below one, every sufficiently small centered interval is contractive and invariant.
assumptions_latex: \text{Global test: }f\text{ is continuous on }I\text{ and differentiable on }\operatorname{int}(I)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal-dual Newton iteration for a logarithmic barrier problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic formulation for inequality constraints represented by positive slacks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\sigma>0\), define \(A(x)=g'(x)\), \(H(x,\lambda)=\nabla^2f(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\nabla^2g_i(x)\), \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda)\), and \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(z)\). The perturbed KKT system is \(\nabla f(x)+A(x)^T\lambda=0\), \(ZY\mathbf1=\sigma\mathbf1\), and \(g(x)+z=0\). At iteration \(k\), compute \((d_x^k,d_\lambda^k)\) from
\[
\begin{bmatrix}H(x^k,\lambda^k)&A(x^k)^T\\A(x^k)&-(Y^k)^{-1}Z^k\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}d_x^k\\d_\lambda^k\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}-\nabla f(x^k)-A(x^k)^T\lambda^k\\-g(x^k)-\sigma(Y^k)^{-1}\mathbf1\end{bmatrix},
\]
recover \(d_z^k=(Y^k)^{-1}(\sigma\mathbf1-Z^kY^k\mathbf1-Z^kd_\lambda^k)\), and update \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\tau_kd_x^k\), \(z^{k+1}=z^k+\tau_kd_z^k\), and \(\lambda^{k+1}=\lambda^k+\alpha_kd_\lambda^k\), choosing positive steps so that \(z^{k+1}>0\) and \(\lambda^{k+1}\ge0\). Then decrease \(\sigma\) and repeat; exact solution of the current perturbed system need not precede the decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Form the perturbed primal-dual KKT equations, solve their reduced Newton system for the primal and multiplier directions, recover the slack direction, take positivity-preserving primal and dual steps, decrease the barrier parameter, and repeat. The barrier parameter may be reduced before the current system is solved exactly.
assumptions_latex: f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\text{ are twice differentiable where the Newton system is formed}
\text{the displayed reduced Newton system is solvable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z^{k+1}>0,\quad \lambda^{k+1}\ge0,\quad \text{and the iteration continues with a decreased barrier parameter }\sigma.
