knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degree, Local Index, and Invertibility of Continuous Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the defining boundary condition and principal properties of Brouwer degree and local index, together with related invertibility notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:\operatorname{cl}\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuous, where \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^m\) is open and bounded, and let \(\bar a\notin G(\partial\Omega)\). Then \(\deg(G\mid\bar a,\Omega)\in\mathbb Z\) is defined. It has the following properties: nonzero degree implies a solution of \(G(v)=\bar a\) in \(\Omega\); it is unchanged under a continuous perturbation \(\widetilde G\) satisfying \(\sup_{x\in\Omega}\|G(x)-\widetilde G(x)\|<\operatorname{dist}(\bar a,G(\partial\Omega))\); it is invariant under homotopies avoiding \(\bar a\) on the boundary; deleting a compact subset containing no solution does not change it; and \(\deg(G\times\widetilde G\mid(\bar a,\bar b),\Omega\times\Omega')=\deg(G\mid\bar a,\Omega)\deg(\widetilde G\mid\bar b,\Omega')\). If \(\bar v\) is isolated in \(G^{-1}(G(\bar v))\), the common degree over sufficiently small neighborhoods of \(\bar v\) defines \(\operatorname{ind}(G,\bar v)\). If \(G\) is Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar v\) with invertible Jacobian, then \(\operatorname{ind}(G,\bar v)=\operatorname{sgn}\det\nabla G(\bar v)\in\{-1,1\}\); local injectivity also implies \(\operatorname{ind}(G,\bar v)\in\{-1,1\}\). A continuous map is locally or globally invertible when it is bijective on a neighborhood or its full domain, respectively; on an open domain its image is open. It is a Lipschitz homeomorphism when it and its inverse are Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Brouwer degree is defined when the target value is avoided on the boundary. It supplies existence, perturbation, homotopy, excision, and product rules. At an isolated preimage it induces a neighborhood-independent local index; a nonsingular derivative gives the sign of the determinant, and local injectivity gives index plus or minus one. The extract also defines local and global invertibility and Lipschitz homeomorphisms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \deg(G\mid\bar a,\Omega)\text{ is defined and satisfies solvability, perturbation, homotopy, excision, and Cartesian-product properties; isolated preimages define a local index with the stated determinant and injectivity formulas.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Self-Maps, Fixed Points, and Contractions on an Interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic scalar fixed-point terminology, with the source's inconsistent map symbol normalized to \(\varphi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R\) and let \(\varphi:S\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. If \(\varphi(S)\subseteq S\), then \(\varphi\) is a self-map of \(S\). A point \(x\in S\) is a fixed point if \(\varphi(x)=x\). The self-map \(\varphi\) is a contraction if there exists \(q\in(0,1)\) such that \[|\varphi(x_1)-\varphi(x_2)|\le q|x_1-x_2|\qquad\forall x_1,x_2\in S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A self-map sends the interval into itself, a fixed point is unchanged by the map, and a contraction uniformly reduces pairwise distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varphi(S)\subseteq S;\quad \varphi(x)=x\text{ defines a fixed point};\quad \exists q\in(0,1)\ \forall x_1,x_2\in S:\ |\varphi(x_1)-\varphi(x_2)|\le q|x_1-x_2|\text{ defines a contraction}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Damped cofactor iteration for the periodic Monge–Ampère equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration for solving \(\det(I-D^2\varphi)=\rho\) on \(\mathbb T^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a smooth \(\varphi_0\) such that \(I-D^2\varphi_0\succ0\), and fix a small \(\tau>0\). At step \(n\), set \(\rho_n:=\det(I-D^2\varphi_n)\) and \(M_n:=\operatorname{cof}(I-D^2\varphi_n)\). Provided \(M_n\succ0\), solve on \(\mathbb T^d\) with periodic boundary conditions \(\operatorname{Tr}(M_nD^2\psi_n)=\rho_n-\rho\), selecting, for example, the zero-mean representative, and update \(\varphi_{n+1}:=\varphi_n+\tau\psi_n\). The periodic solution is unique up to an additive constant under the stated positivity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with a smooth potential whose identity-minus-Hessian is positive definite. At each step, form its determinant and cofactor matrix, solve the periodic linear elliptic correction equation, choose a normalization such as zero mean, and apply the damped correction. Under positive definiteness of the cofactor matrix, the correction is unique up to a constant.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{Tr}(M_nD^2\psi_n)=\rho_n-\rho\text{ is solved on }\mathbb T^d\text{ with periodic boundary conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_n=\det(I-D^2\varphi_n),\qquad \varphi_{n+1}=\varphi_n+\tau\psi_n,\qquad \psi_n\text{ is unique modulo constants and is fixed uniquely by zero mean.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Auxiliary-variable reformulations of one- and infinity-norm residual minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise epigraph representations and their consequence for optimization over a smooth residual map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r:X\to\mathbb{R}^m. For every x\in X,\qquad \|r(x)\|_1=\min_{t\in\mathbb{R}^m}\left\{\mathbf{1}^\top t:-t_i\le r_i(x)\le t_i\ \text{for all }i\right\},\qquad \|r(x)\|_\infty=\min_{\tau\in\mathbb{R}}\left\{\tau:-\tau\le r_i(x)\le\tau\ \text{for all }i\right\}.\qquad Consequently, minimizing either residual norm over x is equivalent to minimizing the corresponding linear auxiliary objective subject to these inequalities; if every r_i is smooth, the resulting formulation is a smooth constrained optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a vector residual r(x), its one-norm equals the minimum sum of componentwise upper bounds on the absolute residuals, and its infinity norm equals the minimum common upper bound on all absolute residuals. Thus minimizing either norm is equivalent to a constrained problem with a linear auxiliary objective. When the residual components are smooth, this is a smooth constrained optimization formulation.
assumptions_latex: r_i\text{ is smooth for every }i\text{ when claiming a smooth constrained formulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|r(x)\|_1=\min_t\{\mathbf{1}^\top t:-t_i\le r_i(x)\le t_i\ \forall i\},\quad \|r(x)\|_\infty=\min_\tau\{\tau:-\tau\le r_i(x)\le\tau\ \forall i\},\quad\text{and the corresponding minimization problems admit equivalent smooth constrained formulations when }r\text{ is smooth}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global and Local Convergence of minFBLSA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of accumulation points, recovery of NCP solutions under FB regularity, whole-sequence convergence, eventual unit steps, and local Q-superlinear or Q-quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(T_{\min}\) be a linear Newton approximation scheme of \(\mathbf F_{\min}\), and let \(\{x^k\}\) be an infinite sequence generated by Algorithm 9.2.3. Then every accumulation point of \(\{x^k\}\) is stationary for \(\theta_{\mathrm{FB}}\); any such point \(x^*\) that is FB regular solves \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\). If \(\{x^k\}\) has an isolated accumulation point \(x^*\), then \(x^k\to x^*\). If a limit point \(x^*\) solves \(\operatorname{NCP}(F)\) and \(T_{\min}\) is nonsingular at \(x^*\), then the whole sequence converges to \(x^*\). If additionally \(p>2\) and \(\gamma<\tfrac12\), then eventually \(d^k\) always solves system (9.1.5), unit steps are always accepted, and convergence is Q-superlinear. If, further, \(T_{\min}\) is strong at \(x^*\) and \(JF\) is Lipschitz at \(x^*\), convergence is Q-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every accumulation point of an infinite minFBLSA sequence is stationary for the Fischer–Burmeister merit function, and FB regularity makes such a point an NCP solution. An isolated accumulation point attracts the whole sequence. A solution accumulation point also attracts the whole sequence when the minimum-function Newton approximation is nonsingular there. With p greater than 2 and gamma below one half, the method eventually uses the referenced Newton direction and unit steps and converges Q-superlinearly; strong approximation and a locally Lipschitz Jacobian strengthen the rate to Q-quadratic.

T_{\min}\text{ is strong at }x^*\text{ and }JF\text{ is Lipschitz at }x^*\text{ for Q-quadratic convergence}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton model step, exactness, and convergence boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained minimization, including the full Newton step and common safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q_x(\delta)=f(x)+g(x)^T\delta+\tfrac12\delta^TH(x)\delta\), nonsingularity of \(H(x)\) gives the stationary Newton step \(\delta_N=-H(x)^{-1}g(x)\); if \(H(x)\succ0\), this is the unique minimizer of \(q_x\) and is a descent direction whenever \(g(x)\ne0\). For a strictly convex quadratic objective, the full step reaches its unique minimizer from every starting point in one iteration. For a general nonquadratic objective, a singular Hessian can make the Newton equation nonunique or inconsistent, while an indefinite Hessian need not produce descent; positive-definite Hessian modification and a line search \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kd_k\) provide safeguards. Near a nondegenerate minimizer, full Newton convergence is superlinear for a continuous Hessian and quadratic when the Hessian is locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Newton step minimizes the local quadratic model when the Hessian is positive definite. It solves a strictly convex quadratic in one iteration, but singular or indefinite Hessians can destroy uniqueness or descent, motivating positive-definite modification and line search. Near a nondegenerate minimizer, full Newton is superlinear with a continuous Hessian and quadratic with a locally Lipschitz Hessian.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is twice continuously differentiable near the points considered}
\nabla^2f\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x^*\text{ for quadratic convergence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_N=-H(x)^{-1}g(x),\quad H(x)\succ0\Rightarrow g(x)^T\delta_N<0\text{ for }g(x)\ne0;\text{ quadratic objectives are solved in one full step, subject to the stated boundaries.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Model Formation from Factored Secant Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square nonlinear systems whose scaled Jacobian approximation is maintained in QR-factored form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a scaled Jacobian approximation in the form \(D_FJ\approx QR\). On restart, factor the current \(D_FJ(x_c)\) and store \(Q^T\) and \(R\); otherwise reuse the supplied factors. Test whether \(R\) is singular and estimate \(\kappa_1(RD_x^{-1})\). If \(R\) is singular or the estimate exceeds \(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\), set \(G=R^TR\), \(\tau=\sqrt{n\varepsilon}\,\|D_x^{-1}GD_x^{-1}\|_1\), form \(H=G+\tau D_x^2\), factor it, and compute \(s_N=-H^{-1}g\), where \(g=R^TQ^TD_FF_c\). Otherwise compute \(s_N=-R^{-1}Q^TD_FF_c\). When requested by the globalization mode, also return \(R^T\) and the corresponding quadratic-model matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reuse the QR factors maintained by factored secant updates, recomputing them on restart. Take the factored Newton step when the scaled triangular factor is well conditioned; otherwise solve a scaled, diagonally regularized normal-equation model.
assumptions_latex: D_FJ\approx QR,\quad Q\text{ orthogonal},\quad R\text{ upper triangular}
\mathrm{restart}\text{ indicates whether the QR factors are recomputed}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative Criterion for a Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient contraction condition for a continuously differentiable self-map of a compact interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R\), and let \(\varphi:S\to S\) have a continuous derivative on \(S\). If \(|\varphi'(x)|<1\) for every \(x\in S\), then \(\varphi\) is a contraction on \(S\); equivalently, there exists \(q\in(0,1)\) such that \[|\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)|\le q|x-y|\qquad\forall x,y\in S.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable self-map of a closed interval is a contraction when its derivative has absolute value strictly below one everywhere.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic convergence when the fixed-point Jacobian vanishes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit local error bound under Lipschitz continuity of the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $x^{k+1}=g(x^k)$ and let $g(x^*)=x^*$. Suppose $g$ is differentiable on
\[
S=\{x:\|x-x^*\|\le\|x^0-x^*\|\},
\]
its Jacobian is Lipschitz on $S$ with constant $L$, and $g'(x^*)=0$. If
\[
q=\frac{L}{2}\|x^0-x^*\|<1,
\]
then
\[
\|x^k-x^*\|\le\frac{2}{L}q^{2^k}\qquad\forall k\ge0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a fixed-point mapping has a Lipschitz Jacobian on the initial-error ball, its Jacobian vanishes at the fixed point, and the initial error satisfies L times that error divided by two below one, then the stated quadratic error bound holds.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Backtracking line search with a directional forcing function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An abstract feasible Armijo method using directions selected from $\Xi(x)$ and a forcing function dominated by the negative upper directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $x^0\in X$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$, and $\sigma:\mathbb R^{2n}\to\mathbb R_+$ with $0<\sigma(x,d)\le-\theta^D(x;d)$ for every $(x,d)\in\operatorname{gph}\Xi$, repeat until $x^k$ is D-stationary: choose $d^k\in\Xi(x^k)$; choose the smallest $i_k\ge0$ such that $$\theta(x^k+2^{-i_k}d^k)\le\theta(x^k)-\gamma2^{-i_k}\sigma(x^k,d^k);$$ set $\tau_k=2^{-i_k}$ and $x^{k+1}=x^k+\tau_kd^k$. If $X$ is convex and the local acceptance hypotheses hold, the search terminates finitely, $x^k\in X$, and $$\theta(x^{k+1})-\theta(x^k)\le-\gamma\tau_k\sigma(x^k,d^k).$$ Moreover, if $i_k\ge1$, the preceding trial $2^{-(i_k-1)}$ fails the Armijo inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each non-D-stationary iterate, select an admissible direction and halve the step until the forcing-function Armijo decrease holds. The search is finite, preserves feasibility, produces monotone sufficient decrease, and the immediately preceding larger trial fails whenever backtracking occurred.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction Theorem on a Closed Interval
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, global convergence, and a geometric error bound for scalar contraction iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R\), and let \(\varphi:S\to S\) be a contraction with modulus \(q\in(0,1)\). For any \(x^0\in S\), define \(x^{k+1}=\varphi(x^k)\). Then \(\varphi\) has a unique fixed point \(\bar x\in S\), the sequence \(x^k\) converges to \(\bar x\), and \[|x^{k+1}-\bar x|\le q^{k+1}|x^0-\bar x|\qquad(k=0,1,\ldots).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every contraction of a closed real interval has a unique fixed point, and iteration converges to it geometrically from every starting point in the interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\bar x\in S:\ \varphi(\bar x)=\bar x,\qquad x^k\to\bar x,\qquad |x^{k+1}-\bar x|\le q^{k+1}|x^0-\bar x|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Square nonlinear systems and roots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the problem class and records its residual-squares representation and possible absence or multiplicity of roots.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let r:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n, with r(x)=(r_1(x),\ldots,r_n(x))^T, and suppose each r_i is smooth. The square nonlinear-equation problem is to find x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n such that r(x^*)=0; such an x^* is called a solution or root. Moreover, r(x^*)=0 if and only if \sum_{i=1}^n r_i(x^*)^2=0. The solution set may be empty, a singleton, or contain multiple points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth vector function from R^n to R^n, solving the square nonlinear system means finding a point where every residual is zero; that point is a solution or root. This is equivalent to attaining zero in the residual sum of squares. A system can have no root, one root, or multiple roots.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is a root}\iff r(x^*)=0\iff \sum_{i=1}^n r_i(x^*)^2=0,\qquad \{x:r(x)=0\}\text{ may be empty, singleton, or non-singleton.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Model Formation with Ill-Conditioned-Jacobian Regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Square nonlinear systems with positive residual and variable scalings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F_c=F(x_c)\), a Jacobian or Jacobian approximation \(J\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g=J^TD_F^2F_c\), positive diagonal scalings \(D_F,D_x\), and machine precision \(\varepsilon\), compute a QR factorization \(D_FJ=QR\) and estimate \(\kappa_1(RD_x^{-1})\). If \(R\) is singular or the estimate exceeds \(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon}\), set \(G=J^TD_F^2J\), \(\tau=\sqrt{n\varepsilon}\,\|D_x^{-1}GD_x^{-1}\|_1\), form \(H=G+\tau D_x^2\), factor it, and compute \(s_N=-H^{-1}g\). Otherwise compute \(s_N=-J^{-1}F_c\). When requested by the globalization mode, also return the triangular model factor and the corresponding quadratic-model matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor the scaled Jacobian and test its scaled triangular factor. Use the ordinary Newton step when it is well conditioned; otherwise solve a diagonally regularized normal-equation model. Return the model factors required by the selected globalization mode.
assumptions_latex: F_c=F(x_c),\quad J\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\text{ is }J(x_c)\text{ or an approximation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: s_N=\begin{cases}-H^{-1}g,&R\text{ singular or }\widehat\kappa_1(RD_x^{-1})>1/\sqrt\varepsilon,\\-J^{-1}F_c,&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\quad H=J^TD_F^2J+\sqrt{n\varepsilon}\,\|D_x^{-1}(J^TD_F^2J)D_x^{-1}\|_1D_x^2\text{ in the regularized branch.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar nonlinear equations and their functional iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define f(x):=x+g(x). Then g(x)=0 if and only if f(x)=x. Thus the roots of g are exactly the fixed points of f, and the associated functional iteration is x_n=f(x_{n-1}).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Defining f(x)=x+g(x) converts g(x)=0 equivalently into the fixed-point equation f(x)=x. Functional iteration repeatedly applies f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton Method for a Square Nonlinear System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J(x)=F'(x)\), and choose \(x_0\in\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure finite-dimensional Newton iteration for square systems; damping, trust regions, inexact linear solves, and singular-Jacobian variants are neighboring extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every iteration \(k\) for which the linear system is solvable and the new point remains in \(\mathcal D\), the Newton step \(s_k\) is defined by \[J(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k.\] Equivalently, \(s_k\) is a zero of the affine residual model \(M_k(s)=F(x_k)+J(x_k)s\). If \(J(x_k)\) is nonsingular, the step is uniquely \(s_k=-J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's method linearizes the nonlinear residual at the current iterate, chooses the step that makes this affine model zero, and adds that step to the current point. A nonsingular current Jacobian makes the step unique.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(J(x_k)\) is invertible, \(x_{k+1}=x_k-J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(F=\nabla f\), the iteration is the pure Newton method for unconstrained stationary equations.
If \(F\) is affine with nonsingular Jacobian, one Newton step reaches its unique root.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F(x_k)=0\), then \(s_k=0\) is a Newton step.
A singular Jacobian can make the pure Newton step nonexistent or nonunique.
boundary_notes: This definition makes no global-convergence assertion from a remote initial point.
Solving \(J(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k)\) only approximately defines an inexact Newton method, not the pure method in this slot.
Least-squares solutions of inconsistent Newton equations require a separately specified rectangular or singular-system variant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optional Jacobian Evaluation and Storage Contract
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interface and storage contract for the optional user-supplied Jacobian routine in the described modular nonlinear-equation system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=(f_1,\ldots,f_n):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If supplied, the optional Jacobian routine returns every entry of the Jacobian of F at x_c, does not modify n or x_c, and provides the full matrix used by the system.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent error-step tests for superlinear convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between successive-error and step-based little-o conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf h^{(k)}\to\mathbf0\) and define \(\boldsymbol\delta^{(k)}=\mathbf h^{(k+1)}-\mathbf h^{(k)}\). Then the following conditions are equivalent: \(\mathbf h^{(k+1)}=o(\|\mathbf h^{(k)}\|)\); \(\boldsymbol\delta^{(k)}=-\mathbf h^{(k)}+o(\|\mathbf h^{(k)}\|)\); \(\mathbf h^{(k+1)}=o(\|\boldsymbol\delta^{(k)}\|)\); and \(\boldsymbol\delta^{(k)}=-\mathbf h^{(k)}+o(\|\boldsymbol\delta^{(k)}\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For errors tending to zero, superlinear decay of the next error is equivalent to the step asymptotically cancelling the current error, whether the remainder is measured relative to the current error or to the step.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical Newton iteration for a scalar nonlinear equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic exact Newton iteration for solving a scalar equation. The extract mentions, but does not formulate, the extension to nonlinear mappings on normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable function \(P:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\), Newton's method for \(P(x)=0\) defines, whenever \(P'(x_n)\neq 0\),
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n-\frac{P(x_n)}{P'(x_n)}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable scalar function P, Newton's method approximates P by its tangent at the current iterate and takes the tangent's zero as the next iterate: x_(n+1)=x_n-P(x_n)/P'(x_n), provided P'(x_n) is nonzero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: NEINCK input validation and initialization for nonlinear-equation drivers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract denotes the variable-scale output as S_z in the output list but as S_x in its initialization step; this notation inconsistency is preserved rather than silently resolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $n\in\mathbb Z$, machine precision $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}\in\mathbb R$, and $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, NEINCK checks or initializes the options and tolerances of a nonlinear-equation driver. If $n<1$, it sets $\mathrm{termcode}=-1$ and terminates. When scaling is implemented, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ it sets the variable scale—denoted $S_z$ in the output list and $S_x$ in step 2—to $1/(\mathrm{typx})_i$ when $\mathrm{typx}$ is supplied and to $1$ otherwise; similarly, $(S_F)_i=1/(\mathrm{typF})_i$ when $\mathrm{typF}$ is supplied and $(S_F)_i=1$ otherwise. If $\mathrm{Fdigits}}$ is supplied, then $\eta=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ for $\mathrm{Fdigits}=-1$ and $\eta=\max\{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mach}},10^{-\mathrm{Fdigits}}\}$ otherwise; if it is absent, $\eta$ is set to $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}$ or estimated. A negative return code is recommended when $\eta>0.01$. If $\mathrm{global}\in\{2,3\}$ and $\delta$ is absent, the routine sets $\delta=-1$; $\delta$ is ignored when $\mathrm{global}=1$. Unspecified options and tolerances receive implementor-selected values, and supplied values may be checked. Return code $0$ means all inputs were satisfactory or corrected, while a negative code denotes a fatal input error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: NEINCK validates or supplies a nonlinear-equation driver's options and tolerances. It rejects dimensions below one, optionally constructs reciprocal variable and residual scales, derives a residual-noise estimate from machine precision and an optional digit count, and initializes a missing globalization parameter when required. If scaling is not implemented, both scale outputs and their initialization steps are omitted. No additional vector or matrix storage is required, and supplied typical-value arrays may share storage with their corresponding scale arrays.
assumptions_latex: \mathrm{typx},\mathrm{typF}\in\mathbb R^n\text{ and }\mathrm{Fdigits}\in\mathbb Z\text{ are optional inputs}
\text{If scaling is not implemented, the variable- and residual-scale outputs and steps are omitted}
\text{The required option set may be reduced when only a subset of the nonlinear-equation system is implemented}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n<1\Rightarrow\mathrm{termcode}=-1;\qquad n\ge1\Rightarrow\text{the stated validation, scaling, noise-estimation, and default-initialization rules are applied, with }\mathrm{termcode}=0\text{ for satisfactory or corrected input and }\mathrm{termcode}<0\text{ for fatal error}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Banach-space Newton convergence under a Kantorovich bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-definedness and convergence of exact Newton iteration for a nonlinear equation between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces and let \(P:X\to Y\) be twice Fréchet differentiable with \(\|P''(x)\|\le K\) for every \(x\in X\). Suppose that \(x_1\in X\), \(p_1=P'(x_1)\) has a bounded inverse, \(\|p_1^{-1}\|\le\beta_1\), \(\|p_1^{-1}[P(x_1)]\|\le\eta_1\), and \(h_1=\beta_1\eta_1K<\tfrac12\). Then, writing \(p_n=P'(x_n)\), the iteration
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n-p_n^{-1}[P(x_n)]
\]
is well-defined for every \(n>1\) and converges to a point \(x^*\) satisfying \(P(x^*)=\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let P map a Banach space X into a Banach space Y and be twice Fréchet differentiable with globally bounded second derivative. If P'(x1) has a bounded inverse, the inverse and initial Newton correction satisfy the stated bounds, and beta1 eta1 K is less than one half, then all subsequent Newton iterates exist and converge to a zero of P.
assumptions_latex: P:X\to Y\text{ is twice Fréchet differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall n>1,\ x_{n+1}=x_n-P'(x_n)^{-1}[P(x_n)]\text{ is well-defined, and }x_n\to x^*\text{ with }P(x^*)=\theta

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Stability of a Nonsingular Jacobian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local inverse stability for the Jacobian of a continuously differentiable nonlinear residual map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n be continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of x^*\in D, and suppose that F'(x^*) is nonsingular. Then there exist \delta>0 and \xi>0 such that every y\in D satisfying \|y-x^*\|<\delta has nonsingular F'(y) and
\[
\|F'(y)^{-1}\|\leq\xi.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\lim_{\substack{y\to x^*\\y\in D}}\|F'(y)^{-1}-F'(x^*)^{-1}\|=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If F is continuously differentiable near x* and its Jacobian at x* is nonsingular, then all sufficiently nearby Jacobians are nonsingular, their inverses are locally uniformly bounded, and the inverse Jacobian is continuous at x*.
assumptions_latex: F\in C^1\text{ on a neighborhood of }x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\delta,\xi>0\ \forall y\in D:\ \|y-x^*\|<\delta\Rightarrow\left(F'(y)\text{ is nonsingular and }\|F'(y)^{-1}\|\leq\xi\right),\quad F'(y)^{-1}\to F'(x^*)^{-1}\text{ as }y\to x^*.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient asymptotic step condition for superlinear convergence to a regular zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Newton Root Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Newton iteration for a square nonlinear system with an exact Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an initial point \(x_0\), and tolerance \(\tau>0\), evaluate the exact Jacobian \(J_F(x_k)\) and solve \(J_F(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\); a globalized variant may replace the full step by an accepted damped or trust-region step without changing the exact-Jacobian Newton model. Terminate successfully when \(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert\le\tau\), and report failure if the linear system is unsolvable or the globalization mechanism cannot accept a step. The output is the final iterate and its residual norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the exact Jacobian linearization of a square nonlinear system at each iterate and update toward a root.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of the iterates.
The exact Jacobian can be evaluated.
The Newton linear system is nonsingular whenever a full Newton step is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-J_F(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\) is the exact Newton root iteration.

notation.meaning: Exact Jacobian of F at the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Newton iteration for a square nonlinear system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(F:D\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, and write \(J(x)=F'(x)\). The problem is to find \(x_*\in D\) satisfying \(F(x_*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, deterministic root finding. “Exact” means that the current analytic Jacobian is used and the Newton linear equation is solved exactly; it does not assert exact arithmetic or global convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An exact Newton root method is the iteration defined, whenever \(J(x_k)\) is nonsingular and \(x_k+s_k\in D\), by \[J(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k.\] Equivalently, \(x_{k+1}\) is the zero of the current affine model \(M_k(x_k+p)=F(x_k)+J(x_k)p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable square residual map, exact Newton forms the affine model at the current iterate, solves the current Jacobian equation \(J(x_k)s_k=-F(x_k)\) without a linear-solve residual, and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). The iteration is defined only when the required linear equation is solvable and the new point remains in the domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x_{k+1}=x_k-J(x_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\quad\text{when }J(x_k)^{-1}\text{ exists}.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-F(x_k)/F'(x_k)\).
If \(F(x)=Ax-b\) with nonsingular \(A\), one Newton update produces the root from every starting point.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Newton step is uniquely determined whenever \(J(x_k)\) is nonsingular.
The defining linear residual \(J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\) is zero.
boundary_notes: A damped update \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\) with \(\alpha_k\ne1\) is a globalization variant, not the pure iteration defined here.
Inexact, reused, approximated, or regularized Jacobian equations belong to neighboring method families.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Newton Iteration, Local Rate, and Initialization Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines exact scalar Newton iteration for nonlinear equations, gives its local quadratic error relation at a regular root, contrasts the local linear rate of a general fixed-point iteration, and records the absence of unconditional global convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_*\) satisfy \(g(x_*)=0\), and suppose Newton's map \(f(x)=x-g(x)/g'(x)\) is twice differentiable near \(x_*\), with \(g'(x_*)\neq0\) and continuous \(f''\). The Newton iteration is
\[
x_n=f(x_{n-1})=x_{n-1}-\frac{g(x_{n-1})}{g'(x_{n-1})}.
\]
For \(x_0\) sufficiently close to \(x_*\), \(f'(x_*)=0\), and, writing \(e_n=x_n-x_*\),
\[
e_n=\frac12 f''(z_n)e_{n-1}^2,
\qquad
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{e_n}{e_{n-1}^2}=\frac12 f''(x_*),
\]
where \(z_n\) lies between \(x_{n-1}\) and \(x_*\). Hence the error is at least quadratic locally; it is Q-quadratic with the displayed nonzero asymptotic constant when \(f''(x_*)\neq0\). Separately, for a sufficiently smooth fixed-point iteration with \(f(x_*)=x_*\) and \(0<|f'(x_*)|<1\), sufficiently close convergent iterates satisfy
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{e_n}{e_{n-1}}=f'(x_*),
\]
which is linear convergence. Newton's iteration has no unconditional global convergence guarantee and can fail from a starting point too far from the desired root.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Newton's scalar root iteration subtracts the function value divided by its derivative. At a regular root, continuity of the second derivative of the iteration map and a sufficiently close initial point give a quadratic error relation and the stated asymptotic constant. If that constant is nonzero, the convergence is Q-quadratic; if it vanishes, the rate may be faster. A general fixed-point iteration with derivative magnitude strictly between zero and one has a local linear error ratio. Newton's method can fail when initialized too far from the desired root.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is sufficiently close to }x_*\text{ and the Newton iterates are well-defined}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Connections and failure boundaries of exact Newton root iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method connections, singular-Jacobian failure, remote-start behavior, and a degenerate-root rate counterexample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the iteration $J(x_k)p_k=-r(x_k)$, $x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k$, choosing $r=\nabla f$ recovers Newton's method for unconstrained optimization, and applying the iteration to the first-order optimality equations of an equality-constrained problem gives the associated sequential quadratic programming construction. In the usual case where $J(x_k)$ is nonsingular, the displayed Newton equation is also equivalent to the cited Gauss--Newton equation. A remote starting point may lead to erratic behavior, and if $J(x_k)$ is singular the Newton step may fail to be defined. For the degenerate scalar residual $r(x)=x^2$ with $x_0\ne0$, $$x_{k+1}=\frac12x_k,\qquad x_k=2^{-k}x_0,$$ so the iterates converge to $0$ only Q-linearly. Jacobian Lipschitz continuity on a domain means that some $\beta_L\ge0$ satisfies $$\|J(x)-J(y)\|\le\beta_L\|x-y\|$$ for all $x,y$ in that domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Root-finding Newton recovers optimization Newton when the residual is a gradient and produces the equality-constrained SQP construction when applied to the first-order optimality system. Under the stated nonsingularity qualification it also agrees with the cited Gauss–Newton equation. Remote starts may behave erratically, and a singular Jacobian may leave the Newton step undefined. For the degenerate residual r(x)=x², every nonzero starting value is halved at each iteration, giving only linear convergence to zero. The paragraph also defines Lipschitz continuity of the Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: J(x_k)\text{ is nonsingular for the stated Gauss--Newton equivalence}
r(x)=x^2,\quad x_0\ne0\text{ for the degenerate-root example}
\exists\beta_L\ge0\ \forall x,y\text{ in the domain}:\ \|J(x)-J(y)\|\le\beta_L\|x-y\|\text{ for Jacobian Lipschitz continuity}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r=\nabla f\Rightarrow\text{unconstrained-optimization Newton};\quad r(x)=x^2\Rightarrow x_k=2^{-k}x_0\text{ with Q-linear convergence};\quad J(x_k)\text{ singular permits failure of step definition}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Multidimensional Newton Root Iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Newton iteration for a square nonlinear system; the source gives an invertibility condition for each step and only a qualitative local-performance statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^p\to\mathbb{R}^p\), linearization of \(f(y)=0\) about \(x_n\) yields \(-f(x_n)\approx df(x_n)(y-x_n)\). If \(df(x_n)\) is invertible, Newton's root-finding iteration is
\[
x_{n+1}=x_n-df(x_n)^{-1}f(x_n).
\]
The iteration generally works well when the initial point is close to a root \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a mapping from R^p to R^p, Newton's root method linearizes the residual at the current iterate. When the derivative matrix is invertible, the next iterate is the current point minus the inverse derivative applied to the residual. The source describes good performance only qualitatively for an initial point close to a root.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar Newton root iteration and square-root error identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scalar Newton iteration, its square-root specialization, and the precise one-step error-decrease condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a scalar equation f(x)=0, if f is differentiable at x_c and f'(x_c)\ne0, the zero of the affine model M_c(x)=f(x_c)+f'(x_c)(x-x_c) is the Newton iterate x_+=x_c-f(x_c)/f'(x_c). For f(x)=x^2-\alpha with \alpha>0 and x_c\ne0, x_+=\tfrac12(x_c+\alpha/x_c) and x_+-\sqrt{\alpha}=(x_c-\sqrt{\alpha})^2/(2x_c). Hence 0<|x_c-\sqrt{\alpha}|<2|x_c| implies |x_+-\sqrt{\alpha}|<|x_c-\sqrt{\alpha}|.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalar Newton step is the zero of the affine model at the current iterate. For the positive square-root equation, the update averages the current value with alpha divided by that value, and its exact signed error equals the squared current error divided by twice the current iterate. A nonzero error strictly decreases whenever its magnitude is less than twice the magnitude of the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton iterations with a reused Jacobian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable with Jacobian \(J\), and let \(\tau:\mathbb{N}_0\to\mathbb{N}_0\) satisfy \(0\leq\tau(k)\leq k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding with exact derivative evaluations performed only at selected refresh iterations. The definition covers chord and block-reuse variants but excludes secant updates that alter the stored matrix without reevaluating the derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative-reuse Newton method selects refresh indices through \(\tau(k)\), forms \(B_k=J(x_{\tau(k)})\), and, whenever \(B_k\) is nonsingular, defines \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k.\] Reuse occurs at iteration \(k\) precisely when \(\tau(k)<k\), equivalently \(B_k=B_{k-1}\) without a new Jacobian evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative-reuse Newton method solves the Newton-like equation with an exact Jacobian evaluated at an earlier retained iterate. A refresh map \(\tau(k)\) chooses the stored matrix \(B_k=J(x_{\tau(k)})\); the method solves \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\) and accepts \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). At reuse iterations no new derivative matrix is formed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: On a refresh block \(k=r,\ldots,r+q-1\), \[J(x_r)s_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k.\]
special_cases_latex: Pure Newton is recovered by \(\tau(k)=k\).
The chord method is recovered by \(\tau(k)=0\) for every \(k\).
Periodic refresh with period \(q\) uses \(\tau(k)=q\lfloor k/q\rfloor\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every reuse block requires only one Jacobian formation and factorization, although it may require several triangular solves.
The equation residual relative to the stored matrix is zero, while \(J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\) need not vanish.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe a refresh test or claim a convergence rate.
If \(B_k\) is updated by secant data rather than set equal to a previously evaluated Jacobian, the method is quasi-Newton rather than derivative-reuse Newton.

notation.meaning: index of the iterate whose Jacobian is retained at iteration k

review_flags: No inspected source in the supplied locator set gave a precise canonical definition of chord, periodic-refresh, and general refresh-map variants in this root-equation scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Modified Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton root iteration using a deliberately modified or reused Jacobian matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), choose an initial point \(x_0\) and construct nonsingular matrices \(B_k\) that approximate \(J_F(x_k)\), possibly by retaining selected derivative information across iterations. Solve \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\), select \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) through the prescribed globalization rule, and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\). Refresh or modify \(B_k\) whenever its update criterion is triggered. Stop when \(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert\) or an accepted correction norm is below tolerance; output the iterate, residual norm, and final approximation \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace the current exact Jacobian by a nonsingular modified approximation, solve the resulting Newton equation, and refresh that approximation according to a rule.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near the iterates.
Every matrix \(B_k\) used in a step is nonsingular.
The globalization and matrix-refresh rules are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed scheme is a modified Newton family, reducing to exact Newton when \(B_k=J_F(x_k)\).

notation.meaning: Modified Jacobian approximation used at iteration k.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is suitable, but the formulation permits arbitrary Jacobian approximations and therefore extends beyond the derivative-reuse branch into quasi-Newton and other inexact-Newton families. A source is required to determine the intended meaning of modified Newton in this exact container and to delimit the admissible matrix modifications or reuse rules.

children.title: Chord Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Chord Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton-like root iteration with one Jacobian matrix fixed across all corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(x_0\), form the fixed matrix \(B=J_F(x_0)\), or another prescribed nonsingular approximation constructed once. For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), solve \(Bs_k=-F(x_k)\) and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\), where \(\alpha_k=1\) for the classical local chord method and may be reduced by a stated globalization test. Reuse the same factorization of \(B\) at every iteration. Stop when the residual or correction meets tolerance, and report breakdown if the fixed linear system cannot be solved or no step is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix one Jacobian approximation, reuse its factorization for every Newton-like correction, and iterate until the nonlinear residual is small.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near the iterates.
Residual evaluations remain available throughout the iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kB^{-1}F(x_k)\) defines the chord method.

notation.meaning: Single fixed Jacobian or Jacobian approximation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-matrix iteration correctly captures the core chord-method idea and the algorithm kind fits the container. An authoritative source is nevertheless required, particularly for the broadened version allowing a matrix other than J_F(x_0) and an added globalization mechanism.

children.title: Derivative-Refresh Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing derivative reuse and refresh frequency.

knowledge_statements.title: Derivative-Refresh Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rules specifying when a reused derivative model must be recomputed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B_k\) be the derivative matrix used to compute \(s_k\) from \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\). A derivative-refresh regime is a predicate \(R_k\in\{0,1\}\) determined from available iteration data, together with the update rule \(B_{k+1}=J_F(x_{k+1})\) when \(R_k=1\) and \(B_{k+1}=B_k\) when \(R_k=0\). Admissible examples include periodic refresh, refresh after rejected or insufficiently decreasing steps, and refresh when a discrepancy such as \(\lVert F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)-B_ks_k\rVert\) exceeds a specified threshold. The regime must also declare mandatory refresh after singularity or linear-solve breakdown.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refresh regime is an explicit predicate deciding whether to recompute the Jacobian or retain the matrix used in the preceding correction.
assumptions_latex: The iteration data required by \(R_k\) are observable.
An exact or designated replacement derivative can be computed when refresh is requested.
All thresholds and mandatory-refresh events are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((R_k,B_{k+1})\) completely determines derivative reuse versus refresh after iteration \(k\).

notation.meaning: Derivative matrix currently used by the root solver.
Correction computed with the current derivative matrix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind appropriately describes a refresh rule rather than a complete solver. However, the proposed predicate formalization, discrepancy trigger, and mandatory refresh events are method-dependent and unsupported, so a source is needed to establish the intended derivative-refresh regime taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Newton root methods using a freshly approximated Jacobian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose function values are available while the exact Jacobian is unavailable or deliberately not used. Let \(A_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be constructed at \(x_k\) as an approximation to \(J(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional root finding with a derivative approximation freshly constructed at each designated iteration. This includes finite-difference and other direct derivative approximations, but not secant matrices propagated solely from earlier steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A derivative-approximation Newton method is an iteration \[A_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] where \(A_k\) is computed as an approximation to \(J(x_k)\) without evaluating the exact Jacobian. In the forward-difference instance, for nonzero increments \(h_{k,j}\), \[A_ke_j=\frac{F(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-F(x_k)}{h_{k,j}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each iteration, this family constructs a matrix \(A_k\) intended to approximate the current Jacobian without evaluating the exact derivative, solves \(A_ks_k=-F(x_k)\), and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). A canonical instance builds each column by a forward difference of residual values along a coordinate direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The step is the zero of the approximate affine model \(\widetilde M_k(x_k+p)=F(x_k)+A_kp\).
special_cases_latex: Forward differences use \(A_ke_j=[F(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-F(x_k)]/h_{k,j}\).
Central differences may use \(A_ke_j=[F(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-F(x_k-h_{k,j}e_j)]/(2h_{k,j})\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Even when the equation with \(A_k\) is solved exactly, the true Newton residual \(J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\) generally is nonzero.
A dense coordinate forward-difference Jacobian requires \(n\) perturbed residual evaluations in addition to an available value \(F(x_k)\).
boundary_notes: The finite-difference increment must be nonzero and keep every sampled point inside \(D\).
Jacobian-free products used only inside an iterative Krylov solve belong to the Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov family.
Matrices updated from secant pairs rather than reconstructed at the current point belong to quasi-Newton methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Difference Newton Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-step or line-search Newton root iteration using coordinate finite differences to approximate the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an initial point \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and a tolerance \(\tau>0\), choose nonzero increments \(h_{k,j}\) at iteration \(k\) and define the finite-difference matrix by \((B_k)_{:,j}=[F(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j)-F(x_k)]/h_{k,j}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,n\), where \(e_j\) is the \(j\)-th coordinate vector. Solve \(B_ks_k=-F(x_k)\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) for the full-step method, or choose \(\alpha_k\in(0,1]\) using a specified line-search acceptance rule and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\). Select or adapt the increments to account for truncation and function-evaluation errors. Stop successfully when \(\lVert F(x_k)\rVert_2\le\tau\), and report breakdown if \(B_k\) is unusable or the prescribed line search cannot accept a step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate every Jacobian column by coordinate finite differences, solve the resulting approximate Newton equation, optionally globalize the correction by a line search, and stop when the nonlinear residual reaches the stated tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuously differentiable near all evaluated points.
Every perturbed point \(x_k+h_{k,j}e_j\) required by the difference formula is feasible to evaluate.
Each matrix \(B_k\) used to compute a correction is nonsingular.
For the line-search variant, the acceptance rule and its failure condition are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed procedure is a coordinate finite-difference Newton method for solving \(F(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: Coordinate finite-difference approximation to the Jacobian at iteration k.
Nonzero finite-difference increment for coordinate j at iteration k.
The j-th coordinate unit vector in R^n.
Accepted line-search step length when globalization is used.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local rates of coordinate finite-difference Newton
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local well-definedness and linear, superlinear, and quadratic convergence regimes determined by the differencing scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable on an open convex set \(D\). Suppose \(N(x^*,r)\subset D\), \(F(x^*)=0\), \(J(x^*)\) is nonsingular with \(\|J(x^*)^{-1}\|\le\beta\), and \(J\) is Lipschitz continuous on \(N(x^*,r)\). Then there exist \(\epsilon,h>0\) such that, for every \(x_0\in N(x^*,\epsilon)\) and every real sequence \(\{h_k\}\) satisfying \(0<|h_k|\le h\), the coordinate forward-difference Newton iteration is well-defined and converges linearly to \(x^*\). If \(h_k\to0\), the convergence is superlinear. If, for some constant \(c_1\), \(|h_k|\le c_1\|x_k-x^*\|\), or equivalently locally for some \(c_2\), \(|h_k|\le c_2\|F(x_k)\|\), the convergence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a regular root with a locally Lipschitz Jacobian, sufficiently small bounded nonzero differencing scales make finite-difference Newton well-defined and linearly convergent. Vanishing scales give superlinear convergence, while scales proportional to either the current error or residual give quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to x^*\text{ linearly};\quad h_k\to0\Rightarrow x_k\to x^*\text{ superlinearly};\quad |h_k|=O(\|x_k-x^*\|)\ \text{(equiv. locally }|h_k|=O(\|F(x_k)\|)\text{)}\Rightarrow x_k\to x^*\text{ quadratically}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convergence rates of forward finite-difference Newton iteration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded evidence. The hypotheses are retained by reference because Theorem 5.2.1 is not restated. The displayed limit with index k tending to 0 is malformed; in the sequence-convergence context it is interpreted as h_k tending to 0 as k tends to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(x_*\) satisfy the assumptions of the referenced Theorem 5.2.1, with the \(\ell_1\) vector norm and corresponding induced matrix norm. There exist \(\varepsilon,h>0\) such that, for every real sequence \(\{h_k\}\) satisfying \(0<|h_k|\le h\) and every \(x_0\in N(x_*,\varepsilon)\), the iteration \((A_k)_{\cdot j}=\frac{F(x_k+h_ke_j)-F(x_k)}{h_k}\), \(j=1,\ldots,n\), and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-A_k^{-1}F(x_k)\) is well defined and converges \(q\)-linearly to \(x_*\). If \(h_k\to0\) as \(k\to\infty\), convergence is \(q\)-superlinear. If \(|h_k|\le c_1\|x_k-x_*\|_1\) for some constant \(c_1\), or equivalently \(|h_k|\le c_2\|F(x_k)\|_1\) for some constant \(c_2\), convergence is \(q\)-quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the referenced local Newton hypotheses, sufficiently small nonzero forward-difference increments and a sufficiently close initial point yield a well-defined finite-difference Newton sequence converging q-linearly to the solution. Increments tending to zero give q-superlinear convergence, while increments bounded proportionally to the current error—or equivalently to the residual—give q-quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ and }x_*\text{ satisfy the assumptions of the referenced Theorem 5.2.1.}
\|\cdot\|=\|\cdot\|_1\text{ for vectors, with the corresponding induced matrix norm.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_k\to x_*\text{ q-linearly};\quad h_k\to0\text{ as }k\to\infty\Rightarrow\text{ q-superlinear convergence};\quad |h_k|\le c_1\|x_k-x_*\|_1\ \text{or equivalently}\ |h_k|\le c_2\|F(x_k)\|_1\Rightarrow\text{ q-quadratic convergence}.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference-Quality Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence regimes determined by the quality of a derivative approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable near a root \(x_*\), let \(J=F'\) be Lipschitz continuous there, and suppose \(J(x_*)\) is nonsingular. Consider steps satisfying \(B_k s_k=-F(x_k)\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). There exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) and a constant \(\delta>0\) such that, if \(x_0\in U\), every \(B_k\) is nonsingular, and \(\|B_k-J(x_k)\|\leq\delta\), then the iteration is locally linearly convergent. If additionally \(\|(B_k-J(x_k))s_k\|/\|s_k\|\to0\) for nonzero steps, the convergence is superlinear. If instead \(\|B_k-J(x_k)\|=O(\|x_k-x_*\|)\), the convergence is quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a nonsingular root with a Lipschitz Jacobian, a sufficiently small uniform derivative-model error gives local linear convergence; vanishing derivative error along the computed steps gives superlinear convergence; and derivative-model error proportional to the current iterate error gives quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is Lipschitz continuous in a neighborhood of \(x_*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Regularized Newton Equation Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton equation stabilized by an additive regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), an iterate \(x_k\), and \(\lambda_k\geq0\), choose \(\lambda_k\) so that \(J(x_k)+\lambda_k I\) is acceptably conditioned. Solve \((J(x_k)+\lambda_k I)s_k=-F(x_k)\), test the trial point \(x_k+s_k\) with a residual merit function, and accept it when the prescribed decrease test holds. Otherwise increase \(\lambda_k\) and recompute the step; after successful steps, \(\lambda_k\) may be decreased. Stop when the residual or step tolerance is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a nonnegative shift to the Newton matrix, solve the stabilized equation, and adapt the shift according to trial-point residual decrease.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood containing all trial points.
\(J(x_k)+\lambda_k I\) is nonsingular for every computed step.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Additively regularized Newton equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable with Jacobian \(J\). For each iteration choose \(\lambda_k\geq0\) and a regularization matrix \(R_k\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding. The defining mechanism regularizes the Newton linear equation by an additive matrix term; trust-region and normal-equation regularizations are nearby variants unless they reduce to this form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An additively regularized Newton equation method defines \(s_k\) by \[(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k)s_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] subject to nonsingularity of \(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k\). A genuine regularization iteration has \(\lambda_kR_k\ne0\); allowing \(\lambda_k=0\) makes exact Newton a limiting special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family replaces the possibly singular, ill-conditioned, or otherwise unsuitable Newton matrix by \(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k\). It solves the resulting regularized equation for \(s_k\) and updates \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). The parameter is nonnegative, and the modified matrix must be nonsingular for the step to be uniquely defined.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s_k=-(J(x_k)+\lambda_kR_k)^{-1}F(x_k)\] whenever the inverse exists.
special_cases_latex: Scalar shifting uses \(R_k=I\), giving \((J(x_k)+\lambda_kI)s_k=-F(x_k)\).
Setting \(\lambda_k=0\) recovers the exact Newton equation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The unregularized Newton residual satisfies \(J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)=-\lambda_kR_ks_k\).
Regularization changes the defining linear model unless \(\lambda_kR_ks_k=0\).
boundary_notes: For nonsymmetric Jacobians, a positive scalar shift does not by itself guarantee nonsingularity or desirable conditioning.
Levenberg–Marquardt equations based on \(J(x_k)^TJ(x_k)+\lambda_kI\) are normal-equation regularizations and are not automatically identical to this additive-Jacobian definition.
No rule for choosing \(\lambda_k\) or accepting the step is included.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-controlled Newton–Krylov iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J_k=J(x_k)\), and let \(\mathcal K_m(J_k,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,J_kr_0,\ldots,J_k^{m-1}r_0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding with an iterative Krylov solution of each Newton equation. The outer method is inexact because the inner linear residual need not vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact Newton–Krylov method chooses \(0\leq\eta_k<1\) and computes a correction \(s_k\) by a Krylov subspace linear solver such that \[r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}=J_ks_k+F(x_k),\qquad \|r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|,\] then sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), possibly after an independently specified globalization. For a zero initial inner guess, the computed step lies in a Krylov space generated by \(J_k\) and \(-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each outer iterate, an inexact Newton–Krylov method applies a Krylov linear solver to the Newton equation. The inner solve stops when the linear residual \(J_ks_k+F(x_k)\) is no larger than a forcing fraction \(\eta_k\) of the nonlinear residual norm. The resulting correction, rather than the exact Newton correction, defines the next outer iterate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: There exists \(e_k\) with \(\|e_k\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\) such that \[J_ks_k=-F(x_k)+e_k.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(\eta_k=0\) and the Krylov process reaches an exact solution, the outer step is exact Newton.
GMRES, MINRES, and CG are possible inner solvers only when their respective algebraic requirements match the Newton matrix.
immediate_consequences_latex: The forcing term separates the permitted linear-solve error from the nonlinear residual scale.
No explicit factorization of \(J_k\) is required by the family definition.
boundary_notes: Krylov membership depends on the initial inner guess and changes under left or right preconditioning.
The definition does not require Jacobian-free products; explicitly assembled Jacobians are allowed.
A convergence rate requires additional regularity and forcing-sequence hypotheses.

notation.meaning: residual of the inexact Newton linear equation

Inexact Newton Forcing Strategies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-based accuracy conditions for approximate Newton equation solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), an inexact Newton step \(s_k\) has linear residual \(r_k=J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\) and must satisfy \(\|r_k\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\), where \(0\leq\eta_k<1\). A fixed bound \(\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) defines a linear forcing regime; \(\eta_k\to0\) defines a superlinear forcing regime; and \(\eta_k=O(\|F(x_k)\|)\) defines a quadratic forcing regime under the usual nonsingular-root and Lipschitz-Jacobian hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forcing term bounds the relative residual of each approximate Newton solve; constant, vanishing, and residual-proportional choices target linear, superlinear, and quadratic local convergence.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forcing strategy for an inexact Newton equation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable. At iteration \(k\), an inexact Newton step has linear residual \(r_k^{\mathrm{lin}}=J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic relative-residual stopping strategies for inner Newton solves. This definition specifies admissible forcing values, not a convergence theorem or a particular adaptive formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact Newton forcing strategy is a rule \(\Phi_k\) that, from information available through iteration \(k\), chooses \[\eta_k=\Phi_k(x_0,\ldots,x_k,F(x_0),\ldots,F(x_k),\ldots)\in[0,\eta_{\max}],\qquad \eta_{\max}<1,\] and terminates the inner solve only after \[\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|.\] Smaller \(\eta_k\) requests a more accurate Newton equation solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forcing strategy is the rule that chooses the relative inner tolerance \(\eta_k\). The selected value lies between zero and a fixed bound below one, may depend only on information already available, and controls termination through \(\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(F(x_k)\ne0\), the admissibility test is \[\frac{\|J(x_k)s_k+F(x_k)\|}{\|F(x_k)\|}\leq\eta_k.\]
special_cases_latex: A constant forcing strategy sets \(\eta_k\equiv\bar\eta\) with \(0\leq\bar\eta<1\).
A tightening strategy has \(\eta_k\to0\) as the nonlinear residual approaches zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: At an exact root \(F(x_k)=0\), the relative test forces \(J(x_k)s_k=0\); implementations normally terminate the outer iteration instead.
The forcing rule is independent of the particular Krylov recurrence used to meet its residual test.
boundary_notes: An absolute tolerance without normalization by \(\|F(x_k)\|\) is a different stopping convention.
The bound \(\eta_{\max}<1\) is part of this canonical admissibility definition; sharper rate conditions are not asserted.
Finite-precision stagnation may prevent a requested tolerance from being attained.

notation.meaning: uniform upper bound on relative inner residuals

The selected inner solver must preserve its stated structural assumptions, and the outer stopping test remains the inexact Newton residual condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projection-defined Newton–Krylov solver variant
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), consider the Newton equation \(J_ks=-F_k\), where \(J_k=J(x_k)\), \(F_k=F(x_k)\), and an inner process builds trial and test spaces \(\mathcal V_{k,m},\mathcal W_{k,m}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear Krylov variants used as inner solvers. The distinguishing object is the projection or residual-optimality condition, not the outer Newton update or forcing rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–Krylov solver variant is specified by nested Krylov trial spaces \(\mathcal V_{k,m}\), test spaces \(\mathcal W_{k,m}\), and an inner iterate \(s_{k,m}\in s_{k,0}+\mathcal V_{k,m}\) satisfying either the Petrov–Galerkin condition \[F_k+J_ks_{k,m}\perp\mathcal W_{k,m}\] or the minimum-residual condition \[s_{k,m}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{s\in s_{k,0}+\mathcal V_{k,m}}\|F_k+J_ks\|.\] The accepted \(s_k=s_{k,m_k}\) must also meet the outer forcing tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver variant chooses how a Krylov trial space is generated and how the approximate Newton correction is selected from it. The correction either makes the linear residual orthogonal to a test space or minimizes its norm over the trial affine space. The outer method accepts an inner iterate only after it satisfies the prescribed forcing condition.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For zero initial guess, a standard unpreconditioned trial space is \[\mathcal V_{k,m}=\mathcal K_m(J_k,-F_k).\]
special_cases_latex: GMRES uses the minimum-residual condition for a general square matrix.
FOM uses a Galerkin condition with matching trial and test Krylov spaces.
CG requires an appropriate symmetric positive-definite linear system; MINRES requires symmetry.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different projection conditions can produce different corrections from the same Krylov space.
Restarted variants replace an indefinitely growing space by successive spaces of bounded dimension.
boundary_notes: Solver names alone do not guarantee applicability; matrix symmetry and definiteness requirements remain operative.
Preconditioning changes the operator and spaces and is defined separately.
Breakdown, stagnation, and finite-precision loss of orthogonality are not characterized here.

Jacobian-Free Newton–Krylov Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free Newton–Krylov iteration using residual differences for Jacobian products.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_k\), run a Krylov method for the Newton equation without forming \(J(x_k)\). Whenever the inner method requests a product with \(v\neq0\), return \(J(x_k)v\approx[F(x_k+\sigma_{k,v}v)-F(x_k)]/\sigma_{k,v}\), with a nonzero scale \(\sigma_{k,v}\) chosen to balance truncation and evaluation error. Stop the inner iteration when its computed linear residual satisfies the forcing tolerance, set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), and stop the outer iteration when \(\|F(x_k)\|\) meets the requested tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov solver receives Jacobian-vector products from residual differences, avoiding explicit Jacobian assembly while retaining an inexact Newton stopping rule.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is differentiable near all sampled points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov iteration
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be differentiable. A Krylov solver for \(J(x_k)s=-F(x_k)\) requires products of the current Jacobian with vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth root finding. Jacobian-free means that Krylov matrix–vector products are supplied without assembling or storing the full Jacobian; preconditioners may still contain derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov method is an inexact Newton–Krylov method in which each requested product \(J(x_k)v\) is replaced by a matrix-free directional approximation, canonically \[\mathcal J_{k,\varepsilon}(v)=\frac{F(x_k+\varepsilon_{k,v}v)-F(x_k)}{\varepsilon_{k,v}},\qquad \varepsilon_{k,v}\ne0,\] with sampled points in \(D\). The Krylov process approximately solves the resulting Newton equation until its chosen residual test is met, and no full matrix \(J(x_k)\) is formed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This method applies an inexact Newton–Krylov iteration while supplying every Jacobian–vector product through residual evaluations, typically a directional finite difference. The full Jacobian is neither assembled nor stored. The inner solver uses these products to obtain a correction satisfying its forcing tolerance, after which the outer iterate is updated.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If the exact directional derivative is available without matrix assembly, one may use \[\mathcal J_k(v)=\left.\frac{d}{dt}F(x_k+tv)\right|_{t=0}.\]
special_cases_latex: Forward directional differencing uses one perturbed residual evaluation per requested product when \(F(x_k)\) is cached.
Centered directional differencing uses two perturbed evaluations and \([F(x_k+\varepsilon v)-F(x_k-\varepsilon v)]/(2\varepsilon)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Storage of a dense \(n\times n\) Jacobian is not required by the outer–inner iteration.
The finite-difference map \(v\mapsto\mathcal J_{k,\varepsilon}(v)\) may fail to be exactly linear when \(\varepsilon_{k,v}\) depends on \(v\) or arithmetic is finite.
boundary_notes: The perturbation must keep \(x_k+\varepsilon_{k,v}v\) in the domain.
Jacobian-free does not mean derivative-free in the mathematical limit, because the product approximates a directional derivative.
A separately assembled preconditioner is compatible with this definition.

notation.meaning: matrix-free approximation to the current Jacobian action

Newton–Krylov Preconditioning Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent left- and right-preconditioned interfaces for Newton–Krylov inner solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Newton equation \(J_k s=-F_k\), an invertible left preconditioner \(M_k\) gives \(M_k^{-1}J_k s=-M_k^{-1}F_k\). An invertible right preconditioner gives \(J_kM_k^{-1}y=-F_k\) followed by \(s=M_k^{-1}y\). A split interface with \(M_k=M_{L,k}M_{R,k}\) gives \(M_{L,k}^{-1}J_kM_{R,k}^{-1}y=-M_{L,k}^{-1}F_k\) and \(s=M_{R,k}^{-1}y\). Right and split interfaces retain the original nonlinear residual for outer acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Preconditioning may act on the left, right, or both sides; right-preconditioned variables must be mapped back before updating the nonlinear iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left and right preconditioning interfaces for Newton–Krylov solves
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At outer iteration \(k\), let \(J_k=J(x_k)\), \(F_k=F(x_k)\), and let \(P_k:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be an invertible linear operator whose action or approximate inverse action is computationally available.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Newton–Krylov linear solves. The interface is algebraic and does not prescribe how the preconditioner is constructed or updated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A left-preconditioned interface presents the Krylov solver with \[P_k^{-1}J_ks=-P_k^{-1}F_k,\] and measures the transformed residual unless an additional true-residual test is imposed. A right-preconditioned interface solves \[J_kP_k^{-1}z=-F_k,\qquad s=P_k^{-1}z,\] so the residual in the original Newton equation is \(J_ks+F_k\). A split interface factors the transformation into compatible left and right operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton–Krylov preconditioning interface specifies how an invertible auxiliary operator is inserted into the Newton equation and which residual the inner solver exposes. Left preconditioning transforms both equation sides. Right preconditioning changes variables and recovers the physical Newton correction after the Krylov solve. Split preconditioning combines both transformations.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For right preconditioning, \[J_kP_k^{-1}z+F_k=J_ks+F_k.\]
For left preconditioning, the displayed inner residual is \[P_k^{-1}(J_ks+F_k).\]
special_cases_latex: The identity choice \(P_k=I\) gives the unpreconditioned Newton equation.
A fixed preconditioner uses \(P_k=P\) for all outer iterations; a variable preconditioner permits dependence on \(k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Left and right preconditioning generally generate different Krylov spaces even with the same \(P_k\).
A small left-preconditioned residual does not automatically imply a small unpreconditioned residual without norm-control information for \(P_k\).
boundary_notes: Flexible Krylov methods may be required when the applied right-preconditioner action changes between inner iterations.
The definition assumes an invertible mathematical operator even if its inverse action is computed approximately.
Preconditioning does not alter the desired root of \(F(x)=0\), but it changes the inner linear iteration.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Secant quasi-Newton method for nonlinear equations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(x_k,x_{k+1}\in D\), and define \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) and \(y_k=F(x_{k+1})-F(x_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square nonlinear equations. The family approximates the Jacobian or its inverse using secant data and does not require a fresh exact Jacobian at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct secant quasi-Newton equation method maintains a nonsingular matrix \(B_k\), computes \[B_ks_k=-F(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k,\] and selects the next approximation from the secant set \[B_{k+1}s_k=y_k.\] An inverse form maintains \(H_k\approx J(x_k)^{-1}\), uses \(s_k=-H_kF(x_k)\), and imposes \(H_{k+1}y_k=s_k\). Additional conditions are required because a single vector secant equation does not uniquely determine an \(n\times n\) matrix when \(n>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A secant quasi-Newton method replaces the current Jacobian or inverse Jacobian by an evolving matrix inferred from changes in iterates and residuals. The direct form solves with \(B_k\) and requires the new matrix to map the latest step \(s_k\) to the latest residual change \(y_k\). The inverse form requires the new inverse approximation to map \(y_k\) back to \(s_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The direct secant equation is equivalent to interpolation by the new affine model at the two consecutive iterates.
When \(B_{k+1}\) is invertible and \(H_{k+1}=B_{k+1}^{-1}\), \[B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\iff H_{k+1}y_k=s_k.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the direct secant equation uniquely gives \(B_{k+1}=y_k/s_k\) when \(s_k\ne0\).
Broyden methods choose a rank-one member of the direct or inverse secant set.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(n>1\) and \(s_k\ne0\), the direct secant constraint alone leaves multiple admissible matrices.
The method requires no evaluation of \(J(x_{k+1})\) in its defining update.
boundary_notes: A finite-difference Jacobian reconstructed independently at each iterate is not a propagated secant update.
Nonsingularity of the updated matrix is not guaranteed by the secant equation alone.
Globalization and update-skipping rules are outside this definition.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean smooth quasi-Newton models. The source's claim that positive curvature implies positive definiteness is corrected: positive curvature is necessary for a positive-definite matrix satisfying the secant equation, but is not sufficient to establish positive definiteness of an unspecified matrix.

Let \(f:D\subset\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable on open \(D\), and define \(s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k\) and \(y_k=

abla f(x_k)\). The inverse-Hessian quasi-Newton condition is \(H_{k+1}y_k=s_k\). If \(H_{k+1}\) is nonsingular and \(B_{k+1}=H_{k+1}^{-1}\), its Hessian form is \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\). The latter condition is equivalent to requiring the quadratic model centered at \(x_{k+1}\) to interpolate the gradient at \(x_k\) as well as at its center. e0\) and a positive-definite \(B_{k+1}\) satisfies \(B_{k+1}s_k=y_k\), then \(s_k^Ty_k>0\). The converse does not hold for an otherwise unspecified \(B_{k+1}\).

It represents two-point gradient interpolation and is exact for a quadratic objective with constant Hessian. A positive-definite secant matrix requires positive s_k transpose y_k, but that scalar condition alone does not prove that an arbitrary matrix is positive definite.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exponential relative-scale convergence bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-iterate and weighted-average guarantee for the stated adaptive-metric method applied to the quadratic transform of a strictly positive objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_0\succ0\) induce \(\|\cdot\|_{G_0}\), let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be strictly positive, and set \(\hat f(x)=\tfrac12f(x)^2\). Fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\), assume \(g(x)\in\partial\hat f(x)\) satisfies \(\|g(x)\|_{G_0}^*\le L\) for every \(x\in Q\), and let \(x^*\) be an optimal solution. For the best points \(x_k^*\) generated by the stated method and \(R=\|x_0-x^*\|_{G_0}\), every \(k\ge0\) satisfies \[(1-\delta)\hat f(x_k^*)\le\hat f(x^*)+\frac{L^2R^2}{2n\left(e^{\delta(k+1)/n}-1\right)}.\] The same bound holds with \(\hat f(\tilde x_{k+1})\) in place of \(\hat f(x_k^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the stated relative-scale adaptive-metric method, a uniform dual-norm bound on subgradients of one half the squared positive objective yields an exponentially decaying additive term in the mixed relative-accuracy bound. The guarantee applies both to the best iterate and to the specified weighted average.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: General Hybrid Quasi-Newton Algorithm for One Scalar Nonlinear Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract local-model iteration with a globalization fallback; the extract supplies neither a specific model nor an acceptance rule or convergence guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}\), for \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), test whether to stop. If not, construct a local model of \(f\) around \(x_k\) and find a point \(x_N\) that solves, or comes closest to solving, the model problem. Decide whether to set \(x_{k+1}=x_N\); if not, choose \(x_{k+1}\) using a global strategy that makes more conservative use of the model solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each nonterminal iteration, build a local model of the scalar equation and obtain a model solution or closest available point. Either take that point as the next iterate or use it more conservatively through a globalization strategy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{At each nonterminal iteration, either }x_{k+1}=x_N\text{ or }x_{k+1}\text{ is selected by a more conservative global strategy based on the model solution.}
