knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward and Central Finite-Difference Jacobians
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(x\in\mathcal D\), and choose nonzero steps \(h_j\) such that all sampled points remain in \(\mathcal D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional componentwise differences are covered. The approximations include truncation and floating-point evaluation error.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The forward finite-difference Jacobian \(J_h^+(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) is defined columnwise by \[J_h^+(x)e_j=\frac{F(x+h_je_j)-F(x)}{h_j},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n.\] If both displaced points are admissible, the central finite-difference Jacobian is \[J_h^0(x)e_j=\frac{F(x+h_je_j)-F(x-h_je_j)}{2h_j}.\] If \(J\) is Lipschitz near the sampled segment, then \(\|J_h^+(x)e_j-J(x)e_j\|=O(|h_j|)\). If the relevant third directional derivatives are bounded, then \(\|J_h^0(x)e_j-J(x)e_j\|=O(h_j^2)\). In floating-point arithmetic the steps are chosen away from zero because subtractive cancellation and function-evaluation error grow as \(|h_j|\) decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward finite-difference Jacobian approximates column \(j\) by the residual change caused by perturbing variable \(j\), divided by the perturbation. A central Jacobian uses symmetric positive and negative perturbations. Under standard smoothness, forward truncation error is first order and central truncation error is second order. Steps cannot be reduced indefinitely in floating-point arithmetic because cancellation and evaluation noise eventually dominate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Entrywise, \((J_h^+)_{ij}=[F_i(x+h_je_j)-F_i(x)]/h_j\).
For a direction \(v\), \([F(x+hv)-F(x)]/h\) is a matrix-free finite-difference approximation to \(J(x)v\).
special_cases_latex: A common relative perturbation has the form \(h_j\asymp\sqrt{\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}}\max\{1,|x_j|\}\) for forward differences when function values are accurate to machine precision.
immediate_consequences_latex: A dense forward-difference Jacobian needs \(n\) additional residual evaluations after \(F(x)\) is known.
Central differences typically double the number of displaced evaluations.
boundary_notes: The displayed asymptotic orders are truncation-error statements and do not include noisy evaluations.
One-sided differences must replace central differences near a domain boundary unless another feasible perturbation rule is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward finite-difference Jacobian error bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Columnwise forward differences for a vector-valued map under a quadratic Taylor-remainder bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) have Jacobian \(J\), and suppose \(\|F(x+s)-F(x)-J(x)s\|\le \frac{\gamma}{2}\|s\|^2\) for \(s=he_j\), \(j=1,\ldots,n\). Assume \(h\ne0\), \(x,x+he_j\in D\), and \(\|e_j\|=1\). Define \(A_{\cdot j}=[F(x+he_j)-F(x)]/h\). Then \(\|A_{\cdot j}-J(x)_{\cdot j}\|\le \frac{\gamma}{2}|h|\) for every \(j\). If the vector norm is \(\ell_1\) and the corresponding induced matrix norm is used, then \(\|A-J(x)\|_1\le \frac{\gamma}{2}|h|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the first-order Taylor remainder of a vector-valued map is bounded by gamma times half the squared step norm, every forward-difference Jacobian column has error at most gamma |h|/2. With the l1 norm, the full induced matrix-norm error satisfies the same bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward-Difference Jacobian Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a columnwise forward-difference approximation to a Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m have Jacobian J(x), let h\ne 0, and let e_j be the j\text{-th coordinate vector}. Define A=(a_{ij}) by
\[
a_{ij}=\frac{f_i(x+h e_j)-f_i(x)}{h}.
\]
Equivalently, the j\text{-th column is
\[
A_{\cdot j}=\frac{F(x+h e_j)-F(x)}{h},\qquad j=1,\ldots,n,
\]
which is a forward-difference approximation to J(x)_{\cdot j}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a map F from R^n to R^m with a Jacobian at x and a nonzero increment h, the j-th Jacobian column is approximated by [F(x+h e_j)-F(x)]/h. Componentwise, a_ij=[f_i(x+h e_j)-f_i(x)]/h.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a_{ij}=\frac{f_i(x+h e_j)-f_i(x)}{h},\qquad A_{\cdot j}=\frac{F(x+h e_j)-F(x)}{h}\approx J(x)_{\cdot j}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward-Difference Jacobian Error Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the columnwise error and, under the stated norm choice, the matrix one-norm error of a forward-difference Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m satisfy the conditions referenced as Theorem 1.2.22, with constant \gamma. Let the relevant norm satisfy \|e_j\|=1 for j=1,\ldots,n, let h\ne0, and define
\[
A_{\cdot j}=\frac{F(x+h e_j)-F(x)}{h}.
\]
Then, for every j=1,\ldots,n,
\[
\|A_{\cdot j}-J(x)_{\cdot j}\|\le \frac{\gamma}{2}|h|.
\]
If the \ell_1 norm is used, then
\[
\|A-J(x)\|_1\le \frac{\gamma}{2}|h|.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the smoothness conditions referenced by the source, each forward-difference Jacobian column differs from the true column by at most gamma times |h| divided by two. When the l1 norm is used, the full matrix error obeys the same bound.
assumptions_latex: F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\text{ satisfies the conditions of the referenced Theorem 1.2.22 with constant }\gamma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall j\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \|A_{\cdot j}-J(x)_{\cdot j}\|\le\frac{\gamma}{2}|h|;\qquad \|A-J(x)\|_1\le\frac{\gamma}{2}|h|\ \text{when the }\ell_1\text{ norm is used}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structurally Orthogonal Coloring and Compressed Jacobian Recovery
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have a known structural nonzero pattern \(\mathcal Z\). Let \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) partition \(\{1,ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition covers column coloring for sparse Jacobians and compressed directional evaluations. The sparsity pattern is assumed known and valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The partition is structurally orthogonal if \[j\ne\ell,\ j,\ell\in C_c\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nexists i\text{ with }(i,j)\in\mathcal Z\text{ and }(i,\ell)\in\mathcal Z.\] For nonzero scaling coefficients \(d_j\), define seed vectors \[s_c=\sum_{j\in C_c}d_je_j,\qquad c=1,\ldots,q,\] and compressed products \(y_c=J(x)s_c\), or finite-difference approximations to these products. The recovery operator \(\mathcal R_{\mathcal Z,C,d}\) is defined on every structural nonzero by \[\widehat J_{ij}=\frac{(y_c)_i}{d_j}\quad\text{when }j\in C_c\text{ and }(i,j)\in\mathcal Z,\] and sets entries outside \(\mathcal Z\) to zero. Structural orthogonality makes the contributing column unique in every row-color pair, so exact compressed products recover \(J(x)\) exactly on \(\mathcal Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Columns with no possible nonzero in a common row may share one color. A seed combines all columns of a color, and one Jacobian-vector product or one simultaneous finite-difference perturbation produces their compressed information. Because at most one column of the color contributes to any row, each structural nonzero is recovered by dividing the corresponding compressed component by its seed coefficient. With exact products and a correct pattern, recovery is exact; finite-difference products add approximation error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R_{\mathcal Z,C,d}\bigl(JS\bigr)=J,\qquad S=[s_1\ \cdots\ s_q],\] whenever the coloring is structurally orthogonal and \(\operatorname{supp}(J)\subseteq\mathcal Z\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The column-intersection graph joins columns sharing a structural row; \(C_1,\ldots,C_q\) are the color classes of a proper coloring of that graph.
special_cases_latex: A structurally tridiagonal Jacobian admits three repeating column colors, independent of \(n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The number of compressed evaluations is \(q\), rather than \(n\).
An invalid sparsity pattern can alias two contributions and corrupt recovery.
boundary_notes: Minimum coloring is not required; any valid coloring defines a correct interface.
The extraction artifact in the ambient partition range must be read as \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Jacobian Coloring
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column-intersection coloring used to group structurally noninterfering Jacobian columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have known structural sparsity pattern \(\mathcal S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\times\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Its column-intersection graph has vertices \(1,\ldots,n\) and an edge \(\{j,k\}\) whenever some row \(i\) satisfies \((i,j)\in\mathcal S\) and \((i,k)\in\mathcal S\). A sparse Jacobian column coloring is a map \(c:\{1,\ldots,n\}\to\{1,\ldots,q\}\) that is proper on this graph. Consequently, columns assigned the same color have disjoint structural row supports and may be combined in one directional derivative without rowwise interference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Color Jacobian columns so that columns sharing a potentially nonzero row receive different colors. Same-colored columns can then be probed simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: The structural sparsity pattern \(\mathcal S\) contains every position that can be nonzero at the point of interest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(j)=c(k)\) and \(j\neq k\) imply no \(i\) has both \((i,j)\in\mathcal S\) and \((i,k)\in\mathcal S\).

notation.meaning: structural nonzero pattern of the Jacobian

children.top_down_role: Compressed derivative storage, recovery interfaces, structural requirements, and ambiguity risks.

knowledge_statements.title: Compressed Jacobian Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Seed-matrix compression of a structurally sparse Jacobian using noninterfering column groups.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c\) be a proper coloring of the column-intersection graph of \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), using \(q\) colors. Define the seed matrix \(S\in\{0,1\}^{n\times q}\) by \(S_{jk}=1\) exactly when \(c(j)=k\). The compressed Jacobian is \(Y=JS\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times q}\), whose color column satisfies \(Y_{:k}=\sum_{j:c(j)=k}J_{:j}\). Because same-colored columns have disjoint structural row supports, every structurally permitted entry of \(J\) appears without collision in the corresponding entry of \(Y\); thus \((Y,S,\mathcal S)\) represents \(J\) uniquely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A seed matrix sums same-colored Jacobian columns into fewer compressed columns. Structural noninterference makes the original sparse entries uniquely identifiable.
assumptions_latex: The sparsity pattern \(\mathcal S\) is known and structurally valid.
The coloring \(c\) is proper for the column-intersection graph induced by \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y=JS\), with \(Y_{:k}=\sum_{j:c(j)=k}J_{:j}\), uniquely determines all entries allowed by \(\mathcal S\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the container, and the seed-matrix dimensions, compressed product, and collision-free uniqueness claim are mathematically coherent under the stated structural-pattern assumption. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Coloring-Based Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct rowwise recovery of sparse Jacobian entries from a coloring-compressed product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a structural pattern \(\mathcal S\), a proper column coloring \(c\), its seed matrix \(S\), and the compressed product \(Y=JS\). Initialize \(\widehat J=0\). For every \((i,j)\in\mathcal S\), set \(\widehat J_{ij}=Y_{i,c(j)}\); retain zero outside \(\mathcal S\). Proper coloring ensures that, in row \(i\), column \(j\) is the only structurally nonzero column of color \(c(j)\), so \(Y_{i,c(j)}=J_{ij}\). Output \(\widehat J\). If the pattern omits a nonzero or the coloring permits a collision, this direct recovery rule need not equal \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recover each permitted Jacobian entry from its row and color in the compressed product. Exact recovery requires a complete pattern and collision-free coloring.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) contains all nonzeros of \(J\), and \(c\) is proper for its column-intersection graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the recovery container, and the direct recovery rule is correct under a complete structural pattern and proper column coloring. No inspectable source is supplied for the recovery algorithm and its failure boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matrix-Free Jacobian and Transpose-Jacobian Actions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathcal D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be differentiable at \(x\), and let \(J=F'(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pair exposes linear actions without requiring storage or assembly of the matrix \(J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A primal-adjoint matrix-free product pair at \(x\) is a pair of linear operators \[\mathsf P_x:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m,\qquad \mathsf A_x:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n\] satisfying \[\mathsf P_x(v)=Jv,qquad \mathsf A_x(w)=J^Tw,\qquad w^T\mathsf P_x(v)=v^T\mathsf A_x(w)\] for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(w\in\mathbb R^m\). The interface is matrix-free when these actions are evaluated from the residual computation, automatic differentiation, an adjoint program, or a directional approximation without forming all entries of \(J\). An approximate pair \((\widetilde{\mathsf P}_x,\widetilde{\mathsf A}_x)\) must state action-error bounds or a transpose-consistency tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The primal operator maps a parameter-space direction to its linearized residual change, \(Jv\). The adjoint operator maps a residual-space weight to \(J^Tw\). They represent the same Jacobian precisely when their bilinear products agree for every pair of vectors. Matrix-free means that callers can request these actions without receiving or storing the full matrix. Forward automatic differentiation naturally supplies the primal action, while reverse differentiation of \(w^TF(x)\) supplies the adjoint action.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mathsf A_x\) is the Euclidean adjoint of \(\mathsf P_x\).
The residual gradient is obtained matrix-free as \(\nabla\tfrac12\|F(x)\|^2=\mathsf A_x(F(x))\).
special_cases_latex: A finite-difference primal action is \([F(x+hv)-F(x)]/h\).
For square Newton-Krylov methods, Krylov iterations may require only \(v\mapsto\mathsf P_x(v)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Normal-equation products can be computed as \(v\mapsto\mathsf A_x(\mathsf P_x(v))\).
A dot-product test detects incompatibility between independently implemented primal and adjoint products.
boundary_notes: A primal-only interface cannot generally compute least-squares gradients.
The control character before “qquad” in the formal statement is an extraction artifact and requires correction to \(\qquad\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Jacobian Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional-derivative access to Jacobian-vector products without materializing the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Fréchet differentiable at \(x\), with Jacobian \(J_F(x)\). For any direction \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the matrix-free Jacobian product is represented by the directional derivative \[J_F(x)v=DF(x)[v]=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{F(x+tv)-F(x)}{t}.\] An implementation may evaluate this product by forward-mode automatic differentiation or approximate it by a directional finite difference, without storing the entries of \(J_F(x)\). A linearized solver using this interface must receive a mapping that is linear in \(v\) to the accuracy required by that solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Jacobian-vector product is the residual's directional derivative. It can be evaluated by tangent propagation or approximated by finite differences without assembling the Jacobian.

notation.meaning: directional action of the derivative at x on v

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Free Adjoint Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse scalarization representation of transposed-Jacobian products without forming the Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be differentiable at \(x\), and fix \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Define the scalarized residual \(\phi_u(z)=u^{\mathsf T}F(z)\), treating \(u\) as constant. Then \[\nabla\phi_u(x)=J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}u.\] Hence a matrix-free adjoint-product oracle may compute \(J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}u\) by one reverse differentiation of the residual program seeded by the output cotangent \(u\), without forming \(J_F(x)\). The formula uses Euclidean inner products; under other inner products, the adjoint includes the corresponding Riesz maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transpose-Jacobian times a vector equals the gradient of the vector-weighted residual scalarization, enabling reverse-mode evaluation without storing the Jacobian.
assumptions_latex: \(u\) is constant with respect to the differentiation variable.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the adjoint-product container, and the Euclidean scalarization identity, reverse-mode interpretation, and non-Euclidean caveat are consistent. An authoritative source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint representation of the reduced gradient
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a differentiable reduced objective defined through an implicit state equation, the adjoint equation eliminates the state sensitivity from the gradient formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let J:Y\times V\to\mathbb{R} and E:Y\times V\to W, let E(y(u),u)=0, and define j(u)=J(y(u),u). If J and E are Fréchet differentiable near (y(u),u), the state map u\mapsto y(u) is Fréchet differentiable there, and E_y(y(u),u) is continuously invertible, then the unique adjoint state w(u)\in W^* satisfies E_y(y(u),u)^*w(u)=-J_y(y(u),u), and the reduced derivative is j'(u)=J_u(y(u),u)+E_u(y(u),u)^*w(u). Thus j'(u) is obtained by solving the state equation, solving the adjoint equation, and evaluating this formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let the state y(u) be determined by E(y(u),u)=0 and let the reduced objective be j(u)=J(y(u),u). If J and E are Fréchet differentiable, the state map is Fréchet differentiable, and the state derivative with respect to y is continuously invertible, then the adjoint equation has a unique solution. The reduced gradient equals the partial control derivative of J plus the adjoint action of the partial control derivative of E. It can therefore be computed by solving the state equation, then the adjoint equation, and finally evaluating the reduced-gradient formula.
assumptions_latex: J\text{ and }E\text{ are Fréchet differentiable near }(y(u),u)
u\mapsto y(u)\text{ is Fréchet differentiable near }u

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirectional Product Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean adjoint identity connecting matrix-free primal and transposed-Jacobian product oracles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_x:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(A_x:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be linear oracles intended to implement \(J_F(x)v\) and \(J_F(x)^{\mathsf T}u\). They are bidirectionally consistent at \(x\) exactly when \[u^{\mathsf T}P_x(v)=v^{\mathsf T}A_x(u)\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^m,v\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] In exact arithmetic this condition is equivalent to \(A_x=P_x^{\mathsf T}\). For approximate implementations, a scale-aware defect is \(\delta(u,v)=|u^{\mathsf T}P_x(v)-v^{\mathsf T}A_x(u)|/(\|u\|\,\|P_x(v)\|+\|v\|\,\|A_x(u)\|)\) whenever the denominator is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Primal and adjoint product oracles are consistent when their inner products agree for every input pair; a normalized inner-product defect supports numerical checking.
assumptions_latex: \(P_x\) and \(A_x\) are linear maps between Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u^{\mathsf T}P_x(v)=v^{\mathsf T}A_x(u)\) for all \(u,v\), equivalently \(A_x=P_x^{\mathsf T}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representation Family for the Linearized Residual Subproblem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At a point \(x\), let \(r=F(x)\in\mathbb R^m\), \(J=F'(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and consider \(\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\|Js+r\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns unconstrained finite-dimensional linear least squares. Rank-deficient cases use the minimum-norm convention when a unique step is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linearized-subproblem representation is any algebraically equivalent specification of the solution set \[\mathcal S_* = \operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\|Js+r\|_2.\] The canonical representations are: the normal equations \[J^T(Js+r)=0;\] the residual-augmented equations with \(z=Js+r\), \[\begin{bmatrix}I&-J\\J^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r\\0\end{bmatrix};\] an orthogonal factorization of \(J\); and the spectral formula \(s_*=-J^+r\) for the minimum-norm minimizer. If \(J\) has full column rank, \(\mathcal S_*\) is a singleton and all four representations return the same step. If \(J\) is rank deficient, the normal and augmented equations characterize all least-squares minimizers, while the pseudoinverse selects the one orthogonal to \(\ker J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The linearized residual subproblem minimizes \(\|Js+r\|_2\). It can be represented by normal equations, a larger symmetric augmented system, an orthogonal factorization, or an SVD and pseudoinverse. With full column rank these descriptions identify one common step. With rank deficiency, the least-squares minimizer need not be unique; the pseudoinverse representation selects the unique minimizer of smallest Euclidean norm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The residual \(z_*=Js_*+r\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(J)\).
The model \(\tfrac12\|Js+r\|_2^2\) has gradient \(J^T(Js+r)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(m=n\) and \(J\) is nonsingular, the solution is the Newton step \(s_*=-J^{-1}r\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Representation choice changes numerical conditioning and storage but not the exact solution set.
Forming \(J^TJ\) squares the two-norm condition number when \(J\) has full column rank.
boundary_notes: Regularized and trust-region subproblems modify the exact solution set and are not equivalent representations of the unregularized problem.
Weighted norms require corresponding weighted normal and augmented systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Equation Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal-equation form of the unconstrained linearized residual least-squares subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(f\in\mathbb{R}^m\), consider \(\min_{p\in\mathbb{R}^n}\tfrac12\|f+Jp\|_2^2\). A vector \(p_*\) solves this convex problem exactly when it satisfies the normal equations \[J^{\mathsf T}Jp_*=-J^{\mathsf T}f.\] If \(J\) has full column rank, \(J^{\mathsf T}J\) is positive definite and \(p_*\) is unique. Forming the normal equations squares the spectral condition number in the full-rank case: \(\kappa_2(J^{\mathsf T}J)=\kappa_2(J)^2\), which can magnify numerical sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearized least-squares step satisfies the normal equations. Full column rank gives a unique solution, but forming the Gram matrix squares the spectral condition number.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean least-squares problem is unconstrained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Equations for a Linearized Residual Model
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(r\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(q(s)=\tfrac12\|Js+r\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The representation is exact in real arithmetic for unweighted linear least squares. Both full-rank and rank-deficient matrices are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The normal-equation representation of the linearized residual subproblem is \[J^TJs=-J^Tr.\] Its solution set equals \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in\mathbb R^n}q(s)=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:J^T(Js+r)=0\}.\] If \(\operatorname{rank}(J)=n\), then \(J^TJ\) is positive definite and the unique step is \[s_*=-(J^TJ)^{-1}J^Tr.\] If \(J\) is rank deficient, the system remains consistent but may have multiple solutions; all solutions give the same projected residual \(Js_*+r\), and the minimum-norm member is \(-J^+r\). A weighted representation for symmetric positive definite \(W\) is \(J^TWJs=-J^TWr\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal equations set the gradient of the squared linearized residual to zero. Their solutions are exactly the least-squares minimizers. Full column rank makes \(J^TJ\) positive definite and the step unique. Rank deficiency makes the coefficient matrix singular but does not make the normal equations inconsistent; instead, multiple steps can produce the same optimal residual. A pseudoinverse is needed when the minimum-norm step is required.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The optimal residual is orthogonal to every column of \(J\).
For full column rank, the normal equations are the first-order conditions of a strictly convex quadratic.
special_cases_latex: If \(J\) is square and nonsingular, the normal-equation solution equals \(-J^{-1}r\).
With Levenberg regularization, the modified equations are \((J^TJ+\lambda I)s=-J^Tr\), which define a different problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: For full column rank, \(\kappa_2(J^TJ)=\kappa_2(J)^2\).
Cholesky factorization is applicable to \(J^TJ\) only when positive definiteness is numerically reliable.
boundary_notes: Explicit formation of \(J^TJ\) may magnify conditioning and rounding difficulties.
The regularized equations are not equivalent to the unregularized normal equations when \(\lambda>0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-System Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric saddle-point representation of the unconstrained linearized residual least-squares problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(f\in\mathbb{R}^m\), introduce \(r=-(f+Jp)\). The first-order conditions for \(\min_p\tfrac12\|f+Jp\|_2^2\) are equivalently represented by the augmented system \[\begin{pmatrix}I_m&J\\J^{\mathsf T}&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}r\\p\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-f\\0\end{pmatrix}.\] Its first block equation defines the signed residual, while its second imposes \(J^{\mathsf T}r=0\). Eliminating \(r\) yields \(J^{\mathsf T}Jp=-J^{\mathsf T}f\). If \(J\) has full column rank, the augmented coefficient matrix is nonsingular and the step is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Introducing the signed linearized residual converts least squares into a symmetric augmented system. Eliminating that residual recovers the normal equations.
assumptions_latex: For nonsingularity, \(J\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((r,p)\) solves the augmented system if and only if \(r=-(f+Jp)\) and \(p\) satisfies the least-squares first-order conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the augmented-system container. The sign convention, block equations, elimination to the normal equations, and nonsingularity claim under full column rank are consistent. No inspectable source with a relevant locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Augmented Saddle-Point System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(r\in\mathbb R^m\), and define the linearized least-squares problem \(\min_s\tfrac12\|Js+r\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition concerns the unweighted Euclidean least-squares augmented system. It avoids explicitly forming \(J^TJ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The augmented-system representation introduces the linearized residual variable \(z=Js+r\) and defines \((z,s)\) by \[\begin{bmatrix}I_m&-J\\J^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}z\\s\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}r\\0\end{bmatrix}.\] Equivalently, \[z-Js=r,\qquad J^Tz=0.\] Eliminating \(z\) yields \(J^TJs=-J^Tr\), so every augmented-system solution produces a least-squares step. Conversely, every least-squares minimizer \(s\) paired with \(z=Js+r\) solves the block equations. If \(J\) has full column rank, the block matrix is nonsingular and the pair is unique. Under rank deficiency, \(z\) remains unique but \(s\) may not be unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The augmented representation keeps the optimal residual as an explicit variable and couples it to the step in a symmetric indefinite block system. The first block equation defines the residual; the second imposes its orthogonality to the Jacobian range. Eliminating the residual gives the normal equations, while inserting any least-squares minimizer gives an augmented-system solution. Full column rank makes the block system nonsingular. Rank deficiency leaves the optimal residual unique but permits multiple steps.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Changing variables to \(y=-s\) gives the sign convention \(z+Jy=r\), \(J^Tz=0\).
For positive-definite weight \(W\), one augmented form uses \(W^{-1}z-Js=r\) and \(J^Tz=0\).
special_cases_latex: When \(J\) is square and nonsingular, \(z=0\) and \(s=-J^{-1}r\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The block form avoids explicit multiplication \(J^TJ\).
Its coefficient matrix is symmetric but indefinite whenever both block dimensions are positive.
boundary_notes: No supplied source was inspected that states this exact residual-augmented system for general linear least squares.
Alternative augmented systems in constrained optimization may have different blocks and signs.
review_flags: A precise authoritative source for the displayed general least-squares augmented system is required.

Orthogonal-Factorization Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Thin-QR representation of a full-column-rank linearized residual least-squares step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\), have full column rank and thin QR factorization \(J=QR\), where \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_n\) and \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular upper triangular. Then the unique solution of \(\min_p\tfrac12\|f+Jp\|_2^2\) is represented by \[Rp_*=-Q^{\mathsf T}f,\qquad p_*=-R^{-1}Q^{\mathsf T}f.\] Extending \(Q\) to an orthogonal matrix shows that the minimum residual norm is the norm of the component of \(f\) orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}(J)\). This representation avoids explicitly forming \(J^{\mathsf T}J\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A thin QR factorization reduces full-rank least squares to triangular solution and exposes the residual component orthogonal to the Jacobian range.
assumptions_latex: \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(m\ge n\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*=-R^{-1}Q^{\mathsf T}f\) is the unique minimizer of \(\tfrac12\|f+Jp\|_2^2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the orthogonal-factorization container. The thin-QR dimensions, triangular system, unique minimizer, orthogonal residual interpretation, and avoidance of the Gram matrix are coherent under full column rank. An inspectable authoritative source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: QR Representation of a Linearized Least-Squares Step
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\geq n\), let \(r\in\mathbb R^m\), and suppose initially that \(\operatorname{rank}(J)=n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The primary definition uses full-column-rank QR. Rank-revealing pivoted QR is identified as the nearby rank-deficient variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An orthogonal-factorization representation writes \[J=Q\begin{bmatrix}R\\0\end{bmatrix},\qquad Q=[Q_1\ Q_2],\] where \(Q\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is orthogonal and \(R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular upper triangular. The unique minimizer of \(\|Js+r\|_2\) is defined by the triangular system \[Rs=-Q_1^Tr,\qquad s_*=-R^{-1}Q_1^Tr.\] Its optimal residual is \[Js_*+r=Q_2Q_2^Tr,\qquad \|Js_*+r\|_2=\|Q_2^Tr\|_2.\] For a column-pivoted factorization \(J\Pi=Q[R_{11}\ R_{12};0\ R_{22};0\ 0]\), the numerical rank is determined from the leading triangular block and the solution convention must state how free components are chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The QR representation rotates residual space without changing Euclidean norms. With full column rank, the transformed least-squares problem separates into a triangular equation for the step and an orthogonal residual component that cannot be reduced. The step is obtained without forming \(J^TJ\). Column pivoting and a rank decision extend the representation to rank-deficient or nearly rank-deficient matrices, but a minimum-norm convention then requires additional specification.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A thin QR factorization \(J=Q_1R\) suffices to compute the step, while an orthogonal complement describes the irreducible residual.
The normal equations factor as \(J^TJ=R^TR\).
special_cases_latex: If \(m=n\), the zero block is absent and QR solves the square Newton equation.
Givens rotations or Householder transformations may realize the same orthogonal factorization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Orthogonal transformations preserve the two-norm.
QR avoids the condition-number squaring caused by explicitly forming normal equations.
boundary_notes: Unpivoted QR does not by itself define a reliable numerical-rank decision.
For \(m<n\), an LQ or transposed-QR representation is more natural.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular-Value and Moore–Penrose Representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r_J\), and let \(J=U\Sigma V^T\) be a singular value decomposition with singular values \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{r_J}>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition covers rectangular and rank-deficient linearized residual systems and selects the exact minimum-norm least-squares step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The spectral representation of \(J\) is \[J=U\Sigma V^T=\sum_{i=1}^{r_J}\sigma_i u_iv_i^T.\] Its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is \[J^+=V\Sigma^+U^T=\sum_{i=1}^{r_J}\sigma_i^{-1}v_iu_i^T,\] where zero singular values remain zero in \(\Sigma^+\). For the linearized residual problem \(\min_s\|Js+r\|_2\), the pseudoinverse representation selects \[s_*=-J^+r=-\sum_{i=1}^{r_J}\frac{u_i^Tr}{\sigma_i}v_i.\] This \(s_*\) is the unique vector of minimum Euclidean norm among all least-squares minimizers. The corresponding residual is \[(I-JJ^+)r,\] and the orthogonal projectors onto \(\operatorname{range}(J)\) and \(\operatorname{range}(J^T)\) are \(JJ^+\) and \(J^+J\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectral representation resolves the Jacobian into singular directions and gains. The pseudoinverse reciprocates each positive singular value and leaves null directions at zero. Applying it to the negative residual gives the unique least-squares step of smallest Euclidean norm, including for rectangular or rank-deficient systems. The unreduced residual is the component of \(r\) orthogonal to the Jacobian range. Small singular values reveal directions in which the step is highly sensitive.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The minimum-norm step satisfies \(s_*\in\operatorname{range}(J^T)=\ker(J)^\perp\).
If \(J\) has full column rank, \(J^+=(J^TJ)^{-1}J^T\).
If \(J\) is square and nonsingular, \(J^+=J^{-1}\).
special_cases_latex: A truncated pseudoinverse replaces reciprocals below a threshold by zero, thereby defining a regularized problem rather than the exact pseudoinverse problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: The number of positive singular values equals \(\operatorname{rank}(J)\).
boundary_notes: Numerical rank requires a tolerance and may differ from exact algebraic rank.
Truncation or Tikhonov damping changes the step and must be declared separately.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Value Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact SVD representation of a linearized least-squares subproblem and its minimum-norm solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r\) and compact singular-value decomposition \(A=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^{\mathsf T}\), where \(\Sigma_r=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)\) and \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_r>0\). For \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), every least-squares minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|_2\) has the representation \[x=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{\mathsf T}b+z,\qquad z\in\ker(A).\] The unique minimum-Euclidean-norm minimizer is \[x_{\min}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{u_i^{\mathsf T}b}{\sigma_i}v_i.\] Thus singular directions scale residual data by reciprocal nonzero singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SVD decomposes a linear least-squares solution into singular directions; reciprocal nonzero singular values produce the unique minimum-norm solution, while null-space components parameterize all other minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{\min}=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r^{\mathsf T}b\), and all minimizers equal \(x_{\min}+z\) with \(z\in\ker(A)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pseudoinverse Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moore–Penrose representation of solutions and residual projections for a linearized least-squares system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), let \(A^{\dagger}\) be the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. The complete set of least-squares minimizers is \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\|Ax-b\|_2=\{A^{\dagger}b+(I-A^{\dagger}A)w:w\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\}.\] Its unique minimum-norm member is \(x_{\min}=A^{\dagger}b\). The fitted vector and residual are \(Ax_{\min}=AA^{\dagger}b\) and \(b-Ax_{\min}=(I-AA^{\dagger})b\), respectively, where \(AA^{\dagger}\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\operatorname{range}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution, while a null-space projector parameterizes all solutions and a range projector determines the fitted residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{min}=A^{\dagger}b\), with all least-squares minimizers given by \(A^{\dagger}b+(I-A^{\dagger}A)w\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the null space of A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pseudoinverse as the minimum-norm least-squares solution operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for a linear operator between normed inner-product spaces whenever the stated unique minimum-norm least-squares solution exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an operator \(A:G\to H\) and \(y\in H\), let \(x_0\) be the unique minimum-norm vector among all \(x_1\in G\) satisfying \[\|Ax_1-y\|=\min_{x\in G}\|Ax-y\|.\] The pseudoinverse \(A^\dagger\) is defined by \(A^\dagger y=x_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse maps each target vector to the unique minimum-norm vector among all least-squares minimizers of the residual norm.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is the unique minimum-norm element of }\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in G}\|Ax-y\|

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oblique pseudoinverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the pseudoinverse associated with a chosen complementary subspace and records its orthogonal special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), \(p\le n\), and let \(\mathcal Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be such that the oblique projector \(E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)}\) onto \(\mathcal Y\) along \(\mathcal N(X)\) is well-defined. The oblique pseudoinverse of \(X\) associated with \(\mathcal Y\) is \[X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}:=E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)}X^{\dagger}.\] If \(\mathcal Y=\mathcal N(X)^\perp=\mathcal R(X^T)\), then \(E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)}=P_{\mathcal N(X)^\perp}\) and \(X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=X^{\dagger}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a p-by-n matrix X and a subspace Y complementary to the nullspace of X, the oblique pseudoinverse is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse followed by projection onto Y along the nullspace. Choosing the orthogonal complement of the nullspace recovers the ordinary pseudoinverse.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)}X^{\dagger},\qquad X_{\mathcal N(X)^\perp}^{\dagger}=X^{\dagger}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Algebraic and adjoint identities for a closed-range pseudoinverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties of the pseudoinverse of a bounded closed-range linear operator between Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a bounded linear operator with closed range. Its pseudoinverse \(A^\dagger\) is linear and bounded, and satisfies \[(A^\dagger)^\dagger=A,\qquad (A^*)^\dagger=(A^\dagger)^*,\] \[A^\dagger A A^\dagger=A^\dagger,\qquad A A^\dagger A=A,\qquad (A^\dagger A)^*=A^\dagger A,\] and \[A^\dagger=(A^*A)^\dagger A^*=A^*(AA^*)^\dagger.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a bounded closed-range linear operator, the pseudoinverse is bounded and linear, is involutive under pseudoinversion, commutes with taking adjoints, satisfies the generalized-inverse and self-adjointness identities, and admits representations through the pseudoinverses of A-star A and A A-star.
assumptions_latex: A:G\to H\text{ is bounded and linear}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A^\dagger\text{ is bounded and linear},\quad (A^\dagger)^\dagger=A,\quad (A^*)^\dagger=(A^\dagger)^*,\quad A^\dagger A A^\dagger=A^\dagger,\quad A A^\dagger A=A,\quad (A^\dagger A)^*=A^\dagger A,\quad A^\dagger=(A^*A)^\dagger A^*=A^*(AA^*)^\dagger

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Identities for an oblique pseudoinverse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the two associated projection products, recovery of the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, and a range-factor representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}\), let \(\mathcal X=\mathcal R(X)\), and let \(\mathcal Y\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be complementary to \(\mathcal N(X)\). For \(X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)}X^{\dagger}\), \[XX_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=P_{\mathcal X},\qquad X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}X=E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)},\qquad X^{\dagger}=P_{\mathcal R(X^T)}X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}.\] Moreover, if \(\mathcal Y=\mathcal R(Y)\) for a matrix \(Y\), then \[X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=Y(XY)^{\dagger}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oblique pseudoinverse is a right inverse up to orthogonal projection onto the range of X, while its product with X is the oblique projector onto Y along the nullspace. Orthogonally projecting it onto the row space recovers the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. If Y is represented as the range of a matrix Y, the oblique pseudoinverse equals Y times the pseudoinverse of XY.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: XX_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=P_{\mathcal X},\quad X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}X=E_{\mathcal Y,\mathcal N(X)},\quad X^{\dagger}=P_{\mathcal R(X^T)}X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger};\quad \mathcal Y=\mathcal R(Y)\Rightarrow X_{\mathcal Y}^{\dagger}=Y(XY)^{\dagger}

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Rank Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based numerical-rank rule for truncated spectral solution operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) with singular values \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_p\geq0\), where \(p=\min(m,n)\). Given an absolute tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm{abs}}\geq0\) and relative tolerance \(\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\geq0\), define \(\tau=\max\{\tau_{\mathrm{abs}},\tau_{\mathrm{rel}}\sigma_1\}\). The thresholded numerical rank and pseudoinverse are \[r_{\tau}=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\},\qquad A^{\dagger}_{\tau}=\sum_{\sigma_i>\tau}\sigma_i^{-1}v_i u_i^{\mathsf T}.\] A singular direction is retained exactly when \(\sigma_i>\tau\); discarded directions contribute neither to \(r_{\tau}\) nor to the computed step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined absolute-relative singular-value tolerance defines numerical rank and a truncated pseudoinverse by retaining exactly the singular values above the threshold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear least-squares solve with numerical-rank certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(\tau\ge0\) be a rank threshold. Write an SVD as \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_q)V^T\), where \(q=\min\{m,n\}\) and \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real linear least squares, including rectangular and numerically rank-deficient matrices; the definition specifies a mathematical interface rather than a particular factorization implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear solve-rank management interface at threshold \(\tau\) is a map \(\mathcal S_\tau:(A,b)\mapsto(p,\widehat r,\eta)\) satisfying \(\widehat r=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}\), \(p=\sum_{\sigma_i>\tau}(u_i^Tb/\sigma_i)v_i\), and \(\eta=\|Ap-b\|_2\). Thus \(p\) is the minimum-norm solution of the truncated least-squares problem on the retained right-singular subspace, \(\widehat r\) is its declared numerical rank, and \(\eta\) is the returned residual certificate. At \(\tau=0\), all nonzero singular directions are retained and \(p=A^\dagger b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a real matrix, right-hand side, and nonnegative rank threshold, the interface returns the truncated-SVD least-squares vector, the number of singular values exceeding the threshold, and the norm of the resulting residual. The returned vector is the minimum-norm solution on the retained singular subspace. With zero threshold it is the Moore–Penrose least-squares solution.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(V_\tau\) and \(U_\tau\) contain the retained singular vectors and \(\Sigma_\tau\) the retained singular values, then \(p=V_\tau\Sigma_\tau^{-1}U_\tau^Tb\).
For \(\tau=0\), \(p\in\arg\min_x\|Ax-b\|_2\) and \(p\perp\ker A\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full column rank and \(\tau<\sigma_n\), then \(p=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb\).
If \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\) and every nonzero singular direction is retained, then \(\eta=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The declared nullity is \(n-\widehat r\).
Discarded directions cannot enlarge \(\|p\|_2\) relative to retaining the same directions with smaller threshold.
boundary_notes: The threshold defines numerical rank; it need not equal exact algebraic rank.
Backward-error estimates, pivot-growth diagnostics, and floating-point status codes are outside this mathematical interface.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear least-squares solve with numerical-rank certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparsity regimes for direct least-squares solution
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\operatorname{nnz}(M)\) denote the number of nonzeros of a matrix \(M\). A direct method obtains a least-squares solution through a finite matrix factorization and triangular or orthogonal-factor solves.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct solution of overdetermined or square least-squares systems; sparsity is classified by the matrix actually formed and factored.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct least-squares solve belongs to the normal-equations sparsity regime when it forms or accumulates \(G=A^TA\) and factors \(G=R^TR\); it belongs to the orthogonal-factor sparsity regime when it factors \(A\Pi=Q\begin{bmatrix}R\\0\end{bmatrix}\) without forming \(A^TA\); and it belongs to the dense spectral regime when it computes \(A=U\Sigma V^T\). For a factor \(L\), its fill ratio is \(\phi(L;M)=\operatorname{nnz}(L)/\operatorname{nnz}(M)\), where \(M=G\) in the normal-equations regime and \(M=A\) in the orthogonal regime. A regime is called sparsity-preserving for a matrix family when the relevant factor storage is \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(M))\) uniformly over that family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct least-squares solver is classified by whether it factors the normal-equations matrix, directly factors the rectangular matrix with orthogonal transformations, or computes a dense singular-value decomposition. Its sparsity regime is measured against the matrix being factored, using the number of factor nonzeros relative to input nonzeros. A family is sparsity-preserving when factor storage remains proportional to the stored input structure.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The normal-equations regime solves \(A^TAx=A^Tb\), whereas the QR and SVD regimes act directly on \(A\).
Sparsity preservation may equivalently be stated as the existence of \(C>0\) such that \(\operatorname{nnz}(L)\le C\operatorname{nnz}(M)\) throughout the matrix family.
special_cases_latex: When \(m\gg n\) and \(A^TA\) is affordable but \(A\) is not stored, accumulated normal equations form a natural direct regime.
For dense moderate-size matrices, \(\operatorname{nnz}\) distinctions disappear, leaving conditioning and robustness as the principal distinctions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Forming \(A^TA\) squares the spectral condition number when \(A\) has full column rank.
QR avoids the conditioning degradation caused by explicitly forming normal equations; SVD additionally exposes singular directions.
boundary_notes: Fill depends on ordering as well as the original sparsity pattern.
The definition does not assert that a sparsity-preserving ordering exists for every sparse matrix family.

notation.meaning: factor fill ratio relative to the factored input

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Direct Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense QR solution of a full-column-rank linearized least-squares subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), with \(m\geq n\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\). Compute a dense Householder QR factorization \(A=QR\), where \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has orthonormal columns and \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is upper triangular. Form \(c=Q^{\mathsf T}b\), solve \(Rx=c\) by backward substitution, and return \(x\). The output is the unique least-squares minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|_2\). In dense arithmetic, factorization costs \(O(mn^2)\) operations and stores \(O(mn)\) numbers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense Householder QR followed by triangular substitution computes the unique full-rank least-squares solution using cubic-scale work for square systems.

notation.meaning: Thin QR factors of the dense matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Sparse Direct Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-aware sparse QR solution of a full-column-rank linearized least-squares subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a sparse matrix \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), a vector \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), with \(m\geq n\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\), and a column permutation matrix \(P\) chosen to reduce fill. Compute a sparse thin QR factorization \(AP=QR\), where \(Q\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has orthonormal columns and \(R\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is nonsingular and upper triangular. Apply the stored orthogonal transformations to form \(c=Q^{\mathsf T}b\), solve \(Ry=c\) by backward substitution, and return \(x=Py\). The returned vector is the unique minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|_2\). Storage and work depend on fill in the sparse factors and elimination structure rather than solely on \(m\) and \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-column-rank sparse least-squares system, sparse QR uses a fill-reducing column permutation, sparse orthogonal factors, and triangular substitution to compute the unique solution; its cost is governed by fill-in.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) is stored sparsely, with \(m\geq n\).
\(P\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is a column permutation matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned vector \(x=PR^{-1}Q^{\mathsf T}b\) uniquely minimizes \(\|Ax-b\|_2\).

notation.meaning: Thin sparse QR factors of the permuted matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense–Sparse Crossover Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational crossover condition based on predicted factorization time and memory, including sparse fill.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed linearized system, let \(T_d,M_d\) denote predicted time and memory for a dense direct factorization, and let \(T_s(P),M_s(P)\) denote the corresponding predictions for a sparse factorization under ordering \(P\), including symbolic analysis and fill. Given available memory \(M_{\max}\), select the sparse regime when \[M_s(P)\leq M_{\max}\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(M_d>M_{\max}\ \text{or}\ T_s(P)<T_d\bigr).\] Select the dense regime when \(M_d\leq M_{\max}\) and \(T_d\leq T_s(P)\). The equality \(T_d=T_s(P)\), subject to both memory constraints, defines the modeled crossover boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dense–sparse crossover occurs where predicted solve times agree; feasibility and selection must also account for memory and ordering-dependent sparse fill.
assumptions_latex: Dense and sparse solvers enforce the same numerical-rank convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The solver regime is selected by the stated feasible-time comparison, with crossover boundary \(T_d=T_s(P)\).

notation.meaning: Predicted dense and ordered-sparse solution times.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operator-based taxonomy of iterative least-squares solvers
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). An iterative least-squares solver produces iterates \(x_k\) using matrix-vector products with \(A\), \(A^T\), or \(A^TA\), without computing a complete direct factorization.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, unconstrained linear least squares; the taxonomy concerns the operator generating the iterate space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An iterative least-squares method is normal-equation Krylov if \(x_k\in x_0+\mathcal K_k(A^TA,A^T(b-Ax_0))\); it is Golub–Kahan or LSQR-type if it generates paired Krylov spaces through alternating products by \(A\) and \(A^T\) and chooses \(x_k\in x_0+\mathcal K_k(A^TA,A^Tr_0)\) from the associated bidiagonal projected problem; and it is augmented-system Krylov if its iterates arise from a Krylov method applied to \(\begin{bmatrix}I&A\\A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}r\\x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}b\\0\end{bmatrix}\). Here \(r_0=b-Ax_0\) and \(\mathcal K_k(H,g)=\operatorname{span}\{g,Hg,\ldots,H^{k-1}g\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iterative least-squares solvers are classified by the operator used to generate their search spaces. Normal-equation methods use Krylov spaces of the squared operator. LSQR-type methods alternate multiplication by the matrix and its transpose and solve projected bidiagonal problems. Augmented-system methods instead apply a Krylov solver to the saddle-point equations that encode the residual and stationarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_k\in x_0+\mathcal K_k(A^TA,A^Tr_0)\) for normal-equation and LSQR-type methods, while augmented-system methods operate on \(\begin{bmatrix}I&A\\A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The least-squares optimality equations are \(A^T(Ax-b)=0\), which are the second block row of the augmented system with \(r=b-Ax\).
A matrix-free method requires only routines computing \(v\mapsto Av\) and \(u\mapsto A^Tu\).
special_cases_latex: Conjugate gradients applied to \(A^TAx=A^Tb\) is a normal-equation Krylov method.
LSQR is a Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization method and does not require explicit formation of \(A^TA\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every iteration can be implemented with at most a small fixed number of products by \(A\) and \(A^T\).
Preconditioning changes the generating operator and therefore must be included when identifying the precise Krylov space.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy does not imply identical floating-point behavior for methods spanning the same exact-arithmetic space.
Stopping rules and regularization by early termination are separate choices.

notation.meaning: order-k Krylov subspace generated by H and g
initial residual b minus A x_0

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov Least-Squares Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Golub–Kahan Krylov iteration for matrix-free linear least squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input linear operators \(v\mapsto Av\) and \(u\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}u\), a right-hand side \(b\), an initial vector \(x_0\), and tolerance \(\eta\geq0\). Set \(r_0=b-Ax_0\). After \(k\) Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization steps, obtain orthonormal \(V_k\) and bidiagonal \(B_k\) satisfying the projected least-squares relation, compute \[y_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{k}}\|\beta e_1-B_k y\|_2,\qquad x_k=x_0+V_k y_k,\] where \(\beta=\|r_0\|_2\). Stop when \(\|A^{\mathsf T}(Ax_k-b)\|_2\leq\eta\), and return \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Golub–Kahan bidiagonalization builds a Krylov subspace using matrix and transpose products, then solves a small projected least-squares problem until normal residual accuracy is met.
assumptions_latex: Products with \(A\) and \(A^{\mathsf T}\) are available.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate gradient least-squares recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: CGLS iteration as extracted; the initialization uses \(y_0\), whereas the displayed iterate update uses \(x_k\), so the notation switch is retained rather than silently resolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(y_0\), set \(r_0=A^Ty_0-g\), \(g_0=Ar_0\), and \(p_0=-g_0\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\) until convergence, compute
\[
q_k=A^Tp_k,\qquad \alpha_k=\frac{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2}{\lVert q_k\rVert_2^2},
\]
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k,\qquad r_{k+1}=r_k+\alpha_kq_k,\qquad g_{k+1}=Ar_{k+1},
\]
\[
\beta_k=\frac{\lVert g_{k+1}\rVert_2^2}{\lVert g_k\rVert_2^2},\qquad p_{k+1}=-g_{k+1}+\beta_kp_k.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialize the residual, its image under A, and the negative initial search direction from y0. Until convergence, form q_k with A transpose, choose alpha_k from the squared norm ratio, update the iterate and residual, recompute g_k, choose beta_k from consecutive squared g-norms, and update the conjugate direction. The extract changes the iterate symbol from y0 at initialization to x_k in the update.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ and the vectors have compatible dimensions.}
\lVert q_k\rVert_2\ne0\text{ and }\lVert g_k\rVert_2\ne0\text{ whenever the corresponding quotients are evaluated.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x_{k+1},r_{k+1},g_{k+1},p_{k+1})\text{ are generated by the stated CGLS recurrences until convergence.}

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Krylov Iterative Least-Squares Solvers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Landweber iteration as a canonical stationary, non-Krylov least-squares solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) with \(A\neq0\), \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\), \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), a tolerance \(\eta\geq0\), and a stepsize \(0<\alpha<2/\|A\|_2^2\). For \(k=0,1,\ldots\), perform the Landweber update \[x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha A^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax_k).\] Stop and return \(x_k\) when \(\|A^{\mathsf T}(Ax_k-b)\|_2\leq\eta\). In exact arithmetic, the infinite sequence of iterates converges to a least-squares solution. If \(x_0\in\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})\), its limit is the minimum-norm solution \(A^{\dagger}b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Landweber iteration repeatedly applies a fixed gradient step to a nonzero least-squares matrix. A stable stepsize ensures convergence, and a row-space initialization selects the minimum-norm solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The infinite sequence converges to a least-squares solution; if \(x_0\in\operatorname{range}(A^{\mathsf T})\), then \(x_k\to A^{\dagger}b\).

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the least-squares matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Inner-Solve Accuracy Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forcing-term conditions linking linearized inner residuals to local nonlinear residual convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(J_k=F'(x_k)\), and let an inexact Newton step \(s_k\) satisfy \[\|J_k s_k+F(x_k)\|_2\leq\eta_k\|F(x_k)\|_2.\] The fixed-accuracy regime has \(0\leq\eta_k\leq\bar\eta<1\) and supports local linear residual reduction under standard nonsingularity and Lipschitz assumptions. The vanishing-accuracy regime has \(\eta_k\to0\) and yields superlinear convergence. If additionally \(\eta_k=O(\|F(x_k)\|_2)\), the regime is compatible with local quadratic convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inner solve may use a bounded forcing tolerance for linear convergence, a vanishing tolerance for superlinear convergence, or residual-proportional tolerance for quadratic convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near a root \(x_*\).
\(F'\) is locally Lipschitz for the quadratic regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bounded, vanishing, and residual-proportional \(\eta_k\) correspond respectively to local linear, superlinear, and quadratic convergence regimes.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the nonlinear residual at the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Paired QR and SVD numerical-rank diagnostics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(q=\min\{m,n\}\), and \(\tau\ge0\). Let \(A\Pi=QR\) be a column-pivoted QR factorization and \(A=U\Sigma V^T\) an SVD with \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_q\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional numerical rank diagnosis; QR supplies a triangular pivot diagnostic, while SVD supplies the reference singular-value diagnostic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The QR–SVD rank-diagnostic pair at threshold \(\tau\) is \((r_{\mathrm{QR}},r_{\mathrm{SVD}})\), where \(r_{\mathrm{QR}}=\max\{j:|R_{jj}|>\tau\}\), with the maximum defined as zero if the set is empty, and \(r_{\mathrm{SVD}}=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}\). The associated SVD condition diagnostic is \(\kappa_\tau(A)=\sigma_1/\sigma_{r_{\mathrm{SVD}}}\) when \(r_{\mathrm{SVD}}>0\). Agreement means \(r_{\mathrm{QR}}=r_{\mathrm{SVD}}\); disagreement flags threshold sensitivity or insufficient rank revelation by the chosen pivoted QR factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The diagnostic pair compares a rank inferred from the diagonal pivots of a column-pivoted QR factorization with the rank obtained by counting singular values above the same threshold. The smallest retained singular value also defines a retained-subspace condition estimate. Equal ranks constitute agreement; unequal ranks flag a threshold-sensitive or inadequately rank-revealing QR diagnosis.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The SVD diagnosis identifies the retained right-singular subspace \(\operatorname{span}\{v_i:\sigma_i>\tau\}\).
Exact rank is recovered from the SVD diagnostic when \(\tau=0\) and singular values are interpreted in exact arithmetic.
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full column rank and \(\tau<\sigma_n\), then \(r_{\mathrm{SVD}}=n\).
If \(A=0\), both diagnostics are zero for every \(\tau\ge0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Small \(\sigma_{r_{\mathrm{SVD}}}\) indicates sensitivity of coefficients in the retained singular direction.
The SVD diagnostic directly determines the dimension of the truncated-pseudoinverse solution space.
boundary_notes: Diagonal entries of a generic pivoted QR factorization are not singular values; equality of the two ranks is diagnostic rather than automatic.
Relative thresholds such as \(\tau=\varepsilon\sigma_1\) are nearby conventions but are not imposed here.

notation.meaning: condition ratio on retained singular directions

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Revealing QR Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Permutation-aware QR certificate for thresholded numerical rank and column-space dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a column-pivoted QR factorization satisfy \(AP=QR\), and partition \[R=\begin{pmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{pmatrix},\qquad R_{11}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r}.\] For tolerance \(\tau>0\), the factorization supplies a numerical-rank certificate when \(R_{11}\) is nonsingular, \(\sigma_{\min}(R_{11})>\tau\), and \(\|R_{22}\|_2\leq\tau\). These inequalities certify \(r\) resolved independent directions and a trailing block whose action is below tolerance. The permutation \(P\) identifies the selected columns, while \(R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}\) diagnoses how remaining columns depend on them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pivoted QR factorization certifies numerical rank when the leading triangular block is safely nonsingular and the trailing block lies below tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) admits the displayed pivoted QR factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(\sigma_{\min}(R_{11})>\tau\) and \(\|R_{22}\|_2\leq\tau\) certify thresholded rank \(r\).

notation.meaning: Leading resolved and trailing unresolved triangular blocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subspace-Angle Bounds for Truncated Rank-Revealing QR
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds comparing QR-derived range and null-space approximations with the corresponding singular subspaces of a matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Phi_k^{\mathrm{QR}} be the angle between \mathcal R_k(A) and the range of the first k columns of Q, let \Psi_k^{\mathrm{QR}} be the angle between \mathcal N_k(A) and \mathcal R(Y_k), and let \widetilde\Psi_k^{\mathrm{QR}} be the angle between \mathcal N_k(A) and \mathcal R(\Pi W_k). Then \[\sin\Phi_k^{\mathrm{QR}}\le \operatorname{cond}(R_{11})\frac{\|R_{22}\|_2}{\|R_{11}\|_2},\] \[\sin\Psi_k^{\mathrm{QR}}\le \frac{\operatorname{cond}(R_{11})^2\|R_{22}\|_2^2/\|R_{11}\|_2^2}{1-\operatorname{cond}(R_{11})^2\|R_{22}\|_2^2/\|R_{11}\|_2^2},\] and \[\sin\widetilde\Psi_k^{\mathrm{QR}}\le (1+f_{k+1}^{\mathrm{alg}})\frac{\sigma_{k+1}}{\sigma_k}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The QR-derived range and null-space approximations satisfy explicit subspace-angle bounds involving the leading-block condition number, trailing-block ratio, or adjacent singular-value ratio.

knowledge_statements.title: SVD Rank Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular-value separation certificate for thresholded numerical rank, retained and discarded right subspaces, and effective conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have singular values \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_p\geq0\), where \(p=\min(m,n)\), and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) be a full orthonormal right singular basis, including any additional right-null vectors when \(n>p\). For a tolerance \(\tau>0\), an index \(r\in\{0,\ldots,p\}\) satisfying \[\sigma_r>\tau\geq\sigma_{r+1}\] certifies thresholded numerical rank \(r\), with conventions \(\sigma_0=+\infty\) and \(\sigma_{p+1}=0\). The retained right subspace is \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,ldots,v_r\}\), and the discarded right subspace is \(\operatorname{span}\{v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n\}\). When \(r>0\), the effective condition number of the retained operator is \(\kappa_{\tau}=\sigma_1/\sigma_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tolerance between consecutive singular values certifies numerical rank, identifies the complete retained and discarded right-singular subspaces, and determines the effective condition number of the retained operator.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) is a full orthonormal right singular basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\sigma_r>\tau\geq\sigma_{r+1}\), then the thresholded numerical rank is \(r\), with retained right subspace \(\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\) and discarded right subspace \(\operatorname{span}\{v_{r+1},\ldots,v_n\}\).

notation.meaning: Vectors in a full orthonormal right singular basis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Selective SVD regularization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines selective SVD by thresholding right-hand-side SVD coefficients and records the extract's differing equality conventions at the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let A=U\Sigma V^T with singular triplets (\sigma_i,u_i,v_i), and let \tau\ge 0. The selective-SVD solution is
\[
x_\tau:=\sum_{|u_i^Tb|>\tau}\frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}v_i.
\]
The stated filter factors are
\[
\varphi_i^{[\tau]}=\begin{cases}1,&|u_i^Tb|\ge\tau,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus the extract uses a strict inequality in the solution sum but a non-strict inequality in the filter definition. If the additive noise in b is white with scale \eta, a proposed noise-rejection threshold is \tau=\nu_{\mathrm S}\eta, where \nu_{\mathrm S} is a safety factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an SVD of the forward matrix, selective SVD retains only components whose right-hand-side SVD coefficients exceed a threshold. The extract uses a strict threshold in the solution formula but a non-strict threshold in its filter factors. Under white right-hand-side noise of scale eta, it proposes choosing the threshold as a safety factor times eta.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the noise-based choice, the additive noise in }b\text{ is white with scale }\eta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_\tau=\sum_{|u_i^Tb|>\tau}\frac{u_i^Tb}{\sigma_i}v_i,\qquad \varphi_i^{[\tau]}=\mathbf 1_{\{|u_i^Tb|\ge\tau\}},\qquad \tau=\nu_{\mathrm S}\eta\text{ under the stated white-noise rule.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized singular value decomposition of a matrix pair
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation and structural properties of the GSVD used for general-form Tikhonov regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For matrices \(A\) and \(L\) with the same number \(n\) of columns, where \(L\) has \(p\) rows, a GSVD uses linearly independent common right vectors \(x_i'\), orthonormal left-vector systems \(u_i'\) and \(v_i'\), and nonnegative scalars \(\sigma_i',\mu_i'\) satisfying \((\sigma_i')^2+(\mu_i')^2=1\). If \(p<n\), then \(Ax_i'=\sigma_i'u_i'\) and \(Lx_i'=\mu_i'v_i'\) for \(i=1,\ldots,p\), while \(Ax_i'=u_i'\) and \(Lx_i'=0\) for \(i=p+1,\ldots,n\). If \(p\ge n\), the paired relations hold for \(i=1,\ldots,n\). The ratios \(\sigma_i'/\mu_i'\) are the generalized singular values. Moreover, \(\ker L\) is spanned by the \(x_i'\) with \(\mu_i'=0\), together, when \(p<n\), with \(x_{p+1}',\ldots,x_n'\). Conventionally, the \(\sigma_i'\) are ordered nondecreasingly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For matrices A and L sharing n columns, with L having p rows, the generalized SVD supplies common linearly independent right vectors, two orthonormal left-vector systems, and nonnegative coefficient pairs whose squared entries sum to one. The decomposition has distinct formulas for p<n and p≥n; the coefficient ratios are the generalized singular values. The null space of L is spanned by right vectors having zero L-coefficient and, when p<n, by the additional right vectors indexed p+1 through n. The sigma coefficients are conventionally ordered nondecreasingly.
assumptions_latex: A\text{ and }L\text{ have the same }n\text{ columns}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{cases}Ax_i'=\sigma_i'u_i',\ Lx_i'=\mu_i'v_i',&i\le p,\quad p<n,\\Ax_i'=u_i',\ Lx_i'=0,&p<i\le n,\quad p<n,\\Ax_i'=\sigma_i'u_i',\ Lx_i'=\mu_i'v_i',&1\le i\le n,\quad p\ge n,\end{cases}\quad \ker L=\operatorname{span}\{x_i':\mu_i'=0\}\text{, augmented by }\{x_{p+1}',\ldots,x_n'\}\text{ if }p<n.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Diagnostic Agreement Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient separation conditions for QR- and SVD-based numerical-rank diagnostics to agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(AP=QR\) be a rank-revealing QR factorization partitioned at index \(r\), and let \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_p\) be the singular values of \(A\). For a common tolerance \(\tau>0\), suppose \[\sigma_r>\tau\geq\sigma_{r+1},\qquad \sigma_{\min}(R_{11})>\tau,\qquad \|R_{22}\|_2\leq\tau.\] Then the SVD threshold count and the QR block test both report numerical rank \(r\). If either diagnostic has values within its perturbation or rounding uncertainty of \(\tau\), agreement is not certified and the rank decision must be treated as tolerance-sensitive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: QR and SVD rank tests agree when both separate the same leading and trailing subspaces across a common tolerance; values near that tolerance make agreement uncertified.
assumptions_latex: The QR and SVD diagnostics use the same \(\tau>0\).
The displayed QR and singular-value separation inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Both diagnostics return numerical rank \(r\); absent separation from \(\tau\), agreement is not certified.

notation.meaning: Leading and trailing blocks of the rank-revealing QR factor.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectrally filtered regularized least-squares family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i)V^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and let \(\alpha\ge0\) be a regularization parameter. A spectral filter is a family of scalar functions \(\varphi_\alpha:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear least squares with rank deficiency or ill conditioning; both truncated-SVD and Tikhonov/Levenberg regularization are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rank-aware regularized solve family is \(x_\alpha=\sum_{\sigma_i>0}\varphi_\alpha(\sigma_i)(u_i^Tb)v_i\), where the filter suppresses directions with small \(\sigma_i\). The truncated-SVD member uses \(\varphi_\tau(\sigma)=\sigma^{-1}\mathbf1_{\{\sigma>\tau\}}\). The Tikhonov member uses \(\varphi_\lambda(\sigma)=\sigma/(\sigma^2+\lambda)\) for \(\lambda>0\), equivalently \(x_\lambda\) is the unique minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2\) and satisfies \((A^TA+\lambda I)x_\lambda=A^Tb\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-aware regularized solve applies a scalar filter to every singular component of the data. Truncated SVD removes components whose singular values do not exceed a threshold. Tikhonov regularization continuously damps every component, with the strongest damping in small-singular-value directions, and is equivalently the unique minimizer of a least-squares objective plus a positive quadratic penalty.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_\lambda=\arg\min_x\left(\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2\right)\) for \(\lambda>0\).
The Tikhonov system is the normal equation of \(\min_x\left\|\begin{bmatrix}A\\\sqrt\lambda I\end{bmatrix}x-\begin{bmatrix}b\\0\end{bmatrix}\right\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: At \(\tau=0\), truncated SVD yields \(A^\dagger b\).
If \(A\) has full column rank, then \(x_\lambda\to(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb\) as \(\lambda\downarrow0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(\lambda>0\), \(A^TA+\lambda I\) is positive definite even when \(A\) is rank deficient.
Both filters reduce amplification by reciprocals of small singular values.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe a parameter-choice rule.
General penalties \(\|Lx\|_2^2\) require a generalized spectral decomposition and are outside this slot.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncated Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated-SVD solution of a possibly rank-deficient linearized residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(q=\min\{m,n\}\) and let \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^{q}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\) be a compact singular value decomposition, where \(U\in\mathbb R^{m\times q}\), \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\), and \(\sigma_1\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_q\geq0\). Given \(b\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(\tau>0\), define \(I_\tau=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,q\}:\sigma_i>\tau\}\) and \(A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I_\tau}\sigma_i u_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\). The truncated solve returns
\[
p_\tau=-\sum_{i\in I_\tau}\frac{u_i^{\mathsf T}b}{\sigma_i}v_i=-A_\tau^\dagger b.
\]
No singular component at or below \(\tau\) is retained; if \(I_\tau=\varnothing\), the output is \(p_\tau=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discard singular directions at or below the threshold and solve only in the retained singular subspace, returning zero if no direction is retained.
assumptions_latex: \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf T}\) is a compact singular value decomposition with \(q=\min\{m,n\}\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_\tau=-A_\tau^\dagger b\) using exactly the singular values satisfying \(\sigma_i>\tau\).

notation.meaning: smaller of the row and column dimensions of A
rank-truncated approximation of the linearized operator
Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the truncated operator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truncated SVD Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the TSVD solution and records the source's noise-filtering guidance for selecting the truncation index.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the relevant singular triplets be \((\sigma_i,u_i,v_i)\), ordered as in the SVD, and let \(1\le k\le r\), where \(\sigma_i>0\) for \(i\le r\). The truncated SVD solution retaining the first \(k\) components is
\[
x_k:=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{u_i^{\top}b}{\sigma_i}v_i.
\]
The truncation index \(k\) should discard noise-dominated SVD coefficients; inspection of a Picard plot can often guide its selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The truncated SVD solution retains the first k components of the naive SVD solution. The cutoff should discard noise-dominated coefficients and can often be selected using a Picard plot.

knowledge_statements.title: Damped Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tikhonov-damped least-squares step for a linearized residual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\lambda>0\), define
\[
p_\lambda=\operatorname*{argmin}_{p\in\mathbb R^n}\bigl(\lVert Ap+b\rVert_2^2+\lambda^2\lVert p\rVert_2^2\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, compute \(p_\lambda\) from
\[
(A^{\mathsf T}A+\lambda^2I_n)p_\lambda=-A^{\mathsf T}b,
\]
where \(I_n\) is the \(n\times n\) identity matrix. Because \(\lambda>0\), the coefficient matrix is positive definite and the output \(p_\lambda\) is the unique minimizer. An iterative implementation may stop when its normal-equation residual satisfies a prescribed linear-solve tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Add a positive quadratic penalty to least squares, yielding a unique damped step even when the linearized operator is rank deficient.

notation.meaning: identity matrix on the step space
