knowledge_statements.title: Simple Turning Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local quadratic parametrization of a simple fold of \(F(x,\lambda)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n	imes\mathbb{R}	o\mathbb{R}^n\) be three times continuously differentiable and satisfy \(F(x_*,\lambda_*)=0\). Suppose \(J_*=F_x(x_*,\lambda_*)\) has one-dimensional right and left nullspaces spanned by nonzero vectors \(v\) and \(w\), with \(w^{\mathsf T}F_\lambda(x_*,\lambda_*)
eq0\) and \(w^{\mathsf T}F_{xx}(x_*,\lambda_*)[v,v]
eq0\). The local solution curve admits a parameter \(t\) such that \[x(t)=x_*+tv+O(t^2),\qquad \lambda(t)=\lambda_*- rac{w^{\mathsf T}F_{xx}(x_*,\lambda_*)[v,v]}{2w^{\mathsf T}F_\lambda(x_*,\lambda_*)}t^2+O(t^3).\] Thus \(\lambda'(0)=0\) and \(\lambda''(0)
eq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a simple turning point, the solution curve has a nonzero state-space tangent while the continuation parameter reverses direction quadratically.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is three times continuously differentiable near \((x_*,\lambda_*)\).

notation.meaning: state Jacobian at the turning point
nonzero right and left nullvectors of the state Jacobian

knowledge_statements.title: Fold Singularities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nondegenerate codimension-one fold conditions for a parameterized residual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(F(x_*,\lambda_*)=0\), write \(J_*=F_x(x_*,\lambda_*)\). The point is a nondegenerate fold singularity when \[\operatorname{rank}J_*=n-1,\qquad w^{\mathsf T}F_\lambda(x_*,\lambda_*)\neq0,\qquad w^{\mathsf T}F_{xx}(x_*,\lambda_*)[v,v]\neq0,\] where nonzero \(v\) and \(w\) span \(\ker J_*\) and \(\ker J_*^{\mathsf T}\), respectively. The first inequality makes the parameter direction transverse to \(\operatorname{range}J_*\); the second excludes higher-order tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondegenerate fold has a one-dimensional state-Jacobian nullspace, transverse parameter dependence, and nonzero quadratic curvature along the null direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}J_*=n-1\), \(w^{\mathsf T}F_\lambda\neq0\), and \(w^{\mathsf T}F_{xx}[v,v]\neq0\) characterize a nondegenerate fold.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of F with respect to the state variable
nonzero right nullvector of the state Jacobian
nonzero left nullvector of the state Jacobian

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition content kind is appropriate and the rank, transversality, and quadratic nondegeneracy conditions form the standard simple-fold characterization. No source or inspectable locator is supplied, so the characterization remains source-dependent candidate knowledge.

children.title: Fold Traversal Failure
children.top_down_role: Covers loss of path-following reliability near fold regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Fold Traversal Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of natural-parameter continuation at a nondegenerate fold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a nondegenerate fold, suppose the local representation satisfies \(x(t)=x_*+tv+O(t^2)\) with \(v\neq0\) and \(\lambda(t)=\lambda_*+ct^2+O(t^3)\) with \(c\neq0\). On either nearby branch, \(t=O(|\lambda-\lambda_*|^{1/2})\), and \[\left\lVert\frac{dx}{d\lambda}\right\rVert=O(|\lambda-\lambda_*|^{-1/2}).\] Consequently, continuation that prescribes \(\lambda\) and corrects only \(x\) encounters a singular state Jacobian and an unbounded branch slope as \(\lambda\to\lambda_*\). It cannot traverse both sides while maintaining \(\lambda\) as a monotone local parameter; an arclength-type parameter provides a regular traversal formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural-parameter continuation fails at a fold because the state Jacobian becomes singular and the state derivative with respect to the parameter diverges; an arclength-type parameter can regularize traversal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert dx/d\lambda\rVert=O(|\lambda-\lambda_*|^{-1/2})\), preventing regular traversal with \(\lambda\) as a monotone local parameter.

notation.meaning: nonzero state-space tangent at the fold

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branch-Switching Failure Relative to a Target Solution Branch
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G:U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n\), and suppose distinct local solution branches \(\mathcal C_1,\ldots,\mathcal C_q\subseteq G^{-1}(0)\) meet at \(z_*\). Let \(\mathcal C_i\) be the intended branch and let \(z_k\in\mathcal C_i\) approach \(z_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuation near a point with multiple local solution branches. Failure is defined relative to an explicitly selected target branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a predictor-corrector step from \(z_k\) return \(\widehat z_{k+1}\in G^{-1}(0)\cap B_r(z_*)\). For a branch-separation tolerance \(\delta>0\), a branch-switching failure from \(\mathcal C_i\) occurs when there exists \(j\neq i\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_{k+1},\mathcal C_j)\leq\delta,
\qquad \operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_{k+1},\mathcal C_i)>\delta.\] If \(\widehat z_{k+1}\) lies within \(\delta\) of more than one branch, the step is branch-ambiguous rather than a certified switch. The definition requires a declared intended branch because changing branches may otherwise be a legitimate continuation operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a junction of distinct local solution branches, identify the branch that the computation is intended to follow. A corrected solution is a branch-switching failure when it lies within the prescribed neighborhood of a different branch but farther than the branch-membership tolerance from the intended branch. If the corrected point is close to several branches simultaneously, branch identity is unresolved and the event is classified as ambiguous rather than as a definite switch. Deliberate branch switching is excluded because failure is relative to the continuation objective.
assumptions_latex: The local branches are distinguished subsets of the zero set in \(B_r(z_*)\).
An intended branch \(\mathcal C_i\), a correction output, and a branch-membership tolerance \(\delta\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A failure from \(\mathcal C_i\) occurs when \(\min_{j\neq i}\operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_{k+1},\mathcal C_j)\leq\delta<\operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_{k+1},\mathcal C_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using branch labels \(L_\delta(z)=\{j:\operatorname{dist}(z,\mathcal C_j)\leq\delta\}\), a certified switch means \(i\notin L_\delta(\widehat z_{k+1})\) and \(L_\delta(\widehat z_{k+1})\neq\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: When exactly two separated branches are present, the corrected point transfers from the target branch's tolerance tube to the other tube.
A deliberate switch to \(\mathcal C_j\) is not a failure after \(\mathcal C_j\) is declared the target.
immediate_consequences_latex: Residual smallness alone cannot certify preservation of branch identity.
A branch-aware acceptance test must use information beyond \(G(\widehat z_{k+1})=0\).
boundary_notes: At the common point \(z_*\), distances to all incident branches vanish, so branch identity is necessarily ambiguous.
The definition presumes meaningful local branch sets; unresolved singular geometry requires separate analysis.

notation.meaning: Set of branches whose tolerance tubes contain the point.

review_flags: The distance-to-branch predicate is a precise diagnostic construction but has no inspected canonical source.
A source must support the target-relative distinction between switching and ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Switching Failure Relative to a Target Solution Branch

children.title: Branch-Point Geometry
children.top_down_role: Covers local solution-path structure where multiple branches meet.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch-Point Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-cone geometry of intersecting solution branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(x,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) and \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable with \(F(z_*)=0\). Every differentiable solution branch \(\gamma_j\) through \(z_*\) has tangent \(d_j=\gamma_j'(0)\) satisfying \[F'(z_*)d_j=0.\] Hence the tangent cone of the local solution set is contained in \(\ker F'(z_*)\). A branch point has at least two noncollinear branch tangents; consequently \(\dim\ker F'(z_*)\geq2\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}F'(z_*)\leq n-1\). The nullspace contains the candidate directions that higher-order compatibility equations must distinguish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a branch point, at least two noncollinear solution tangents lie in the nullspace of the full residual derivative, forcing nullity of at least two.
assumptions_latex: At least two differentiable solution branches pass through \(z_*\) with noncollinear nonzero tangents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_j\in\ker F'(z_*)\) for every branch tangent and \(\dim\ker F'(z_*)\geq2\).

notation.meaning: tangent of branch j at the branch point
full derivative with respect to state and parameter

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation correctly places differentiable branch tangents in the kernel of the full derivative and fits the geometry leaf. The adopted branch-point criterion and tangent-cone/nullity conclusions need a direct continuation or bifurcation source, especially because higher-order compatibility is only mentioned and not specified.

children.title: Unintended Path Switching
children.top_down_role: Covers departure from the intended solution branch during continuation.

knowledge_statements.title: Unintended Path Switching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accepted continuation iterate lies on a branch different from the predicted branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let distinct local branches \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) meet near a branch point, and suppose the current iterate belongs to \(\Gamma_1\). Given a predictor \(z_k^{\mathrm p}\), a residual corrector produces an accepted point \(z_{k+1}\). Unintended path switching occurs when \[z_{k+1}\in\Gamma_2\setminus\Gamma_1\quad\text{and}\quad \lVert F(z_{k+1})\rVert\leq	au_F,\] although the predictor was constructed from the tangent of \(\Gamma_1\). A residual test alone cannot reject this event because both branches solve the same equation; branch-sensitive tangent, orientation, or phase constraints are additionally required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Path switching occurs when correction accepts a low-residual point on another branch despite prediction from the intended branch; residual convergence alone cannot detect it.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) are distinct local subsets of \(F^{-1}(0)\).
The predictor uses continuation data from \(\Gamma_1\).
Acceptance requires only \(\lVert F(z_{k+1})\rVert\leq	au_F\) and generic step tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z_{k+1}\in\Gamma_2\setminus\Gamma_1\) with \(\lVert F(z_{k+1})\rVert\leq	au_F\) is an undetectable switch under residual-only acceptance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary definition matches the leaf and correctly observes that residual-only acceptance cannot distinguish exact solution branches. No source is provided for the diagnostic formulation or the claimed need for the listed branch-sensitive constraints.

children.title: Branch Identity Loss
children.top_down_role: Covers ambiguity in preserving the identity of the branch being followed.

knowledge_statements.title: Branch Identity Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-identifiability of a branch from residual information at an intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two distinct continuous solution branches \(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2\subset F^{-1}(0)\) satisfy \(z_*\in\Gamma_1\cap\Gamma_2\). At \(z_*\), the residual value and every acceptance statistic depending only on \(F(z_*)\) are identical for both branches. Thus no branch label can be inferred from residual data at the intersection. Moreover, if stored tangent or orientation information is uncertain enough to admit candidate directions from both branches, continuation history no longer uniquely determines the successor branch. This is branch identity loss; recovery requires additional branch-discriminating information such as a branch invariant, phase condition, symmetry label, or verified tangent-selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an intersection, residual data cannot identify the arriving branch. If historical tangent or orientation information is also ambiguous, the successor branch is not uniquely determined.
assumptions_latex: Stored branch-discriminating data admit successor directions from both branches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual-only information at \(z_*\) cannot determine whether continuation should follow \(\Gamma_1\) or \(\Gamma_2\).

children.title: Switching-Risk Regimes
children.top_down_role: Covers continuation configurations with elevated susceptibility to unintended branch changes.

knowledge_statements.title: Switching-Risk Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric separation test for reliable nearest-branch association.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_{k+1}^*\in\Gamma_1\) be the intended next point and define the competing-branch separation \(d_k=\operatorname{dist}(z_{k+1}^*,\Gamma_2)\). Suppose the predictor lies within \(e_k\) of \(z_{k+1}^*\), and correction plus numerical uncertainty displaces the accepted point by at most \(r_k\) from that predictor. Then the accepted point lies within \(e_k+r_k\) of \(z_{k+1}^*\). Its nearest-branch identity is guaranteed to be \(\Gamma_1\) when \[e_k+r_k<\frac{d_k}{2}.\] When \(e_k+r_k\geq d_k/2\), these bounds no longer guarantee nearest-branch association. Small branch separation, large predictor error, ill-conditioned correction, or numerical noise increases switching risk by shrinking \(d_k\) or enlarging \(e_k+r_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearest-branch association with the intended branch is guaranteed when the total predictor-corrector displacement bound is less than half the competing-branch separation; otherwise these bounds do not exclude switching.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma_1\) and \(\Gamma_2\) are closed local branch segments.
The predictor is within \(e_k\) of \(z_{k+1}^*\), and the accepted point is within \(r_k\) of the predictor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k+r_k<d_k/2\) guarantees that the accepted point is closer to \(\Gamma_1\) than to \(\Gamma_2\); when \(e_k+r_k\geq d_k/2\), the bounds do not guarantee this association.

notation.meaning: distance from the intended next point to the competing branch
predictor error bound relative to the intended next point
correction and numerical displacement bound relative to the predictor

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Intrinsic and Computed Continuation Path Divergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G:U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n\), let \(z:[0,s_*)\to U\) parameterize a selected connected solution path with \(G(z(s))=0\), and let \(\widehat z_k\) be computed continuation points at parameters \(s_k\uparrow s_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuation. Intrinsic unbounded escape and numerical departure from a bounded target path are separated within the divergence taxonomy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The exact continuation path has intrinsic divergence at \(s_*\) when \[\limsup_{s\uparrow s_*}\lVert z(s)\rVert=+\infty.\] If the target segment \(z([0,s_*))\) is bounded, the computed continuation has path divergence when \[\operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_k,z([0,s_*)))\longrightarrow+\infty,\] or, for a prescribed admissible tube radius \(R>0\), when \(\operatorname{dist}(\widehat z_k,z([0,s_*)))>R\) for the first accepted index. The first predicate is geometric escape of the exact component; the second is algorithmic departure from a bounded intended component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact continuation path diverges intrinsically when its norm is unbounded as its continuation coordinate approaches an endpoint. If the intended exact path segment is bounded, a computed path diverges when its distance from that segment grows without bound. A finite operational failure boundary may instead be declared when an accepted computed point first leaves a prescribed tube around the intended path. This definition distinguishes an unbounded solution component from an algorithm that departs from a bounded component; these cases demand different diagnoses.
assumptions_latex: The exact target path and computed continuation points are defined in a common normed space.
Algorithmic divergence is assessed only when the intended exact path segment is bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Intrinsic divergence is \(\limsup_{s\uparrow s_*}\lVert z(s)\rVert=+\infty\); computed divergence is unbounded distance from the bounded target path, with tube exit as its finite-threshold version.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Intrinsic divergence means that for every \(M>0\) and every \(s_0<s_*\), some \(s\in(s_0,s_*)\) satisfies \(\lVert z(s)\rVert>M\).
special_cases_latex: If \(s_*=+\infty\), the same definition applies as \(s\to+\infty\).
A path may remain bounded while approaching the boundary of an open domain; that is domain termination, not norm divergence.
immediate_consequences_latex: Intrinsic divergence precludes convergence to a finite endpoint.
Leaving a fixed tube does not imply that the residual is large; the computation may have reached a different solution component.
boundary_notes: Oscillation inside a bounded set is not divergence under this norm-based definition.
A singular finite endpoint is classified as singular path termination rather than divergence.

notation.meaning: Endpoint of the selected continuation-parameter interval.
Operational radius of the admissible tube around the target path.

review_flags: No inspected continuation source supports both intrinsic escape and computed tube departure under this title.
A precise locator is required before treating the combined taxonomy as canonical.
knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic and Computed Continuation Path Divergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuation-path outcome: divergence or a conditionally valid endpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded summary of a referenced continuation theorem. The extract does not characterize the exceptional choices of the continuation parameter or restate the theorem's other hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Unless the choice of the continuation parameter \(a\) is exceptional in the unspecified sense of the referenced theorem, the stated continuation algorithms can be applied to obtain a path that either diverges or leads to a point \(\bar{x}\). If the path leads to \(\bar{x}\) and \(J(\bar{x})\) is nonsingular, then \(\bar{x}\) is a solution of the original nonlinear system. Genuine path divergence can occur even for apparently benign problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Except for parameter choices left unspecified in the extract, the referenced continuation algorithms produce a path that either diverges or reaches a point x-bar. If the Jacobian at x-bar is nonsingular, x-bar solves the original nonlinear system. Actual path divergence can occur even for apparently benign problems.
assumptions_latex: a\text{ is not an exceptional choice in the unspecified sense of the referenced theorem}
\text{one of the continuation algorithms referenced by the extract is applied}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\text{the path diverges}\bigr)\ \lor\ \bigl(\text{the path leads to }\bar{x}\bigr),\qquad \bigl(\text{the path leads to }\bar{x}\ \land\ J(\bar{x})\text{ is nonsingular}\bigr)\Rightarrow \bar{x}\text{ solves the original nonlinear system}

children.title: Diverging Continuation Iterates
children.top_down_role: Covers numerical path-following sequences that move away from the intended branch.

knowledge_statements.title: Diverging Continuation Iterates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes numerical divergence along a bounded parameter sequence from ordinary failure to satisfy the residual equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuous, and let \((x_k,t_k)\) be continuation iterates with \(t_k\to t_*\) and residual errors \(\|F(x_k,t_k)\|\to0\). The iterates are diverging at \(t_*\) if \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\), or more generally if \((x_k)\) has no bounded subsequence. If a bounded local solution branch through parameter values approaching \(t_*\) exists, such divergence diagnoses failure of the continuation update, parameterization, scaling, or linear solve rather than nonexistence of nearby solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuation iterates diverge when their parameter values converge and residuals vanish, but the state sequence has no bounded subsequence; a bounded nearby branch then indicates numerical failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k)\) is divergent if it has no bounded subsequence; if a bounded nearby branch exists, divergence is algorithmic rather than intrinsic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The final implication is false without substantially stronger branch-selection or isolation hypotheses. A bounded local branch can coexist with an unbounded exact branch approaching the same finite parameter value, so divergence of the computed sequence does not by itself establish that the failure is algorithmic rather than intrinsic. No source is supplied for the proposed diagnostic.

children.title: Unbounded Solution Branches
children.top_down_role: Covers genuine solution paths that escape every bounded region.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Solution Branches
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines intrinsic state-space escape of an exact connected continuation branch.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a continuous residual map \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^m\), a solution branch is a connected set \(\mathcal{B}\subseteq\{(x,t):F(x,t)=0\}\). The branch is unbounded if \(\sup_{(x,t)\in\mathcal{B}}\|(x,t)\|=\infty\). It is state-unbounded at a finite parameter endpoint \(t_*\) if there exists \((x_k,t_k)\in\mathcal{B}\) such that \(t_k\to t_*\) and \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\). This property belongs to the exact solution set and is therefore distinct from divergence caused solely by a continuation algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact solution branch is unbounded when its state-parameter pairs escape every bounded set; state-unboundedness at a finite endpoint requires states to diverge while parameters converge.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal{B}\) is a connected subset of the zero set of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{B}\) is state-unbounded at \(t_*\) exactly when some \((x_k,t_k)\in\mathcal{B}\) satisfies \(t_k\to t_*\) and \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The state-unboundedness criterion is mathematically coherent and the definition kind fits the leaf. However, no evidence is supplied for treating an arbitrary connected subset of the zero set as a solution branch; continuation references may instead require a connected component, path-connected curve, or maximal branch. An authoritative continuation-specific definition with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Apparent Divergence from Poor Parameterization
children.top_down_role: Covers divergence-like behavior caused by an unsuitable continuation parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Apparent Divergence from Poor Parameterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth bounded geometric branch acquires an unbounded tangent under a singular continuation parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the residual system \(F(u,v,t)=(v-u^2,u^3-t)\). Its solution set near the origin has the smooth geometric parameterization \((u,v,t)=(s,s^2,s^3)\). Parameterizing instead by \(t\geq0\) gives \((u(t),v(t))=(t^{1/3},t^{2/3})\), whose derivative is \((u'(t),v'(t))=(\tfrac13t^{-2/3},\tfrac23t^{-1/3})\) and is unbounded as \(t\downarrow0\). Nevertheless, the solution points converge to \((0,0,0)\). Thus a tangent predictor based on \(t\) can display apparent divergence although the geometric solution path is bounded and regular in the parameter \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded smooth branch can have an unbounded derivative under a singular parameter, causing tangent predictors to appear divergent even though the geometric path converges normally.
assumptions_latex: Continuation uses \(t\) as the local path parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|(u'(t),v'(t))\|\to\infty\) while \((u(t),v(t),t)\to(0,0,0)\), so the divergence is parameterization-induced.
review_flags: explicit counterexample is self-checking but lacks external source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed example and derivative calculations are internally consistent, and counterexample is the correct knowledge kind. Nevertheless, the map's domain and codomain are not explicitly declared, and no source supports the continuation-specific claim about tangent-predictor behavior or the characterization as apparent divergence. A precise continuation reference is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular Termination of a Continuation Path
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G:U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(z:[0,s_*)\to G^{-1}(0)\cap U\) be a regular solution path satisfying \(\operatorname{rank}DG(z(s))=n\) for every \(s<s_*<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuation reaching a finite interior endpoint where the full residual derivative loses maximal row rank. Folds with regular augmented derivative are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The path has singular termination at \(z_*\in U\) when \[\lim_{s\uparrow s_*}z(s)=z_*,\qquad G(z_*)=0,
\qquad\operatorname{rank}DG(z_*)<n,\] and there is no \(\varepsilon>0\) and regular extension \(\widetilde z:[0,s_*+\varepsilon)\to G^{-1}(0)\cap U\) satisfying \(\widetilde z(s)=z(s)\) for \(s<s_*\) and \(\operatorname{rank}DG(\widetilde z(s))=n\) for \(s>s_*\). The endpoint is therefore finite and feasible, but the selected regular path cannot be continued through it as the same regular curve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular continuation path terminates singularly when it approaches a finite solution inside the modeled domain, the full derivative of the residual loses maximal row rank at that endpoint, and the incoming path has no extension through the endpoint that remains a regular solution curve. All three conditions matter: convergence to a finite point, singularity of the full continuation system, and nonexistence of a regular extension of the selected path. A simple parameter fold is excluded because its full state-parameter derivative remains of maximal row rank.
assumptions_latex: The incoming path is regular and has finite arclength-parameter endpoint \(s_*\).
The limit \(z_*\) lies in the interior domain \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Singular termination means finite convergence to \(z_*\in G^{-1}(0)\) with \(\operatorname{rank}DG(z_*)<n\) and no regular continuation of the same incoming path beyond \(s_*\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The endpoint belongs to the closure of the regular path but admits no two-sided regular-curve germ extending that path.
special_cases_latex: If \(n=1\), full singularity means \(G_x(z_*)=G_\lambda(z_*)=0\).
A finite endpoint on \(\partial U\) is domain termination and does not satisfy the stated interior condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The implicit regular-curve theorem does not apply at \(z_*\).
A continuation algorithm cannot certify passage through \(z_*\) merely by changing from parameter to arclength continuation.
boundary_notes: Rank loss alone does not imply termination if a regular extension of the selected branch exists on the far side.
An unbounded path has divergence rather than finite singular termination.
Multiple nonsmooth or stratified branches may require a generalized-derivative definition outside this smooth regime.

notation.meaning: Finite singular endpoint of the selected continuation path.
Hypothetical regular extension whose nonexistence is part of the definition.

review_flags: The definition is mathematically scoped but no continuation-theory source was inspected for the rank-loss plus nonextendability criterion.
A precise authoritative locator is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular Termination of a Continuation Path

children.title: Coalescing Solution Paths
children.top_down_role: Covers distinct solution paths that merge within the continuation domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Coalescing Solution Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional square-system criterion for two distinct branches meeting at one solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable. Suppose two distinct solution paths \(x_1(t)\neq x_2(t)\) satisfy \(F(x_i(t),t)=0\) for \(t<t_*\), and both converge to \(x_*\) as \(t\uparrow t_*\). Then \(F(x_*,t_*)=0\), and the state Jacobian \(D_xF(x_*,t_*)\) is singular. Consequently, coalescence cannot occur at a point where the state Jacobian is invertible; regular local uniqueness excludes two distinct nearby solution graphs meeting there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When two distinct solution paths meet at one finite point in a smooth square residual system, the state Jacobian at that point must be singular.

notation.meaning: Jacobian with respect to the state variable

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The singular-Jacobian conclusion is a standard implicit-function consequence, but the record supplies no theorem or section locator. Because the statement is a hypothesis-to-conclusion result, its mathematical role is theorem rather than property. The common parameter interval on which both paths are defined should also be explicit before promotion.

children.title: Singular Path Endpoints
children.top_down_role: Covers terminal path locations with singular local continuation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Path Endpoints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite limiting endpoint condition for a differentiable square residual system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n\) be continuously differentiable, and let \((x(s),t(s))\) be a solution path on \([0,s_*)\). A finite limit \((x_*,t_*)=\lim_{s\uparrow s_*}(x(s),t(s))\) is a singular path endpoint when \(F(x_*,t_*)=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}D_xF(x_*,t_*)<n\). The definition records loss of state-parameter regularity at the endpoint; it does not by itself determine whether the geometric solution set terminates, folds, branches, crosses, or remains continuable under pseudo-arclength parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite solution-path endpoint is singular when it remains an exact zero but its state Jacobian loses rank; rank loss alone does not classify the geometry.
assumptions_latex: \((x(s),t(s))\) consists of exact solutions and has finite limit \((x_*,t_*)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endpoint is singular exactly when \(F(x_*,t_*)=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}D_xF(x_*,t_*)<n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rank-loss condition is precise, but whether it defines a singular path endpoint is terminology-dependent. In particular, singularity of the state Jacobian does not imply singularity of the full residual derivative or geometric path. Because the statement explicitly introduces terminology, definition would ordinarily fit better than condition. A continuation-specific authoritative definition is required.

children.title: Endpoint Classification Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Covers difficulty distinguishing genuine path termination from coalescence or numerical tracking loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Endpoint Classification Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual vanishing and Jacobian rank loss cannot distinguish folds from intersecting branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Scalar residuals \(F_{m fold}(x,t)=x^2-t\) and \(F_{m cross}(x,t)=x^2-t^2\) both satisfy \(F(0,0)=0\) and \(D_xF(0,0)=0\). For \(F_{m fold}\), real solutions exist only for \(t\geq0\) and form a fold \(x=\pm\sqrt{t}\). For \(F_{m cross}\), the two smooth branches \(x=t\) and \(x=-t\) pass through the endpoint for both signs of \(t\). Hence endpoint residual and state-Jacobian rank data alone do not determine whether a singular point is a fold, crossing, bifurcation, or genuine termination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two residual systems can have identical zero-residual and rank-loss data at an endpoint but different local geometries, so those diagnostics alone cannot classify termination.
assumptions_latex: Solutions are considered over the real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The data \(F(x_*,t_*)=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}D_xF(x_*,t_*)<n\) are insufficient for endpoint classification.
review_flags: explicit examples are self-checking but lack external source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two scalar examples correctly demonstrate that zero residual and state-Jacobian rank loss do not determine local solution geometry, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. No source is supplied, however, for the broader continuation classification terminology or its extension to bifurcation and genuine termination. A specific authoritative locator is required.

children.title: Method Selection by Diagnosed Failure
children.top_down_role: Organizes solver-family choices according to the diagnosed failure regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Method Selection by Diagnosed Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A diagnostic decision rule for selecting the next residual-system recovery mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a residual iteration applied to \(F(z)=0\), select a recovery method by the first verified failure condition: inaccurate evaluations require tighter evaluation or linear-solve tolerances; severe scaling requires variable and residual scaling; rejected or nondecreasing trial residuals with reliable derivatives require damping, line search, or a trust region; rank-deficient Jacobians require rank-revealing factorization, regularization, or a pseudoinverse; and a singular parameterized path with a regular augmented tangent system requires pseudo-arclength continuation. Method selection should target the diagnosed violated condition before changing unrelated algorithmic components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose recovery by diagnosis: improve accuracy first, then scaling or globalization, use rank-aware solves for singular Jacobians, and pseudo-arclength continuation for parameterization singularities.
assumptions_latex: The reported failure condition has been independently checked.
The residual and derivative diagnostics refer to the same iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected intervention is the method associated with the first verified failure condition in the diagnostic rule.

notation.meaning: current state or augmented continuation variable

review_flags: provided Newton and trust-region locators do not support the full rule

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Principle fits the method-selection container, but the asserted first-failure hierarchy and the mapping from diagnoses to required interventions are prescriptive and not universal. The statement does not define how the first verified condition is ordered, and the listed local sources do not support the combined rule. Comparative sources with specific locators are required.

children.title: Cross-Regime Recovery Priorities
children.top_down_role: Organizes recovery options when multiple failure regimes are simultaneously plausible.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Recovery Priorities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic recovery order when several computational, iterative, structural, and continuation failures are simultaneously plausible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the diagnostic state be \(d=(d_{m acc},d_{m scale},d_{m step},d_{m rank},d_{m path})\in\{0,1\}^5\), where an entry equal to one denotes a verified failure of evaluation accuracy, scaling, step globalization, Jacobian rank, or path parameterization. Apply corrections in the lexicographic priority \(d_{m acc}\succ d_{m scale}\succ d_{m step}\succ d_{m rank}\succ d_{m path}\), recomputing all diagnostics after each correction. This order prevents unreliable arithmetic or scaling from being misclassified as structural singularity and prevents a parameterization change from masking an unresolved residual-solve failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When failures overlap, correct accuracy, scaling, and step control before structural rank or path parameterization, recomputing diagnostics after every intervention.
assumptions_latex: Each diagnostic component is defined by a reproducible numerical test.
Only verified active components are eligible for correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At each recovery stage, correct the highest-priority active component of \(d\), then recompute \(d\) before proceeding.
review_flags: proposed priority ordering is methodological rather than universal

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lexicographic order is a proposed methodology rather than an established mathematical principle. Different problems can require rank or path treatment before scaling or globalization, and the binary diagnostics have no specified numerical tests. An authoritative source supporting this exact cross-regime priority, or an explicitly scoped algorithmic context, is required.
